#3578. Judge Leaving Book Club Struck 2 Pedestrians, Arrested 1 Day After Reelection

An Iowa judge found herself on the wrong side of the law after she allegedly drove into two pedestrians while looking at her cellphone, killing one of the victims.

Lynn Poschner was arrested on November 4 and charged with homicide by vehicle and serious injury by vehicle in connection with the fatal crash that took place in September. She was taken into custody one day after voters approved retaining her for a six-year term on November 3.

In a search warrant application filed by the Urbandale Police Department, Poschner, 45, was accused of making “statements that she had reached down to push something on her cellular phone.”

Police said that she allegedly claimed her “audiobook on her phone had stopped working through her vehicle speakers,” according to the warrant reviewed by Law & Crime.

“Poschner was not 100 percent confident if she was on her phone, talking or texting, at the time of the collision but did admit to looking at her phone,” the search warrant application stated. “Poschner was confident she was trying to switch something on her phone as the audiobook stopped playing through her speakers.”

The crash took place on September 25 around 9:17 p.m. in Urbandale. Poschner called 911 and officers reported to the scene.

“Dispatch stated that there was a female on the line screaming and two people are laying on the ground after running in front of her vehicle,” police said.

When the officers arrived, a man was found conscious and a woman was unconscious but breathing. The woman was identified as Jasmira Kadic, and she later succumbed to her injuries more than one month after the crash on October 28.

Poschner allegedly told police that she didn’t see the pedestrian when she was driving and that the crash took place when she was leaving a “book club with friends.”

She claimed that she “heard a bump” at the time of the collision and “thought it was either a deer or a dog.”

Poschner worked as a district associate judge in Judicial District 5C at the time of the crash, according to the Iowa Judicial Branch website. She attended Drake Law School and earned her degree in 2007 before she was appointed to the bench in May 2018. Prior to working for Judicial District 5C, she previously worked at a private practice.

Poschner has since been released on bond. It’s not currently clear if she has entered a plea or retained legal counsel following her arrest.

The Urbandale Police Department did not immediately respond to Us’ request for comment regarding updates in the case. The investigation into the matter remains ongoing.

#3577. You Can Preorder XReal's First Wired XR Glasses

The VR headset may be becoming a thing of the past. At Google's Android Developer Summit this morning, XReal officially debuted XReal Aura XR glasses, smart glasses with full XR capability. They're powered by Android XR and run on a Snapdragon Reality Elite-powered puck, with Xreal's X1S Chip in the glasses themselves. The result: Aura packs a 70° field of view in a pair of glasses that weigh less than 95 grams.

Customers in the United States, Canada, Japan, and South Korea can order XReal Aura on XReal's site starting today, and they're expected to begin shipping in mid-November. The limited-time launch price is $1,099 for the 12GB + 256GB configuration and $1,299 for the 16GB + 512GB configuration, $180 and $200 less, respectively, than XReal announced earlier this month. The lower prices will be available until the end of the year.

If the claim of mixed reality in a pair of sunglasses seems dubious, I tried them out a few months ago, and they are exactly that.

Instead of an enclosed headset, XReal Aura projects digital content on transparent lenses so you can be present in the real world while also in the digital world. Unlike "traditional" virtual reality headsets, the Aura's batteries and main compute are in a wired puck/controller you can slip into your pocket. That keeps the weight down and makes them comfortable enough to wear for longer periods. Because it's built on Android XR, users will have access to millions of 2D and 3D Android apps right out of the box.

If you want to go beyond Android, you can plug a USB-C-compatible computer or gaming console into Aura, and use that device in the same virtual space as native Android XR apps.

XReal Aura is launching with a library of over 150 "made for XR" apps as well, including games like Nevatars, designed by Andy Serkis, Fallout: Factions, a dice-based head-to-head game in the Fallout universe, and Landing Party, "the world's first outdoor roleplaying video game." There will also be companion apps for the NBA, NASCAR, and the San Francisco Ballet Company’s The Nutcracker. In terms of productivity, ShapexXR, a platform for software developer collaboration, is making its debut on Android XR, and you'll be able to use apps like Frontline.io for job training and assistance, and Plynk Spatial for stock research and trading.

If you want to get down to the nitty-gritty, here are the Aura's specs:

Split-compute architecture with compact compute puck

Wired Mirroring for laptops and compatible handheld gaming devices

USB-C connectivity using a standard connection

Electrochromic dimming for more immersive viewing

Support for voice, hand, keyboard, trackpad, and game controller input

Back pain doesn't always originate from your back. For example, tight or weak hips, core muscles, or glutes can cause lower back pain or stiffness, and your back muscles may under- or overfire if you don't focus on proper posture.

That's why exercises that strengthen the muscles around your spine and pelvis, like your core, hips and back, are crucial — it's not just about stretching. There's a specific two-step exercise tucked neatly away that I like to bring out for this exact moment.

It's technically two moves — one for your posterior chain (your back, glutes and hamstrings) and one for your deep core; together, they can strengthen your postural muscles and reduce pain and stiffness.

It gets met with a groan every time I introduce it to my clients' sessions, but if you suffer from a tight lower body or symptoms of sciatica, this could help.

If you struggle with the intensity, reduce the time spent in each position by 10 seconds and try again. Focus on squeezing through your core as you face upward (known as the hollow hold exercise), then squeeze your back and glutes when you are in the prone position (face down, known as the Superman exercise).

You can softly bend your knees if you need to, but otherwise, try to keep your legs straight and toes pointed in both positions. Once you feel comfortable, try adding a gentle rocking motion, a bit like a rocking horse, to the hollow hold.

It's crucial to breathe during exercise, which might sound obvious, but a surprising number of us hold our breath when the body is under stress or strain.

It's crucial to breathe during exercise, which might sound obvious, but a surprising number of us hold our breath when the body is under stress or strain. During workouts, breathing helps regulate blood pressure; did you know your diaphragm also counts as a core muscle? Expansive breathing helps keep your core engaged and posture in check, while diaphragmatic breathing in general is known to help reduce stress.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Focus on generating most of the movement in your Superman position from your mid to upper back rather than excessively arching your lower back, creating a soft banana shape with your body. Switching on your glutes will also help protect your spine as you lift your legs into the air.

It can feel mentally and physically challenging, but done regularly, the two exercises combined can counteract weak postural muscles, which are a negative result of sedentary lifestyles.

Take long, deep breaths and use your exhale to deepen the pose and lift higher.

#3574. Your Discord Messages Will Soon Be Discoverable on Google Search, but You Can Opt Out

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you are a member of a large public Discord, your posts may soon be visible in Google Search—even to those without a Discord account. Starting in November, Discord's Discoverable Servers will have server web pages that show up in web search results, including summaries and messages from public channels. While messages won't be tied to your username or avatar, you may still want to opt out.

This change applies to Discoverable Servers on Discord, which are public spaces that have at least 1,000 members. There's no invite link, so anyone can find and join them as long as they have a Discord account. (Other servers on Discord are either invite-only Community Servers for larger groups or Friend Servers, which are small, private spaces.)

On Nov. 16, Discord is launching server web pages for Discoverable Servers, which will display discussion summaries from public channels as well as some individual messages. By mid-December, these pages may appear in search results. While these servers have always been fairly easy to access since they are public, this removes the requirement to sign up for Discord and join servers in order to view them.

In its announcement detailing the change, Discord notes that private servers and DMs will remain private. Plus, server admins can choose which channels are included in web search or opt them out entirely.

Messages you send before mid-December won't be included in search regardless of your setting preferences. However, if you leave this enabled and decide to turn it off later, anything you send between mid-December and disabling the setting will stay up unless you delete the message from Discord entirely.

Emily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City.

#3573. Exclusive: ‘Breaking Bad’ Star RJ Mitte, in His Own Words

For those of us who managed to land a role on Breaking Bad, the show is a formative part of our lives. It represented a chance to work on what is now considered one of the best shows TV has ever seen, and the cast and crew forged an unbreakable bond. RJ Mitte was part of the show’s heartbeat. When I spoke to him for this book, we reflected on our days shooting in New Mexico fondly.

I’ll always remember him as a young kid—bright, talented, and a real sweetheart—who was so thrilled to be on set with us that it reminded us how lucky we all were. We'll all miss him dearly. Rest in peace, RJ. —Dean Norris

The last person to join the White family was RJ Mitte, cast in the role of Walt Jr., aka “Flynn.” RJ, who was only fourteen years old at the time, joined the project after we had already begun filming the pilot, following multiple rounds of auditions stretching out over several months. You might wonder why casting Walt Jr., a comparatively minor character among the core cast, took so long. Well, it was about verisimilitude. As written, Walt Jr. had cerebral palsy, albeit a relatively minor case. It was a fundamental part of the character, and Vince was adamant that the role not be played by a nondisabled actor.

VINCE GILLIGAN, creator: I was worried at the beginning that people wouldn’t connect with Walt. They’d say, Why is this guy doing this terrible thing? And so I kind of loaded him up for bear in terms of, you know, he had a son with cerebral palsy. You felt bad for him. People bullied him.

SHARON BIALY, casting director: We had a lot of autonomy with casting, once we knew what Vince was looking for, once we all agreed that, aesthetically, we were talking about the same type of actor. A case in point is RJ Mitte’s role. Vince only wanted actors who had CP. So, we conducted a nationwide search.

RJ MITTE, Walt Jr.: Walt Jr. is actually based on a real person, a friend of Vince’s from college who had cerebral palsy. So, Vince was really particular about the role of Walt Jr. and who was going to play him.

Experienced actors who also have mild CP is not the deepest pool, of course, but there are more candidates than you might expect. And RJ Mitte’s casting has to be considered something of a surprise, given his relative lack of experience and a variety of other challenges he faced while growing up.

RJ MITTE: We were living in Houston when my sister got discovered at a water park, and that’s what brought us to LA. My sister got booked on a job at Universal Studios for an ad campaign. She was one and a half at the time. We really didn’t have a lot going on. Things were tough. My mom was a single mom, and she had recently been partially paralyzed in a car accident, and my grandparents, who I was very close to, were both sick and dying, so when we got this offer to go to LA, we took it. It was a paid trip. They put us up in a motel in Hollywood—there was a strip club on one side, and a Ralphs and a library on the other side. That’s LA.

Everything was covered for six months, so I just started acting to meet kids my own age and have a little extra cash while we were there. And it ended up turning into a career for me. I started working at a young age, not in the acting industry, but with my uncle and family jobs and stuff to make money as a young kid. I would like to think I grew up with a strong work ethic. So, when we got to LA, I hit the ground running. Within the first six months, I was on shows like Hannah Montana, Everybody Hates Chris, Weeds, Seventh Heaven, Drillbit Taylor, Epic Movie—­ all as an extra. I think that really helped prepare me for Breaking Bad, just with the quality of work and the type of professionalism that the set had. I’m very grateful, because if I did not get Breaking Bad, I wouldn’t have an acting career.

At any number of points along the journey, RJ’s dream could have died. It’s hard enough for a known actor to land a role in a show of this quality, but for a newcomer, it must have been daunting, although you never would have known it by the way he carried himself on set.

RJ MITTE: Funny story: My very first audition ever in my career was an anti­ meth campaign for the state of California. It was a wild PSA, and I ended up not getting it. A year or so later, I started auditioning for Breaking Bad. The description of the role literally said, “dark hair, big eyebrows, and mild cerebral palsy.” And I was like, that’s me!

Sharon Bialy called me in, and I already had been on quite a few auditions by that point, and I didn’t book any of them, so I knew what rejection felt like. I had a sense of, Don’t hold your breath. But I’m a firm believer that you go in owning it and when you walk out, don’t look back. Every callback was a little more like, Wait, I’m actually still in the running.

Walt Jr. had a somewhat more severe case of CP than RJ, who did not use assistive devices for mobility in real life.

RJ MITTE: When I went in for my first audition, Sharon was there, and she had hurt her foot. So, she actually handed me her crutches that she was using for the audition. Six months went by, four callbacks, four auditions, and in that final one, they’re like, Okay, we’re sending you. You’re going to New Mexico. The next day I was on a 6 a.m. flight to audition for Vince and the team. Then he excused me for a moment and brought me back in to do my test screening with Anna and Bryan.

Think about that. RJ was fourteen years old and trying to land a job that would change his life, a job that would help him support his entire family. Talk about pressure.

RJ MITTE: I think in life I’ve always had pressure. It really didn’t stand out to me too much. I can only do what I can do. And so as long as I’m doing my best, that’s what matters. But it always kind of felt like I was part of the team to some degree, even when I wasn’t. And so when it came to doing the scene with Anna and Bryan, it really felt like a family. It was like, Oh, yeah, this feels right. Apparently, they must have had the same feeling because they hired me.

Like everyone else, RJ made the most of his opportunity and crafted a fully formed portrait of an adolescent at the center of a family storm; one whose disability may have helped shape him but did not define who he was.

RJ MITTE: This was the first time I think people really saw a character with a disability who wasn’t disabled. There’s nothing he couldn’t do that other kids were doing. It wasn’t about the disability, and that’s something that I think Vince really stressed: it’s not about his disability; it’s about being a part of the family and living with it.

Five seasons in, Breaking Bad reached its apotheosis with the monumental episode “Ozymandias,” in which Walter White’s house of cards comes crashing down. It’s also the episode where Flynn learns the truth about his father’s double life, and that Walt has led my character—his brother-in-law, Hank—to his death. The episode builds to a climactic moment where Flynn’s mother, Skyler, grabs a knife and brandishes it at her husband.

RIAN JOHNSON, director, “Ozymandias”: The actual fight itself, I remember being surprisingly fun to shoot—­just making sure to give Anna and Bryan the space that they needed to find it. I think RJ also did a terrific job in that moment—­ he’s kind of the linchpin of the whole thing.

It is indeed Flynn who rises to the occasion. When Walt wrestles the knife away from Skyler, his son jumps on top of him and throws him across the room. He’s a big kid, strong enough to handle Walt despite his disability; strong enough to protect his mother.

RJ MITTE: It was very intense to shoot. At the same time, we’re professionals. Everything was very choreographed. There was one moment when we first started, I got so heated, and so into it, that I kind of accidentally grabbed Bryan the wrong way and kind of like tossed him . . . wrong. And everyone was like, “Whoa, RJ! You can’t throw him like that.” And I was like, “Oh, I’m so sorry. I just got caught up in the moment.”

RIAN JOHNSON: When you see Walt Jr. turn, then you know it’s truly over. And Bryan’s reaction to that just breaks my heart every time I see it.

In the series’s penultimate episode, Walt clandestinely calls Flynn at school. A package is on its way, he says, to be delivered to the home of one of Flynn’s friends. The package contains money, one hundred thousand dollars—­the most he could stuff into one box. “I wanted to give you so much more, but this is all I could do,” Walt explains, leaning into the pay phone as Flynn listens, wordlessly, on the other end.

RJ MITTE: I remember at the time we were shooting that scene it was in this school-slash-doctor’s-office that we were using. Bryan was in the room with me when we did this part. It definitely was heartbreaking to have to feel that way about someone that I admire. And I think that’s what Junior felt as well. I’m a believer that in life, there’s always a moment where you have to choose to either be an adult or to stay a child. This moment comes in many different forms, but it comes down to that moment where you say, Am I going to accept this and give them what they want and be submissive, and still have that child aspect of who I am? Or am I going to take charge and become the person that I need to be—­ the man, the adult?

RJ does some terrific wordless acting in this scene, wrestling with this decision. Then he speaks: “Just shut up! Just stop it. Stop it. I don’t want anything from you.”

“You need this money,” Walt says. “Your mother needs this money. It can’t all be for nothing.”

Yes, it can, as Flynn makes abundantly clear.

RJ MITTE: A lot of the decisions I made for Junior were based on my own experiences as a young adult. At the time I was still a child, but I utilized those moments from my own life of having to stand my ground and make that decision—­ realizing who I am and what I need to do to take care and provide for my family. In the show, Walt was no longer doing that. He was actually creating more danger for his family.

I think it’s very powerful that Walt Jr. had the ability to stand his ground, and to put those boundaries in place: “You’re out. This is my family now, and you’re not a part of it.” I find a lot of young men and women have to take that stance at some point, especially with parents or family figures that live in a volatile world, a world that is corrupt.

Later, in the series finale, Walt is standing over a crib, caressing the hair of baby Holly as she naps. He leaves and then watches from a distance as Flynn gets off a school bus and walks into the apartment.

VINCE GILLIGAN: With Walt, you want him to have a goodbye scene with his wife. We were sad we couldn’t have a goodbye scene with his son, Walt Jr., because RJ is a wonderful actor. We just didn’t have the room.

For those of us who were fortunate enough to be a part of it, Breaking Bad remains a seminal event in our lives, both personally and professionally—­ an opportunity to work on one of the greatest television shows in history, alongside people who became lifelong friends.

BRYAN CRANSTON: I knew when it ended that this was the role of my life.

AARON PAUL: I think I can speak for everyone involved in the show: It changed all of our lives.

RJ MITTE: I will be eighty years old in a nursing home and there will probably be someone looking at me through a window, saying, “There’s Walt Jr.” And I’m okay with that.

Excerpted from the book DO WHAT YOU’RE GONNA DO: The Definitive Oral History of Breaking Bad by Dean Norris with Joe Layden. Copyright © 2026 by Dean Norris. From William Morrow, an imprint of HarperCollins Publishers. Reprinted by permission.

#3572. Jockey Izzy Neale Dead at 22 After Tragic Fall, Family Reveals Final Moments

Australian jockey Izzy Neale has died after a tragic fall during a race on Saturday, November 7. She was 22.

Neale was unconscious when she was airlifted to a hospital in critical condition after falling from her horse, Marnoo, during the Warren Shire Cotton Cup in Warren, Australia. Marnoo was euthanized at the track after suffering a severe injury to its leg.

The jockey’s family announced she Neale had died as a result of the fall in a statement released on Tuesday, November 10.

“It is with deep sadness and broken hearts that we announce the passing of our beloved Izzy, surrounded by her closest friends and family,” the statement read. “Izzy rode horses before she could walk. Her love of horses was a lifelong passion that, more recently, had grown into a love of racing.”

The family added, “We are deeply grateful for the love, kindness and support shown to Izzy and our family by her friends, the racing community and everyone who has been by our side during this heartbreaking time.”

The statement revealed that Neale had chosen to be an organ donor, saying she will posthumously “give others the chance of life, bringing some comfort to our family amid this devastating loss.”

Jockey Diego Montes de Oca was also thrown from his horse during the incident, suffering a leg injury and taken to a local hospital.

“Diego sustained soft tissue injuries to his left foot, with no fractures identified, and has subsequently been discharged,” Racing NSW announced on Sunday, November 8.

Horse trainer John P. Thompson, who worked with Neale, called her “an absolute beacon of shining light.”

“Always Happy, Always Smiling, Loved by everyone who met Her,” Thompson shared via X on Tuesday. “The World is poorer for the loss of a Beautiful young Lady. Heartbreaking. 💔”

The late jockey’s brother, Tommy, wrote a gut-wrenching post about his sister on social media after her death.

“Didn’t expect to be having meetings with doctors about pulling your life support,” Tommy shared via Facebook. “Just know I love you so f***ing much an you’ll always be my lil baby sister, you were my best friend an we always was so close so I dunno how I’m gonna deal with this.”

He added, “I can’t even comprehend how I feel till we meet again sis  gonna miss you so much!!”

It's an exciting time in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Fresh off VisionQuest's run for those with a Disney+ subscription, folks are looking forward to the upcoming Marvel movie release of Avengers: Doomsday. Folks are excited to see entire teams of heroes make up the Doomsday cast, although Kevin Feige confirmed more surprise characters are coming. In a recent interview Anthony Mackie might have spoiled one of those secret appearances.

What we know about Avengers: Doomsday is limited, so there are countless fans and theories about what The Russo Brothers might have up their sleeve. In a clip from ET's Twitter, Mackie spoke about the experience of shooting the mysterious blockbuster offering:

These movies, they're like summer camp. You know, everybody comes together. And it's 'Oh how have you been? Oh, you have a kid now. Oh you're married now.' It's one of those things where you catch up with everybody. I got to hang out with Paul Bettany, who I love.

You hung out with WHO?! Hardcore Marvel fans will know that there's been no official confirmation of Paul Bettany appearing in Avengers: Doomsday. So if Mackie didn't misspeak here, this is huge news that Vision could seemingly appear in the highly anticipated crossover event. Coming straight off VisionQuest, this is a thrilling concept that's sure to quickly go viral.

Only time will tell if the studio responds to these comments, or if we'll have to wait until December to see if Bettany actually appears in the next Avengers flick. So it would be thrilling to see him join the battle against Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom.

Tom Holland is known for accidentally revealing Marvel spoilers, but he might have some competition if Paul Bettany ends up showing up in Doomsday. If Mackie did spill the beans, he'd be in good company, as Mark Ruffalo went so far as to accidentally spoil Infinity War's twist ending.

Marvel is known for its tight security, and the contents of The Russo Brothers' movie is being especially kept under wraps. Although as we get closer to its December release, more information is sure to start trickling out. Only time will tell how many surprise characters end up appearing that weren't in the cast list. I mean just look at Chris Evans' Steve Rogers, who got his own trailer after it leaked online.

Our answers will come when Avengers: Doomsday hits theaters on December 18th as part of the 2026 movie release list. If Mackie's comments are to be believed, we should expect to see Paul Bettany appear. But considering how many characters he's portrayed in the shared universe, there's no guarantee he'll actually be Vision. My head is truly spinning from all the possibilities.

#3570. If You Loved 'East of Eden,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

One of the best things about truly great stories is how they can be endlessly adapted and reinterpreted. John Steinbeck published “East of Eden” in 1952, and each time it’s adapted to a screen, it looks a little different. Netflix’s try at this huge, complex story offers up some searing performances, especially from Florence Pugh as the notorious Cathy Ames. Ames is one of the best characters ever crafted in American literature, but her sociopathic nature has sometimes made her into a simple villain—but the series, and Pugh's performances, adds depth to the charcter. If the limited series has you wanting more complex female characters from classic novels, your next move is obvious: Vanity Fair, starring Reese Witherspoon as Becky Sharp.

First published in the mid-19th century, “Vanity Fair” by William Makepeace Thackeray is an enduring classic of American literature, satirizing the artificial manners and pretensions of Victorian society. At the center of the story is Becky Sharp, whose moral ambiguity and self-serving actions were surprising and unexpected at the time—and have made her a kind of antihero in the modern age. Sharp is a complicated character who, like Cathy Ames, can easily be flattened into a villain, a social climber who uses people.

The 2004 adaptation leans into the more modern take on Sharp’s character, giving her more justification for her actions and humanizing her more than the novel. Sharp is orphaned at a young age, but is almost feral in her determination to secure a position in society—which, at the time, meant securing an advantageous marriage. The story doesn’t have the same sweep as East of Eden, chronicling a relatively short period of time—but that period is the Napoleonic Wars, so there’s a lot going on. This gives the film a similarly epic feel even as it focuses on Sharp’s constant scheming and endless flirtations with people who she thinks can help her out.

In many ways, Sharp is simply playing by the rules imposed on her by men, and if that was scandalous in 1848, it’s almost heroic by today’s standards, and Reese Witherspoon imbues her Sharp with a bit of grace to reflect that. But she’s still someone who does what she must to survive and thrive, and that prickly edge will appeal to fans of Pugh in East of Eden. Rent Vanity Fair on Prime Video.

Need more historical epics with fascinating, complex characters? Luckily, the movies tend to specialize in that—here are a few more movies that fans of East of Eden will love.

If you thought the best thing about East of Eden was Florence Pugh, you’re going to love Lady Macbeth. Pugh plays Katherine, a young woman pushed into an arranged marriage with wealthy landowner Alexander Lester (Paul Hilton) in England in 1865. The marriage is solely intended to produce an heir, and Katherine is initially imprisoned in the house. When Alexander and his father leave Katherine alone for some time, she walks the estate and begins a brazen affair with a worker, setting off a chain of violent events that gets bleaker with each scene. Pugh’s portrayal of another dark, determined woman is mesmerizing. Stream Lady Macbeth on Kanopy or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you want more sprawling family drama in a historical setting, look no further than Legends of the Fall. Set in the early 20th century, it follows Colonel William Ludlow (Anthony Hopkins) and his sons Tristan (Brad Pitt), Alfred (Aidan Quinn), and Samuel (Henry Thomas) as they navigate life choices and deal with the emotional wounds they inflict on each other. From World War I to Prohibition, the Ludlows fall in love (sometimes with each other’s wives), suffer crushing loss, and remain connected to their ranch and the natural beauty of Montana through it all. Anchored by a star turn by Brad Pitt, this movie will scratch the itch left behind by East of Eden. Rent Legends of the Fall on Prime Video.

If you want to see a different take on the novel, check out the 1955 adaptation directed by Elia Kazan (grandfather of Zoe Kazan, who co-wrote and directed the 2026 series). Starring James Dean (who would die a few months after its release), it’s an old-school Hollywood epic that only covers the final third of the book. That makes it a very different narrative experience from the series, which has more room to explore the novel’s complexities—but the film looks amazing, Dean’s performance is terrific, and Kazan directs the heck out of it. Rent East of Eden on Prime Video.

Another choice for epic family drama, Giant was James Dean’s last film, and offers family drama in heaps. Like East of Eden, it follows a family over the course of decades as patriarch Jordan “Bick” Benedict, Jr. (Rock Hudson) tries to maintain his family’s ranching legacy in the face of changing times and a flood of oil money, while his former ranch hand Jett Rink (Dean) pines for Bick’s wife, Leslie (Elizabeth Taylor), and strikes it rich with oil. As money’s corrosive effect takes its toll on Jett, the Benedict family grows and changes, with plenty of drama to spare along the way. Rent Giant on Prime Video.

If East of Eden makes you curious about other adaptations of Steinbeck’s work, your next stop should be John Ford’s 1940 version of The Grapes of Wrath. Set during the Great Depression, it follows Tom Joad (Henry Fonda) after his release from prison for manslaughter. He finds his family has been forced off their land, and joins them in a desperate migration to California in hopes of finding work and security. Along the way, Joad kills again and undergoes what can only be described as radicalization, dedicating his life to organizing labor and fighting back against the predations of capitalist society. It’s a remarkable film pulsing with emotional heft and deep family drama, and if its story and setting are very different from East of Eden, the impact will be similar. Stream The Grapes of Wrath on Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

It sounds dumb, but it's surprisingly effective

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you're clued into social media, or terminally online like I am, you may have noticed posts of people realizing that photos shot on iPhone look different if they stick their hand in the frame. Instead of the drab, washed out browns and greens, you end up with a photo with warmer and more vivid colors than before. The only trade-off is that you need to have your hand in frame to get the effect.

Obviously, I was curious about whether this was actually true, and how much of an impact sticking your hand in shot actually makes to the final photo. As it turns out, yes, I could mimic the same effect by putting my own hand between the camera and the foliage.

And there's a very good reason for it, and that reason means iPhone 18 Pro owners can avoid going to these same extremes.

iphone can’t handle anything colorful unless there’s a hand in the frame https://t.co/C8FVp17gkoOctober 31, 2026

The above pictures were taken on the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the final pair which were shot with the iPhone 17 Pro Max. As you can see, the coloring in all of the images is pretty washed out with a dreary gray sheen that seems pretty typical of the Old English Autumn. Unlike New England, the leaves aren't nearly as vivid here — but they certainly don't look like that.

Once my hand is in frame (with some help of my white sleeve) the coloring changes for the better. The various shades of red and yellow seem to pop a bit more, and even the greens, which are usually rather unremarkable, seem to look a lot more vibrant.

The effect is more prominent in some photos compared to others. The change is most noticeable with the blackberry bush, to the point that you wouldn't even realize that those photos were taken seconds apart.

You can actually see the change happen in real time with the above video. This screen recording was taken on the iPhone 17 Pro Max, and when my hand pops into frame you can see the color of the preview change. The overall color gets warmer, and the colors start to pop a little more than they had before.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

In other words, if you're having trouble with the color of your fall foliage not looking as nice as you thought, it's possible that sticking your hand (or something in a very light color) might help things along.

There's a very good reason why this happens, and it all comes down to the fact that most iPhones rely on automatic white balance. In fact, only the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max give users the chance to adjust white balance, a feature that is more common (and more robust) on other cameras — including non-Apple smartphones.

Auto-white balance is common enough, and is used by the camera app to compensate for the ambient light in a specific scene or location. However, utilizing it over manual controls does leave you at the mercy of computational photography algorithms. And in the case of some phones, like older iPhones, you don't have any choice in the matter.

PetaPixel speculates that the iPhone camera could be confusing warmer Fall lighting with an unwanted color cast. To compensate, the camera cools down the image temperature and dulls the natural coloring in the process.

But if you stick something white, or close enough to it, the iPhone camera app will automatically adjust the color temperature across the photo to compensate. That also means that the foliage in the background takes on a warmer hue, and the fall colors appear to be a lot more vivid than the original washed-put image.

Obviously this technique is only going to work for people with lighter skin tones. While we haven't done any testing to see what happens when someone with darker skin puts their own hand in frame, logically the effect would be totally different compared to my own pasty-white hands.

But in those cases you could experiment with using white objects to help trick the software into tweaking the color temperature.

That said, anyone with an iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max has better control over white balance by tapping the camera menu button on the bottom right of the screen, tapping white balance and then picking one of the five preset options.

#3567. Sonia Gandhi Gives an Intimate Account of Her Husband Rajiv Gandhi’s Final Days and Assassination

A week later the general elections were announced for May 1991. Rajiv was soon immersed in work on the party manifesto and meetings to decide on the Congress candidates. He was well aware of the grave danger he was exposed to from diverse terrorist groups. But it was his task to lead his forces in the electoral battle. As he said whenever the subject came up of the threat to his life, “If it comes to having to die for what one believes in, I don’t hesitate.”

As president of the Congress Party, he would have to cover thirty thousand kilometers and more than six hundred parliamentary and assembly constituencies, in every region and almost every state of the country. It was going to be the longest stretch of time we’d be apart from each other in all the years of our marriage. With him being on the move constantly, in those pre-smartphone days I’d get news from his staff and only occasionally hear directly from him.

If I was exhausted from the one campaign, he was that much more so from weeks of being on the go for almost twenty hours a day. He hadn’t been able to eat or sleep properly, as often one day’s program slipped without break into the next. Rather than cancel an engagement, he’d snatch some rest by closing his eyes briefly in between. On some days he used a small plane or helicopter to cover the distances, occasionally piloting the aircraft. On other days he drove long distances by car, addressing scores of formal and informal meetings, at times till the small hours of the day.

Everywhere he was mobbed and his schedule frequently delayed. I felt stricken to see his hands and arms badly scratched and swollen, his body bruised and aching from all the hugs and handshakes he had received from well-wishers. Stretched out with a bolster under his feet, he talked to us about his punishing tours, and how much he was looking forward to the closing of the campaign. When I asked him, “Do you think we have a good chance?” he answered tentatively, “It’s going to be a tough fight, let’s see . . .” Our daughter, Priyanka, and I were glad to tell him that we were confident of a victory for him in his constituency.

On the morning of May 20, we drove together to the polling booth to cast our vote. On the way back I told him how flustered I’d been looking for the spot where I had to place my mark. The ballot paper was a large sheet, and I was confused by the plethora of party symbols printed on it. For a moment I even thought I’d have to forgo giving him my vote. He laughed, holding my hand with that gentle touch that never failed to dispel my anxiety.

He left for another day’s tour and was scheduled to touch down at Delhi airport later, just to change from a helicopter to a plane that would take him to Orissa. I was excited to get a sudden message that he’d come home briefly at around four fifteen in the afternoon. He had a quick bath and a snack; then it was time to leave. He spoke on the phone to our son, Rahul, to wish him well for a coming test and cautioned him lovingly to be careful about his safety. He said goodbye to Priyanka, then suddenly turned to me, and said, “Why don’t you come with me?” I was tempted for a moment, then replied, “I’m still very tired, Rajiv. I’ll see you when you get back.” “All right,” he laughed. “It’s just two more days anyway.” He was scheduled to return for a break before going on to the last stage of campaigning.

This picture of us embracing in a tree was by a friend.

We gave each other a goodbye hug and he left. I watched him, as was my habit, from behind the curtain, till he disappeared from view. It’s more than thirty years since that fateful evening. I still find it searing to revisit those events. Some parts remain a blur in my mind. I thought then and afterwards, many times—why, why didn’t I go with him? My last living image of him is his smile as he looks back, waves to me, and steps into the car that will drive him to the airport.

Rajiv had completed his campaign rallies in Bhubaneshwar in Orissa, flown to Andhra Pradesh for more rallies, and then was going to Madras (renamed Chennai five years later). He was informed that the plane that was to fly him to Tamil Nadu had developed a snag, then came a second message that it was now in order. He reached Madras and immediately set off by road towards a small town then unknown to most people called Sriperumbudur. That was going to be his last engagement of the day. He’d already covered many important places in the state, but he didn’t want to disappoint the candidate, a senior Congress Party representative, Maragatham Chandrashekhar; she had pleaded with him to stop there for just a brief meeting.

He stepped out of the car to meet party workers who had lined up to welcome him. He walked down the receiving line and was asked by one of the workers to pause and listen to her daughter recite him a poem. Smiling, he cheerfully agreed. Next in line was a woman holding a garland who motioned as if to offer it to him. As he bent his head to receive it, she detonated the explosives strapped to her body. The explosion killed him and fourteen others in his vicinity, as well as the assassin, and injured another forty-three. It was May 20, 1991, and Rajiv was forty-six years old; three months later we would have celebrated his forty-seventh birthday.

My recollection of many details of that time is sketchy. I was so overwhelmed by panic and pain that for years they absented themselves from my memory. As hard as I tried, it was like attempting to read words on a blank piece of paper. Much later, some moments returned to my mind, but to this day my own memories here are mixed with what has been recounted to me by my daughter and others. Some images are etched clearly in my mind, others are blurred and disjointed. I remember that at some point during that night of horror I dragged myself through the corridor towards the porch and drew aside the curtain on the main door to look for Priyanka. I saw a cluster of staff members huddled together, sobbing, tears streaming down their faces, the children’s nanny, Ongmu, wailing loudly. I retreated; my head was spinning. I could barely feel my legs. I was about to fall. Priyanka saw me; she held me up and took me to her room, made me sit on her bed.

On May 27 Rahul, Priyanka, and I set out with relatives and friends by a special train for Allahabad. We travel through the night, an exhausting journey broken by frequent stops. At every break crowds of mourners surge forward for a glimpse of the urn containing Rajiv’s ashes. We reach his constituency, Amethi, at three thirty in the morning. People are waiting, grieving and disconsolate. They had placed their trust in him, shared their pains, hopes, and aspirations with him. They had given him their vote and wanted to see him return as their prime minister. Instead, they are paying their last tearful tribute to their leader’s ashes.

We reach Allahabad later on the morning of May 28 and are driven to Rajiv’s ancestral home. We place the urn on the platform where the ashes of his grandfather, his brother, and his mother had been placed before. In the afternoon we are taken by boat to the sacred Sangam for the immersion.

Two decades earlier, on a pearly dawn, we had set off—Rajiv, his brother Sanjay, and I—on a boat ride to the Sangam at my mother-in-law’s request. Rajiv had pointed out the different colors of the water, the mood of the two rivers, one almost resisting merging with the other. He had explained the religious belief in a third river, the invisible Saraswati flowing below the mighty Ganga and the Yamuna. Finally he had guided me through the meaning of the ritual that we were then to perform.

On this day we are taken on a boat towards the Sangam—Rahul, Priyanka, and I. Crowds on other boats encircle us, chanting Rajiv’s name. We reach a platform raised over the water. We clamber onto it with others, amidst Vedic chanting. Rahul, with the priest by his side, empties his father’s ashes into the river. Priyanka holds me tenderly as my tears blind me to the scene. A military band plays “Abide with Me,” one of Mahatma Gandhi’s favorite hymns. We are taken to the shore and then back to Swaraj Bhawan.

I find Rajiv’s travel bag—someone had brought it back. He had always packed his own bags, whether for official or personal tours—as his mother had brought him up to do things on his own. My heart racing, I open it: two khadi kurta sets, handkerchiefs, a shawl, his underclothes neatly folded. His little toilet bag, toothbrush and shaver, his hairbrush, dark glasses, and a portable radio. In an inside zippered compartment, the portable array of family photographs he always carried with him—the first picture he took of me in Cambridge, and later ones. I look at them one by one: the children at different stages of their growing up, his mother and brother. A separate bag has the clothes he had changed out of. I bend over it, seeking to inhale the elusive scent of my beloved, gone forever.

Rahul and Priyanka supporting me at Rajiv’s funeral in 1991

Many of Rajiv’s friends had also come to attend his funeral. I met them briefly with the children. We were touched that some of them had come all the way from distant countries to bid him their last farewell. They were friends from his time in Cambridge as well as from his school days and his years as a pilot. It was a testament to the bond that had kept them close through the years.

My maternal uncles, my mother, and my sister Nadia had come, too, and both my sisters’ estranged husbands. Mother and Nadia stayed back after the funeral to comfort and support us. From the time they first met Rajiv, they had loved him and looked to him as the special human being he was—caring, joyful, always ready to cheer up and help others, his beautiful eyes and smile a reflection of his inner being.

At times over the next few weeks I could feel a certain restlessness in Nadia. A few days before her departure, while sitting in the drawing room in the afternoon, the two of us alone, she began to talk about our young days when I was still at home before I went to Cambridge—how she always looked up to me and admired me, even though she’d tell tales to our mother on her older sisters, of our games, of my helping her with her homework, of Rajiv when she first saw him.

Suddenly she became very serious and, looking straight into my eyes, she exclaimed, “Sonia, they killed your mother-in-law, now they have killed your husband. What are you still doing here? What are you waiting for? For your children’s turn, and yours? India has brought you so much sorrow. Come home, Sonia, we all want you to come back [to Italy].”

I was stunned by her words. For a moment I couldn’t even speak, but as I regained my composure, I replied firmly, “No, Nadia, no! You can’t understand. This is my home. It is my country, my children’s country.”

#3566. 10 Fun and Quirky iPhone Duo Apps Worth Checking Out

The launch of the iPhone Duo marks the first time that Apple has fundamentally changed the form factor of the iPhone. This is an exciting development because, among other reasons, it allows app developers to get even more creative. If you have an iPhone Duo, plan to get one, or if you're just interested in creative app interfaces, then you should take a look at these apps.

With Tiny Computers ($4), when you use the Duo half-open, it turns the bottom display into a keyboard, and the screen goes up top. The app features computers inspired by Commodore 64, Windows 95, iMac G3, Macintosh, IBM PC, Amiga 500, ThinkPad, iBook G3, Powerbook G4, and Windows XP. The attention to detail is great, but early App Store reviews mention that the app can be buggy.

I miss the tactile nature of playing music on my cassette player at home, and my old Sony Walkman clone. Deck-Man ($5) is an app that brings the Walkman's interface, complete with all the clicks and clacks, to your iPhone Duo. Each time you play an album, Deck-Man lets you "insert" the cassette in the player before it starts playing. The app links to your Apple Music account and it also supports playing local music files.

Foldissimo (free, $10 to unlock all songs) simulates the sound of airflow in an accordion as you fold and unfold your iPhone Duo. It has some songs pre-loaded, and you can pay $10 to unlock all songs. Foldissimo also supports a few other instruments (accordion organ, panpipes, and theremin), but you'll need to pay an additional $10 to unlock those.

With Flipcorder ($5), while the viewfinder and the retro interface are visible to you when you have the Duo in tablet mode, your subjects can also see the frame via the outer display. When you fold the Duo, the app saves the clip, and allows you to record up to 30 minutes of video per day, each of which is saved in a virtual "tape."

Orisuji ($5) is a puzzle game where you solve mazes by folding your iPhone Duo. It has 69 levels, and you'll be solving most of these by folding or unfolding the device to shift the position of the maze to make your characters move, unlock doors, or to find keys to get past locked doors.

Toastie ($3) is a game where you, well, make sandwiches: It has 10 recipes for you to master, with a time limit of 15 seconds per step as your in-game customers wait for you to serve them. You fold the phone to "cook" the sandwich; leave it folded for too long and you'll end up with burnt toast.

Marbles Unhinged (Free, $3/each to unlock all levels in a world) is a puzzle game where you guide a marble towards the exit in each level. When you fold your iPhone, it turns the top half of the level into a ramp, and alters the speed of the marble. You can keep the phone at different angles to change the nature of the stage, which will lead you to the solution.

ChompDuo (Free, $1 to unlock all monsters) uses the Duo's folding mechanics to make monsters "chomp" down, and you'll feel each bite via haptic vibrations. When you close the Duo, the monster's eyes stare at you from the outer display. It's a silly app that you or your kids could enjoy playing around with.

Unfold Your City (Free, $5 to unlock all cities) simulates pop-up books to guide you through the highlights of different cities. It reminds me of Robert Sabuda's beautiful pop-up books, especially when you use the app on iPhone Duo. It slowly pops up the artwork for each city as you unfold the device, and displays the cover when you close the "book."

In the Pokémon anime, the Pokédex is an encyclopedia that catalogs information about your friendly neighborhood pocket monsters. Dex Fold (Free, $3 to unlock optional features) simulates the device from the anime, which means that you can only use the app when you unfold the iPhone Duo.

#3564. Five Hacks Every Suunto Race 3S User Should Know

Suunto's new Race 3S is a lightweight, premium racing watch—but at a retail price of $599, it's a steep climb from the Race S, which is regularly on sale for $299. Still, there are certainly some major upgrades: The battery holds 46% more than the Race S's, and it's good for up to 38 hours of dual-band GPS; storage is double the Race S's, at 64GB. And as always, with the SuuntoPlus store, you can download apps and integrations so your watch can do more than just the default features. After all, the best way to justify the price is to really make use of everything the watch can do. Here are five ways to get more out of your Suunto Race 3S.

(Suunto Race 3S users should also check out these Suunto Run hacks).

There are several ways you can explore new hikes, straight from your watch or app, and all from the comfort of your home. First up, make sure you download offline maps at home. The Race 3S offers free worldwide offline maps with contour lines and place names, and you pay no subscription. Download your regions over wifi before you leave, so you aren't relying on a phone signal at the trailhead. The 64GB of storage leaves room for several regions, so grab the places you actually run, plus anywhere you're traveling. Menu paths can shift with firmware updates, so check the Suunto app if the layout has changed.

From there, build a library of points of interest. A POI is any spot worth returning to, such as a trailhead, water source, campsite, or viewpoint—and with Suunto specifically, you get a broad definition of “POI,” including spots for hunting, fishing, foraging, or wildlife watching. There are built-in POI types for noting where a deer seemed to have rubbed its antlers, where you've seen marine mammals, or where you've spotted mushrooms. And with the Race 3S, you can store up to 250 of them on the watch.

You can create them on the map in the Suunto app without even being there in person, or when you do stumble upon one, you can save your current location from the watch mid-run. You just have to plug in the POI as a Navigation Target under the options for your trail run or other activity. There's also a navigation app, accessible from the bottom of the widget list (select All Apps), and you can navigate without having an activity running. Organize them by area before a hiking trip, and you can navigate to a trailhead or a spring with a few taps, with the map showing the terrain around you.

For all the hikers out there, you can use Climb Guidance to preview the climbs. When you load a route, Climb Guidance splits it into flat, uphill, downhill, climb and descent sections, and shows remaining ascent. Use it to decide where to push and where to hold back. It doesn't set your pace for you, but it lets you pace by terrain.

Suunto’s Race line includes a storm alarm that watches for rapid pressure drops, a warning sign that weather is turning. It only helps if the barometer reading is trustworthy, so set your altitude to a known reference (a trailhead sign or a verified elevation) before you head up. To turn on storm alerts, go into Settings > System notifications > Alerts > Storm. (This is also where you can set up sunrise and sunset notifications.)

Just remember to recalibrate your barometer every time you start from a new elevation. Also under the Settings menu, you can select Alti & Baro, and then you have the option to either Set altitude or Auto adjust altitude. The auto-adjustment uses a GPS reading to make sure the altimeter is calibrated. But if you know your current altitude from a map, you can set it manually.

Training by heart rate is a great idea, but the default zones on your watch are based on broad formulas and guesses. With the SuuntoPlus app store, you can select Anaerobic Threshold and follow the instructions to find the heart rate where effort turns hard, so your zones reflect your body.

Be prepared: A threshold test is a tough workout. After a warm-up, you’ll be asked to run as fast as you can for 30 minutes. At the end, the app will tell you the heart rate that seems to correspond with your lactate threshold.

Now here’s the cool part: On your watch, go into Settings, then Training, then Intensity zones. Choose either the Default HR zones for all sports (what I’d recommend if you aren’t sure) or choose a sport under the advanced setting. Here, you can set the boundaries between your zones. The boundary at the bottom of zone 5 (and thus the top of zone 4) should be set to the number you got from the threshold test. If you’d like to tweak the other zones, Suunto has more information on how to calculate numbers for the other zone boundaries.

And for any threshold test, where precision matters most, I recommend pairing with a chest strap.

SuuntoPlus apps run on the watch and show extra data during activities, and these two are worth setting up during your training:

Cadence Coach shows live cadence and stride length so you can work on running form and, in Suunto's words, avoid injuries. Run a few easy sessions with it, find the cadence that feels smooth, and use it as a target.

Sprint automatically records your strides and sprints, using wrist acceleration. Instead of tapping laps during strides or hill sprints, just run, and review the efforts afterward.

Activate both in the Suunto app's SuuntoPlus store before starting an exercise, and watch your running economy start to improve.

My favorite time-saving shortcut is to pin the timer widget. Widgets are reachable from the watch face by swiping up or turning the crown, and you can choose which ones to show and in what order in the Suunto app. Move the timer to the top, and pin it so a crown press opens it. Then the upper button starts and stops the stopwatch, and the lower button resets it. It's ideal for intervals, cooking, and race-day warm-ups, and you never have to start a full workout for a quick timing job. The timer remembers whether you last used the stopwatch or the countdown.

Finally, I’m keeping my eye on the launch of the Race Planner feature. It's meant to build a pacing plan from your route, weather, and goal time, and then guide your pace on race day. Suunto hasn't announced a date yet, so I wouldn’t exactly buy the watch for it.

60 Minutes has entered a new era amid the 2026 TV schedule, and a person who’s been overseeing much of the work behind the scenes is CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss. In conjunction with the news magazine show’s EP, Nick Bilton, Weiss has been looking to update the program, and those efforts have been accompanied by major staff changes and backlash. Some of the criticisms have come from former staff members, including ex-EP Bill Owens, who recently shared his biggest concerns over the series he once shepherded.

Owens worked at CBS News for 37 years and, in 2019, he was named the EP of 60 Minutes after having spent 12 years overseeing its content in other roles. He ultimately resigned from his post in April 2025 amid a flurry of behind-the-scenes changes at 60. Since his departure, Owens has discussed his time with the show, and he notably shared thoughts ahead of the Season 59 premiere, which aired in September. At Semafor’s New Media & Marketing Playbook event, Owens was asked for his thoughts on his former workplace and said:

Not a lot. [Skydance owns] the company, they can do whatever they want. But the ratings are telling. There’s no doubt that linear television is in decline. But the numbers the other day were less than 6 million people. It’s like the evening news. 60 Minutes? That would have freaked me out.

Ratings for the latest season of 60 have reportedly been down compared to those of Season 58. The season premiere notched lower viewership and, despite some forward progress in subsequent weeks, more recent numbers haven’t been so strong. For instance, per data on the show’s October 25 broadcast, the episode only drew 5.6 million live viewers, which fell well below Season 58’s 9.1 million average. Despite that, when Bari Weiss addressed concerns, she stated that the show was doing “tremendously well.”

As for Owens, he’s been candid about leaving 60 Minutes, and he has attributed that move to no longer having the editorial independence he and his colleagues had long been granted. During the Semafor event, Owens also criticized the show’s interview with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and argued that better questions should’ve been asked. On a separate note, the veteran journalist also admitted that he wished his departure would’ve had a different effect on 60:

When I left, I really hoped that I was going to cause enough of a commotion that they would kind of back off. And the people, my senior team, the correspondents, they’ve tried their best. But it’s just a really difficult circumstance.

May 2026 marked the beginning of major personnel changes at 60 Minutes, as several high-profile staffers were let go, including correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega as well as former EP Tanya Simon. Days later, fellow host Scott Pelley was fired as well after he reportedly accused Weiss of “murdering” the show. Around that time, Owens defended Pelley’s comments, saying that he “stood up the way that I did a year ago and I couldn’t be prouder of him, and I know all the people at 60 Minutes couldn’t be prouder of him.”

Bill Owens has since moved on to other ventures and, beginning in March 2027, he’ll executive-produce a YouTube-based outlet known as NewPress. It’s also been rumored that Owens will spill tea about his time at 60 Minutes through a tell-all memoir, but that’s yet to materialize. At the very least, though, Owens still seems somewhat interested about what the future holds for 60.

#3561. What Happened to Saylor Hayes? Girl's Parents Arrested for Her Death

More than two months after 5-year-old Saylor Hayes was found dead in a South Carolina waterway during a family vacation, authorities have revealed her cause of death — and as the criminal investigation into her parents continues.

Saylor’s father, John Herb Hayes III, and her mother, Geordyn Nichole Hayes, were arrested in Tennessee on September 1, each charged with unlawfully placing a child at risk/wilfully abandoning a child. The kindergartner — who is both nonverbal and autistic — was discovered in the water near her family’s Pawleys Island, South Carolina, rental home on August 31, 2026, following a massive search involving hundreds of people and multiple agencies.

Here’s everything to know about the case, the cause of death ruling and the allegations against Saylor’s parents.

On November 9, 2026, the Washington County, Virginia, Sheriff’s Office shared findings from Georgetown County, South Carolina, coroners, who concluded that Saylor died from asphyxia due to drowning, with child neglect listed as a contributing factor.

The manner of death, however, remains undetermined while the criminal investigation into the circumstances surrounding Saylor’s death continues.

“This classification reflects the inability to conclusively determine whether Saylor’s death was accidental or the result of a homicidal act,” a Georgetown County Coroner’s Office spokesperson told WCBC.

Saylor’s body was found in the waters near Hagley Landing on the morning of August 31, 2026, one day after locals and law enforcement officials launched a large-scale search of the area surrounding the family’s rental property.

John and Geordyn were taken into custody in Tennessee on September 1, 2026, and each charged with unlawfully placing a child at risk/wilfully abandoning a child, the Georgetown County Sheriff’s Office announced that same day. The couple have yet to enter a plea.

“The body of the missing girl, who had been the subject of an intensive search involving hundreds of people and multiple agencies, was found yesterday morning in the waters near Hagley Landing,” police said in the statement. “Once extradition proceedings are complete, the couple will be transported back to Georgetown County.”

According to the arrest affidavit, John and Geordyn allegedly put their daughter “at an unreasonable risk of harm affecting her life and safety by failing to provide supervision and safeguards appropriate for a severely nonverbal, autistic, 5-year-old child with a known affinity to water and a history of elopement.”

Investigators determined that Saylor was not wearing her Project Lifesaver transmitter when she disappeared. The young girl typically wore the device because she had a tendency to wander off when she wasn’t supervised by an adult.

Saylor began wearing the monitoring device in 2024, but it was allegedly removed before the family left their Virginia home for the South Carolina trip. It’s not clear why the transmitter was taken off.

According to authorities, John and Geordyn further complicated search efforts by directing law enforcement to look for Saylor using the very tracking technology she wasn’t wearing.

“[They] encouraged search efforts to be directed toward the use of tracking technology, despite knowing that the child was not wearing the monitoring device,” a warrant stated. “[They] further directed search efforts away from the nearby body of water.”

In a statement issued on September 1, 2026, Georgetown County Sheriff Carter Weaver suggested that the Hayeses may have violated a “fundamental responsibility to protect children who cannot protect themselves.”

“When the evidence establishes probable cause to believe that a child has been unlawfully placed in circumstances that endanger that child’s safety, law enforcement has a responsibility to act,” Weaver said.

The sheriff emphasized that Saylor was a “vulnerable five-year-old child who depended upon the adults responsible for her care and protection.”

“She deserved to be safe. She deserved to be protected,” Weaver continued. “These arrests are based upon the evidence developed during this investigation and the applicable law. They should not be interpreted as a determination of guilt. The defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in a court of law.”

Following Saylor’s death, reports emerged that Geordyn had allegedly been charged with child abuse over a separate matter six months before her daughter’s death.

That earlier case reportedly involved accusations of child abuse/neglect, along with reckless disregard for life, stemming from an alleged incident involving a juvenile male.

Us has reached out to representatives for the Hayes family for comment.

The investigation into Saylor’s death remains active, and the manner of death — whether accidental or homicidal — has yet to be formally classified by authorities. John and Geordyn are expected to be returned to Georgetown County to face their charges once extradition proceedings are complete.

For now, the questions surrounding why Saylor’s Project Lifesaver tracker was removed before the family’s trip and why her parents allegedly misdirected searchers continue to drive the investigation forward.

#3560. The Kindle Click Is the One Accessory Readers Have Been Waiting For

The Kindle is the world's most ubiquitous e-reader, but that's not the same as being the best. Don't get me wrong: Amazon deserves a large share of the credit for bringing e-books into the mainstream, and over the years, the Kindle has consistently offered a top-tier user experience, thanks to both generally good hardware and its integration into the retailer's ecosystem (for better or worse). But the company also rarely innovates in the space, waiting until other players like Barnes & Noble and Boox have tested out new features (like temperature-adjustable lighting and color screens, respectively) before adopting them itself. It's also not shy about dictating to customers what they can and can't do with their Kindles, from removing the ability to directly download copies of their e-books to limiting support for third-party accessories.

One such accessory has been maddeningly absent from the Kindle for years, despite the device having the technology in place to support it: a Bluetooth remote control (all Kindles released since 2018 support Bluetooth for connecting wireless headphones, but only wireless headphones).

A few years ago, third-party e-reader remotes became a big thing on BookTok, prompting competitors like Kobo and Boox to release their own versions of the peripherals. But with the Kindle's Bluetooth protocol locked down, Kindle owners were mostly out of luck; their only option a third-party clip-on accessory that attaches to the side of the device and manually taps the display at the press of a remote button—far from ideal, as they can only turn pages in one direction and block a portion of the screen.But finally, Amazon has seen the light and made its own Bluetooth remote, which it has dubbed the Kindle Click. More importantly, it has opened up the Bluetooth protocol within the Kindle firmware so it can connect to the accessory in the first place—though it will only work on Kindles from 2024 or later. (It pairs well with the new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, no pun intended.)

If you've never used one before, it can be a bit confusing to consider why someone would want a remote for their Kindle—why bother fussing with an extra device when you can just tap the screen or press a button? But for certain scenarios, it really does make sense.

Most practically, a remote can allow you to turn pages in circumstances where holding the e-reader itself is less than convenient, as when you're exercising: Holding a Kindle in your hands is tough when you're on an elliptical, and the words can bounce around too much if you're trying to use a spin bike while gulping down a few chapters of Yesteryear. But if you can prop the e-reader onto the machine's handlebars or a nearby surface, you can turn pages easily without missing a step.

Then there's the coziness factor: Reading under a big blanket in winter is one of the coziest activities I can imagine, but if you have to keep your arms outside of the blanket to turn pages on your Kindle, well, that's going to have an impact on how cozy you feel. (This is a real problem!) But what if you could comfortably arrange the device within your line of sight and turn pages while keeping your hands ensconced within your weighted throw? Some readers are willing to spend multiple tens of dollars to achieve this level of coziness.

How many dollars? In the case of the Kindle Click, around 35 of them (plus tax). Though that may seem like kind of a lot for a simple little remote with two basic functions and four buttons, it's just $5 more than the admittedly much cuter Boox Tappy. Speaking of which, while the new firmware update will also allow the Kindle to support cheaper third-party alternatives, there's no guarantee they will work as well.

So how does the Kindle Click work? Pretty seamlessly: You press and hold one button on the remote to put it in pairing mode. You open up the Settings menu on your 2024 or later Kindle and tap Accessories (you may need to perform a software update, if you aren't seeing that option). You tap Kindle Click in the resulting list to pair it. Once paired, the remote seems to connect to the Kindle automatically if the two devices are nearby and both powered up, provided you keep the latter's Bluetooth functionality turned on; you don't have to manually pair them every time.

That's pretty much it: Once you've opened a book, you can now turn pages with a button press (you can map which of the big grey buttons moves pages forward or back to suit your preferences). The volume-like buttons on the side can be used to adjust the brightness of the front light. You can't use the remote to navigate around the device or open a different book, so choose your reading material carefully before you enter your cocoon.

While the Click definitely works as advertised, Amazon could have been a bit more creative with its functionality. The Boox Tappy, for example, can switch between modes so it can be used to jump backward and forward between tracks in an audiobook or scroll pages in a web browser. While the Kindle can't display websites, it definitely supports audiobooks, but you can't use the Click to jump between chapters or adjust the volume while listening to an Audible book; these both seem like no-brainers to me.And while being able to turn the brightness up or down is nice, why not let the remote control the warmth settings as well, either through enabling different modes (like the Tappy) or via a combination of button presses? I'm not an engineer, so I don't know how complicated it would be to get that to work, but Amazon employs a lot of them, and I bet they could figure it out.
