November is another good month to catch up on some highly rated movies on Paramount’s streaming service. There’s plenty to add to your watchlist this month. Better still, you don’t have to take my word for it when it comes to finding something worth streaming. I’ve rounded up five movies newly available on Paramount+ in November 2026 that have all earned at least 90% on Rotten Tomatoes. That’s an impressive seal of approval, although a high Tomatometer score doesn’t necessarily mean every movie will be to your taste.

From critically acclaimed favorites to films you might have missed the first time around, these picks offer a great starting point if you’re looking for your next movie night. So, if you’re scrolling through Paramount+ wondering what to watch, here are five highly rated additions I’d recommend checking out.

If you're looking for something whimsical, “Hugo” is well worth a watch. Directed and co-produced by Martin Scorsese, this fantasy drama is a heartfelt tribute to the early days of cinema, following a young boy whose adventures bring him into the world of pioneering filmmaker Georges Méliès. Its clockwork-filled version of 1930s Paris has a wonderful storybook quality, while Scorsese uses 3D technology to bring the magic of silent-era filmmaking to life. It’s also a rare family-friendly entry in the director’s filmography, making it a lovely choice for a movie night with all ages.

Hugo Cabret (Asa Butterfield) is a 12-year-old orphan who secretly lives within the walls of a bustling Paris railway station in the 1930s, where he keeps the clocks running following his uncle’s disappearance. Hugo spends his spare time repairing a broken mechanical automaton left behind by his late father, hoping it contains a message from him. When he’s caught stealing parts from a local toy shop owner, Georges (Ben Kingsley), Hugo loses his father’s notebook. With help from Georges’ goddaughter Isabelle (Chloë Grace Moretz), he sets out to recover it and uncover the mystery surrounding the automaton.

Rotten Tomatoes score: 93%Watch "Hugo" on Paramount+ now

“Moonage Daydream” is a feature-length documentary exploring the life and career of legendary musician David Bowie. It offers a very different take on the music documentary, taking viewers through Bowie’s life and career using his own words, music and archival recordings. Rather than relying on interviews with friends, colleagues or music historians, the film lets Bowie’s voice guide the experience, drawing on conversations and reflections recorded over five decades. The result is a visually striking, psychedelic tribute to one of music’s most influential artists.

Using previously unseen archival footage, concert performances, personal recordings and interviews, the film takes viewers through Bowie’s evolution as an artist, from his early musical beginnings to his rise as an international rock star. Featuring narration from Bowie himself, the documentary also explores his work beyond music, including acting, painting, theatre and sculpture. With a collection of 48 remastered tracks, it offers an immersive look at the man behind iconic alter egos such as Ziggy Stardust and the Thin White Duke.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Rotten Tomatoes score: 92%Watch "Moonage Daydream" on Paramount+ now

“Selma” is a powerful historical drama directed by Ava DuVernay that received an Academy Award nomination for Best Picture. Rather than attempting to cover Martin Luther King Jr.’s entire life, the film focuses on the three-month campaign for equal voting rights in Selma, Alabama. DuVernay keeps the story grounded in the people and planning behind the movement, from tense strategy meetings and organizing efforts to moments of personal struggle. It’s a gripping and deeply affecting account of a pivotal moment in American history.

Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. (David Oyelowo) leads a campaign to secure equal voting rights for African Americans in 1965. With local officials continuing to prevent residents from registering to vote, King and fellow activists travel to Selma, Alabama, to organize a series of peaceful demonstrations. However, their efforts are met with violent resistance from police and state authorities. King faces pressure from government officials, threats to his family and difficult decisions about how to move the campaign forward. The story builds towards the historic march from Selma to Montgomery, which helped bring about the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

Rotten Tomatoes score: 99%Watch "Selma" on Paramount+ now

“It’s a Wonderful Life” has become one of the most enduring Christmas movie traditions, even though it wasn’t originally made as a festive film. In fact, the only reason it became such a regular fixture on holiday television schedules was a copyright mistake in 1974. Directed and produced by Frank Capra, this fantasy drama starts with the warmth and nostalgia of small-town American life before taking a much darker turn into a noir-inspired alternate reality. That contrast makes the film all the more memorable, giving its familiar festive message a surprisingly dark edge.

George Bailey (James Stewart) is a small-town businessman who abandons his dreams of travelling the world to take over his late father’s building and loan company. Years later, a financial crisis threatens to leave George bankrupt and facing imprisonment, pushing him to breaking point on Christmas Eve. Just as he contemplates ending his life, he encounters Clarence (Henry Travers), a guardian angel who intervenes by granting George’s wish that he had never been born. Clarence then shows him how different Bedford Falls and the lives of its residents would have been without him.

Rotten Tomatoes score: 94%Watch "It's a Wonderful Life" on Paramount+ now

Comedy fans have a classic worth revisiting with “48 Hours,” now joining Paramount’s lineup. This gritty action-comedy film helped establish the buddy-cop formula that countless movies would follow in later years, while also putting Eddie Murphy on the map as a major movie star. Released in 1982, it was a huge box-office success and showed that Murphy’s comedic talent could work just as well in an R-rated action blockbuster. It’s a fun watch if you enjoy old-school action with plenty of sharp humor.

San Francisco police inspector Jack Cates (Nick Nolte) is hunting two dangerous criminals after they escape from prison and kill two of his fellow officers. Desperate for a lead, Jack arranges a 48-hour release for Reggie Hammond (Eddie Murphy), a fast-talking convict who previously worked with one of the fugitives. With Reggie’s inside knowledge potentially holding the key to finding the men, the unlikely pair hit the streets of San Francisco. However, with Reggie due back behind bars in just two days, they must track down the killers before their time runs out.

Rotten Tomatoes score: 92%Watch "48 Hours" on Paramount+ now

#3558. NCIS’ Katrina Law Details ‘Precarious Balance’ of Acting Alongside Daughter

Katrina Law is one proud mama after getting to share the NCIS screen with real-life daughter Kinley — but there were a few challenges behind the scenes.

“I definitely had my stage mom moments,” Law, who plays Jessica Knight on the CBS series, exclusively told Us ahead of Kinley’s Tuesday, November 10, appearance, admitting that when they yelled cut and “all of a sudden” her daughter was “acting like a normal 7 year old,” she found herself saying, “No, you can’t scream!”

The actress, 41, recalled thinking, “‘Oh God, like, don’t think my child is crazy.’ Forgetting that she’s already been on set and everybody knows her.” (Law shares Kinley with estranged husband Keith Andreen, whom she filed for divorce from in 2025 after 12 years of marriage.)

Law revealed, “I definitely had those moments of like, ‘OK, I want everybody to think that she’s good.’ And then moments where I’m just watching her act and tearing up and crying because I’m so insanely proud of her.”

She confessed it was “between the worry and then the proud moments” that she was “definitely the stage mom.”

Law also had her own challenges during her daughter’s cameo, since she had to keep doing her own job as a special agent trying to find out where a little girl’s (Kinley) mother had disappeared amid a murder case.

“When we were shooting, it was a precarious balance between being an actor, being a mom, and then being an acting coach for my daughter,” Law told Us, thanking director Marc Roskin for allowing her to ebb and flow in shared scenes with Kinley.

She explained, “It was good to be able to be in the scene with her, and when she would look at [the team] and just kind of be like, ‘Hey, back here,’ without having to cut and without having 20 different voices in her ear.”

Law was grateful she was able to “streamline” her daughter’s directions on set, saying overall it was “a lot of fun.”

During Tuesday’s episode of NCIS, Kinley makes her acting debut as an 8-year-old girl named Chloe who is found hiding alone in her apartment when her Marine mother goes missing.

Once Chloe is taken into custody at NCIS — after being found by Knight under a sink — the team learns that she has a surprising skill “that just might crack the case wide open,” according to the official logline.

“As the investigation unfolds, it’s a race against time that tests just how far a parent will go to protect family,” per CBS.

For Law, it was the perfect time for Kinley to join their NCIS family in an official capacity as she speaks fluent Mandarin — a skill that could come in handy on the case — and has been pushing to act with her mother for years.

“I’ve been bringing her to set for the past four years, and then one day she walks up to our writer, who was the writer of this episode, Scott Williams, he did a gorgeous job on this episode, and she says to him, ‘I want to be on the show,’” Law recalled of how the collaboration came about. “He’s like, ‘Oh, OK.’ [She said], ‘I want to help my mommy solve the case.’ He’s like, ‘Oh, great.’ And she goes, ‘And I speak Mandarin,’ and he went, ‘Oh.’”

A year and a half later, Williams asked Law if Kinley was serious and once she auditioned it was clear she was meant to be in front of the camera.

“She knocked the audition out of the park. She memorized six pages of sides in less than 20 minutes,” Law gushed. “That’s how she got her part. Basically, she pitched her own story line.”

#3557. 10 Hacks Every Fitbit Edge User Should Know

The Fitbit Edge really hits a sweet spot for anyone who wants a minimalist fitness tracker but still wants a screen to tell the time and display workout data. Here are my tips on how to get the most out of it, including hidden features and surprising ways to use the device.

It’s not very obvious from the watch or the app, but you can switch watch faces—and if you use the app on your phone, you can change color schemes and sometimes even complications.

On the watch, long-press the middle of the watch face. This brings up a carousel of the faces you’ve selected in the app. The last screen in the carousel gives you a button to bring up the watch face library on your phone. This is the quickest way to open it, but you can also go to your device settings in the app.

From here, tap All Clocks and browse the available faces. Once you’ve installed a face you like, tap Customize to choose a color scheme and select which complications appear (like your steps for the day, or the weather). Sadly, the share button doesn’t seem to work—it sends a broken link to the old Fitbit website—but it’s a nice idea.

The Fitbit Edge is built with the assumption that you’ll want the side button on the right. But if you wear other jewelry or watches with it, or if you wear it low on your wrist and find that flexing your hand pushes the button, you can change this.

Just go into your device settings in the Google Health app, tap Device preferences, and then change Tracker orientation to put the button on the left instead of the right. This turns the display upside down, so take off your watch and turn it around so you can see it properly again.

The AI-powered Health Coach is both the best and the worst thing about the Google Health app. Fortunately, you can turn it off. What’s better, Google added a feature that lets you turn off the unprompted insights while still having the AI available when you need it.

Tap your profile picture in the app, then Google Health Settings, then Coaching, and select No Coach Insights. The chatty summaries (and notifications) will stop popping up throughout the day, but you can always hit the Ask Coach button if you have a question or if you want to use AI-powered food logging or workout logging.

The workout app on the Fitbit Edge is pretty minimal and can’t be customized, but it is possible to get more information during your workouts. Swipe down from the top of your Fitbit Edge screen, and tap the icon that looks like a wifi heart. This turns on heart-rate broadcasting.

Then go into the Strava app, hit Record to start a workout, and swipe up from the bottom of the screen to see workout options. Select the Fitbit Edge as your heart rate sensor, and now your phone can track your workout using heart rate data from the Fitbit. The Strava app gives you a lap button and can show you the time for your previous laps; it also shows you a map of where you are and where you’ve been.

Fitbit devices have always been a little over-enthusiastic about counting steps compared to other wearables, and they know it. Hand and arm movements can mistakenly contribute to your step count, but there’s a way to adjust the device’s sensitivity. If you wear the device on your dominant hand (say, on your right hand if you’re right-handed), go into Device preferences on the phone app and set your Wrist preference to dominant.

If you already wear the device on your non-dominant hand, you may still want to use this hack. Wear it on your left hand (if you’re right-handed) and still change your preference to dominant. This will tell the Fitbit to slightly undercount your steps.

The Fitbit Edge can use its own built-in GPS, or it can use the GPS that is built into your phone. By default, it will switch sources automatically based on what it thinks the best option will be.

But you can change this. Go into Device preferences again, and choose GPS settings. If you always carry your phone with you, and you’d prefer to save battery on your Fitbit, tell the device to always use your phone's GPS. On the other hand, if you want the Fitbit to handle its own GPS without piggybacking on your phone all the time, tell it to use the built-in GPS instead.

If your phone is an older one, switching to the built-in GPS will probably give you more accurate distance and pace than using the default switching. If your phone is newer, choose based on which device you want to preserve battery.

At the same time as the Fitbit Edge came out, Google made it so that the app can work with multiple Fitbits. If you sometimes like to have a screen on your wrist, but sometimes you don’t, you can swap seamlessly back and forth between the Edge and the Air (and a Pixel watch, should you happen to have one of those as well). No extra steps are necessary—just set up both of them, and wear whichever you feel like at any given moment.

Small screens can mean less visibility, but there is a setting that helps. In Device preferences, select Magnification and toggle it on. Now, triple-tapping the screen (three quick taps with one finger) enlarges what you’re looking at. You can use your finger to move the image around the screen to see different parts—for example, to get a better look at the number under the step count complication on some watch faces.

In this part of the app, you can also choose whether the magnification gesture gives you a 2x or a 3x zoom. To zoom out, just triple-tap the screen again.

The charger for the Fitbit Edge (like that for the Pixel Watch) is incredibly fast. If your watch is running low on charge and you don't have time to wait for it to charge, just put it on the charger for five minutes. Google says this gives it enough juice for a full day, and that matches my experience. Just now, three minutes of charging brought the device from 31% up to 41%.

If your Fitbit Edge tends to last about a week, you'll need about 15% to get through a full day. I like to use the always-on display (AOD), so I only get about three days per charge. If you're using the five-minute trick because you're low on battery, turn off the AOD if you have it enabled, and you'll get through the rest of the day. But if you always have the AOD enabled, you may be able to get into the habit of charging your Fitbit for about five minutes every day—maybe 10 every now and then—and never have to walk away from it for an hour like you would with most wearables.

I don’t follow the workouts the AI coach gives me, but it can be nice to have a record of what I did. So I’ll take a screenshot of my workout in Hevy, or a photo of my training journal, and show it to the Coach.

You can do this from the Ask Coach button in the bottom right corner of the app. Tell it which workout it should attach the exercises to (for example, “log this for my strength training session from last night”), and it will fill in the exercises in that workout summary. You can view past workouts in the Fitness tab.

#3556. Why Princess Diana Dressed William and Harry Identically, Even Though They Didn’t Like It

Princess Diana had a keen sense of style. It was a talent the late princess (who arrived at court at a very young age and was therefore still unfamiliar with the ins and outs of high fashion) developed over the years with the help of experts in the field—and which has repeatedly earned her the title of style icon.

It comes as no surprise, then, that her keen eye for new trends and her passion for the most sought-after pieces were also reflected in the fashion choices she made for her two children, Prince William and Prince Harry, whom she loved to dress alike from a very young age, no matter the occasion.

Prince Charles and Princess Diana with their sons, William and Harry. July 1986.

Princess Diana, it must be said, was neither the first nor the last mother to choose identical outfits for her children, but it seems this habit was not merely a fashion game. According to a report by Marie Claire, the princess’s former butler, Paul Burrell, reportedly said that Diana’s choice to dress William and Harry identically was a way to reinforce the idea that, in her eyes, there was no difference between the two—even though everyone around her showed preferential treatment toward the eldest son, the future heir to the throne.

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. August 1986.

That’s why the princess waged her own battle, even choosing to dress her two sons in matching outfits, almost as if to convey a sense of unity and equality in their appearance. If these were indeed some of the reasons behind the brothers’ identical looks, it certainly wouldn’t be surprising. We know full well how Diana insisted on equal treatment for her two sons, who, for their part, apparently didn’t much care for their mother’s tendency to choose identical outfits. “The boys hated that, by the way; they didn’t want to be dressed the same,” Burrell added.

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. July 1988.

This statement has also been confirmed by Prince Harry himself. In the 2017 television documentary, Diana, Our Mother: Her Life and Legacy, which aired on the 20th anniversary of Princess Diana’s death, her two sons spoke openly about their mother. The younger son said with a smile: “I genuinely think she got satisfaction out of dressing myself and William up in the most bizarre outfits—normally matching. It was weird shorts and little shiny shoes with the old clip-on.”

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. August 1989.

Bermuda shorts and patent leather shoes with straps—all the rage in the ’80s and ’90s—were, in fact, two of the key elements of the outfits Diana put together for her boys. The lineup also included matching shirts, polos, and sweaters. “Looking back at the photos, it just makes me laugh, and I think, ‘How could you do that to us?’” Harry added with a touch of irony.

As they grew up, the two, of course, began to rebel against this tradition—particularly William, who, according to Harry’s account, at one point refused to have anything to do with being his brother’s twin. “Funnily enough, we got to the age when William would turn round and go: ‘Oh, this is ridiculous. You know, I’m the older brother. Why do I have to be dressed the same as him?’” he recalled. “Hang on a second. If you’re going to dress differently, I’m not going to be the only person dressed like this. This is just ridiculous!” Harry replied.

As with any growing boy, things gradually began to change, and the two brothers started to develop their own independent style. But one can’t help but pause to consider how every choice—even the most trivial, like picking out an outfit—was a statement of intent for the beloved princess. Always in the name of love.

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. June 1987.

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. October 1990.

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. May 1992.

#3555. British Comedian Josie Long Claims Russell Brand Bit Her Face Backstage

British comedian Josie Long is recalling a past encounter with Russell Brand that she hasn’t forgotten about.

“I actually had an experience with Russell Brand. Backstage, he would bite my face, and I would tell him I didn’t like it, and he would chase me around,” Long, 44, alleged on the Monday, November 9, episode of Novara Live. “I would giggle because I was 22 and it was overwhelming.”

She continued, “It took a lot for him to stop. It’s funny now to reckon with that and be like, ‘Oh, that was a physical assault, wasn’t it?’”

Us has reached out to Brand’s attorney for comment.

Long chose to share her alleged experience after Brand, 51, was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison following his multiple convictions for rape and sexual assault for offenses that took place between 2004 to 2009.

In her latest interview, Long looked back on her journey in the comedy world and recalled seeing and hearing inappropriate behavior directed towards women.

“Even at the smallest end of this spectrum, the culture was designed to tokenize and sexualize women,” Long alleged, “to only allow young, naive women for a short time to be a part of it and to allow a kind of blokey camaraderie that would include, happily and easily, rape jokes, jokes about brutalizing women and would exclude anything from a different perspective.”

When she reflects on her early 20s, Long said, “I can’t tell you how toxic that culture was back then.”

“I really want this to be a changing point for the industry,” she said. “Please let me say this very clearly: All other misogynists in comedy, we are coming for you, and I hope you never sleep again.”

Brand appeared in a London court on Monday and was sentenced to 10 years and six months behind bars after a jury found him guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

He previously entered a not guilty plea before he was tried on the seven sexual offense charges, all of which he denied. (Brand was found guilty on four of the seven counts.)

The Metropolitan Police told Us on Monday that Brand is under investigation for further allegations of rape, made by two unidentified women.

“The suspect has previously been interviewed under caution in connection with the allegations,” a spokesperson stated. “Files have been submitted to the Crown Prosecution Service in relation to both complainants. Detectives remain in close contact with prosecutors as enquiries continue and further investigative work is carried out. Anyone who wishes to speak to detectives or make a report can contact the investigation team by email at CSOU@met.police.uk.”

If you have experienced sexual assault, call the National Sexual Assault Telephone Hotline at 1-800-656-4673 for confidential support.

#3554. 10 Hacks Every iCloud User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you accidentally delete or overwrite a file or contact that's synced to iCloud, you can restore it from the Recovery portal on iCloud.com. This feature works across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Contacts, Mail, Photos, Notes, and Reminders, as well as Drive, Pages, Numbers, and Keynote. When you restore an old version of your data, the current version is archived so you can revert back if you change your mind. Deleted files can be recovered within 30 days.

One benefit of an iCloud+ subscription is Apple's Hide My Email, which allows you to create unique, random aliases to keep your real email address private. These addresses forward to your primary inbox, and replies appear to come from the alias rather than your personal email. There's no limit on how many Hide My Email addresses you can generate, so you can use them for newsletter sign-ups, online shopping, and any other credential you may want to deactivate if you start getting spammed. Hide My Email is compatible with Safari, Mail, Apple Pay, and some third-party apps.

Apple supports legacy contacts for Apple Accounts, meaning you can designate someone to receive access to your data—including photos, files, messages, and backups—after your death. This allows you to use iCloud as a digital vault for storing documents and other important information that can be securely passed down. (Note that legacy contacts will not receive iCloud Keychain data like passwords and passkeys, so you'll need another way to share this information if desired.) To designate a legacy contact, go to Settings > [Your Name] > Sign-In & Security > Legacy Contact and follow the prompts. That person will need the access key you generate and your death certificate to take over your accounts.

Apple's Family Sharing allows up to six users to share a single iCloud+ subscription while maintaining separate Apple Accounts. This means that each user has their own private vault for photos, documents, and backups while gaining access to premium features and a lot more storage overall. iCloud+ offers plans from 50 GB to 12 TB of storage. Family Sharing likely makes the most sense if you can fill most or all of the seats and/or already pay for or plan to use close to the limit of one of the higher-cost plans (compared to each individual paying for their own subscription).

Sorting through photos and adding them to a shared album after a vacation can feel like a huge project—but iCloud can do this work for you in real time if your friends and family have iPhones with Bluetooth enabled and are logged into their Apple Accounts. Set up an iCloud Shared Photo Library in the Photos app under Collections > [Your account] > Shared Library and add up to five participants. Then, from Shared Library, tap Sharing from Camera > Share Automatically. If you take photos when other album participants are nearby, they will be uploaded to the shared album.

If you want to text a large photo or video to someone who doesn't have an Apple Account and access to iCloud photos without compressing the file, you can create a temporary link that gives them access to view and download the file for 30 days. This also allows you to share multiple files with a single link rather than sending them individually, and you can revoke access whenever you'd like. To create an iCloud link, open an image, tap Share, and select Copy iCloud Link.

Note that as of iOS 27 and macOS 27, Apple now supports adding Windows and Android users to iCloud Shared Albums. However, temporary links are still a good solution if you don't want to share whole albums.

iCloud's backup feature will automatically back up your iPhone periodically so you can restore your data if your device is lost or stolen. This includes information that isn't regularly synced to iCloud storage, like settings and app organization. You can disable cellular backups to restrict backups to wifi only—or you can turn on low data mode, which will allow for backing up over your cellular connection except when speeds are low, or your data is capped. Low data mode could also save battery by not straining a slow connection. You can enable low data mode for cellular via Settings > Cellular > Cellular Data Options > Data Mode.

If your Apple device is backing up to iCloud, you could regularly bump up against your storage limit, especially if you aren't paying for a large amount of space. One way to mitigate this is to cut down what gets backed up, which you can do at the app level. If you have apps you don't use regularly or don't need data from, you can disable them from your iCloud backups. Go to your Apple account in the Settings app and tap iCloud > Storage > Backups > [This iPhone] to manage app backups.

If you sync tons of photos and files to iCloud along with device backups, you may find yourself hitting the storage cap. But you don't necessarily have to buy more storage space, nor are you stuck manually deleting items one by one. Instead, go to Settings > [Your Account] > iCloud > Recommended For You to find suggestions for freeing up storage space. This may include deleting inactive backups or reviewing your files or photos and videos, which are categorized by duplicates, screenshots, and videos (the content you're most likely to be able to offload). If you don't see these options under Recommended For You, go back to iCloud > Storage and select the app you want to clean up. Finally, check what's included in your device backups, and disable any apps you don't need under iCloud > Storage > Backups.

The Blade Runner saga is set to continue amid the 2026 TV schedule, thanks to an upcoming limited series. Blade Runner 2099 presents the next chapter in this science-fiction-infused tale of humans and replicants and puts new protagonists at the forefront. Given what’s come before, it’s only natural to wonder whether the show has direct connections to Ridley Scott’s original 1982 film and Denis Villeneuve’s 2017 sequel, 2049. Well, the showrunner is now shedding some light on that front.

If it weren’t already clear due to the title, 2099 picks up fifty years after the events of the critically acclaimed Blade Runner 2049. That film left quite a few plot threads on the table, including the revelation that the late Eldon Tyrell gave replicants the ability to reproduce. Heading up the new show is Silka Luisa, who is a longtime fan of the franchise. Luisa recently spoke with SFX Magazine on CinemaBlend and was asked if events from 2049 would come into play. With that, she gave a very clear answer:

No, [Blade Runner 2049] is not directly connected to the show. What was an important early mandate was that audiences could come to the show not having seen the films, and this could stand alone. This could be an introduction to the world of Blade Runner, and it wouldn’t be dependent on you having watched 2049, you having watched the first Blade Runner. In that sense, we had to divorce ourselves from the narrative.

Why Edward James Olmos Says He Owes His Battlestar Galactica Legacy To Blade Runner

Some fans may be a tad disappointed to learn that replicant reproduction won’t be expanded upon during the events of the show. Yet Luisa’s “mandate” does indeed make a lot of sense. What she and her collaborators ultimately want is a show that fits snugly into the continuity but also doesn’t require watching the movies. (Of course, both of those films are excellent and deserve to be watched regardless.) In short, the Shining Girls creator is promising a series that works on its own, and that could do away with any trepidation newcomers may have about jumping in.

Blade Runner 2099 takes viewers to a Los Angeles that’s now fully controlled by replicants, and humans must essentially live within the lower levels of society. At the center of the story is Olwen, a Replicant Blade Runner (played by Michelle Yeoh) who is only days away from dying. She is eventually partnered with Marion Jessop to take on a case. However, unbeknownst to Olwen, “Marion” is actually a human named Cora (Hunter Schafer), who is only masquerading as a Replicant to achieve her own goals.

Per what’s been shared thus far, Yeoh and Schafer forged a strong bond on set not unlike Harrison Ford and Ryan Gosling did while making 2049. However, as far as we know, Yeoh didn’t accidentally punch Schafer in the face like Ford did to Gosling. In fact, Yeoh was protective of her co-star amid production and, in a truly mom-coded move, she even bought Schafer a baby helmet.

The trailers for 2099 would suggest that such headgear was necessary, because a lot of intense moments have been teased thus far. Although fans won’t see any direct links to the Blade Runner films, Silka Luisa is aiming to dish out the action-infused thrills, heightened visuals and deep themes that have long permeated this franchise.

Check out Blade Runner 2099 when all eight episodes are released for Prime Video subscription holders on November 25. In the meantime, anyone who’s curious can stream the original movie for free on Pluto TV and check out 2049 on Prime as well.

#3552. No Reservations: Jessica Craig-Martin Serves Up a Rowdy, Inside Account of ’80s Indochine

No one is famous when they are at home. In New York in 1984, all it took to be famous was to leave the house with intent to commit fame. Beautiful youths were shot through the fame cannon at a rate that made Warhol’s fifteen minutes seem like a century. A cloud of new money hovered over the city, ominously gathering dollars, dropping sudden fortunes on those who knew how to make it rain. No veneer of philanthropy was needed to whitewash the excesses of the wealthy. Conspicuous consumption was the new normal. The new designer clothes all had giant shoulder pads. So did the buildings. The thick-walleted and soft-bellied moved around the city at night in chauffeur-driven carapaces. Eurotrash was the latest import. Fast-talking cocaine replaced nodding-out heroin. The words supermodel and art star fell from heavily glossed lips. Everyone wanted to see and be seen. But where? Studio 54 was closed, disco was dead. Brian McNally’s new restaurant, Indochine, was poised to become the epicenter of ’80s decadence.

Jessica and another waitress with Rupert E at Indochine, 1986.

Waitressing seemed like the best way to make money. I’d met Brian while traveling with the Mardens in France, and he’d mentioned he was opening a restaurant. I had left New York as a hip urban waif with short dark hair and pale skin. I returned curvy and brown-skinned, with long hair that had turned blond in the sun. I wore no makeup and had no interest in fashion, feeling I’d done all that as a teen. I wore vintage ’40s dresses from flea markets, and plastic jelly sandals. When I dropped by 420 Lafayette to ask for a job, Brian looked me up and down and gave me a sly wink. “Yeah, you’ll do.” The question of waitressing experience did not come up.

On opening day, I arrived to find the staff running around frantically with hammers and paintbrushes; stenciling palm leaves on the walls; putting up wallpaper; accepting deliveries of banana trees, ducks, orchids, MSG, and Champagne. There was no way in hell we were going to be ready. I grabbed a brush.

Indochine opened that night, walls still wet, with a private party for Julian Schnabel’s opening at the Mary Boone Gallery. Art dealer Pat Hearn sang Patsy Cline songs wearing a tight 1950s gold brocade dress. Warhol superstar, writer, and genius-about-town Taylor Mead got up on a table to give a hilarious impromptu speech. The crowd danced all night. With one private event after another, opening night lasted a month.

Brian was truly brilliant with people. He made everyone feel like they were in the right place at the right time, and that they were clever, sexy, witty, charming, or all of the above. He was just as comfortable with Henry Geldzahler as he was with Madonna. He could converse on any topic and did so with an easy British charm and lack of pretension that disarmed even the worst snobs.

Moira Hodgson gave us two stars, but other critics found the food “rather ordinary” or “unspectacular,” and everyone agreed that the service was appalling. Ironically, as Brian pointed out later, this became part of the charm of the place. Brian had a strict policy of never refusing a reservation, no matter how overbooked we were. He knew the frenzy at the bar and long waits for booked tables only increased our status as the most sought-after restaurant in town.

When Brian told me my shirt was wrinkled, I said, “Brian, chill out. This is linen. It’s supposed to be wrinkled.” In fact, the shirt could have done with a quick press, but I had only one white shirt and no intention of buying an iron or paying for dry cleaning. Fortunately the waitstaff started to add increased personal touches to the black-and-white dress code until it disappeared. Brian stopped objecting when he saw that the stylish staff was becoming one of the draws of the place. Soon most of us were unrecognizable as waitstaff, leading to many a black-suited banker being called upon for drinks or the check while navigating his way to the bathroom.

Taylor Mead became a nightly fixture at the bar, offering brilliant quips while dining on Dewar’s. Larissa slept on her barstool, her lit cigarette in an elegantly raised hand until someone said, “Larissa!” causing her to reanimate and flick her ash while shouting: “Dahhhh-ling!” She was a movie star who didn’t need movies. If Larissa came to Indochine to sleep, John F. Kennedy Jr. and Daryl Hannah came to break up and reunite, using the vestibule to break up and the bathroom for make-up sex. Carol Channing brought her own silver. Dolly Parton brought her own food. She was on a raw-vegetable and booze diet: “Just gimme the most expensive bottle in the house, honey.” Bianca Jagger ordered her meals in one low, unsmiling breath: “Steamed vegetables no soy sauce no hot sauce no sugar no salt no MSG.” What she didn’t know was that in the kitchen there were three tubs of white powder that went into every single dish: salt, sugar, and MSG.

Dead-eyed debutantes danced in their Manolo’s on tables strewn with platters of spicy beef salad, celebrating an addition to the Guinness dynasty. I wouldn't start using a camera for another eight years, but my mother says Indochine is where I became a photographer.

One night Lena Horne spat her gum directly into my hand. “Gum,” she’d said, after beckoning me over, after which I’d instinctively put my hand out. I gave it to my boyfriend Nick for his birthday. A strand of Cindy Crawford’s hair was the following year’s gift. (We never did get around to cloning her.) Saturday nights were Bridge and Tunnel. I opened the bathroom door to find a woman in high-heeled white boots giving a blowjob to some guy, his soft leather pants around his ankles. Laurie Anderson and I waited to pee while they finished. After that we referred to Saturdays as “White Boot Nights.” Warren Beatty leaned casually against a column, asking a waitress, “You’re a dancer, right? I can see the dance in your body.” A few months later, there he was, leaning against the column again. He asked the same waitress, Robin, “You’re a dancer, right?” Robert De Niro would sit at the end of the bar checking out the scene. Then he’d leave and call the restaurant from his idling limo. He’d ask the maître d’ to tell a woman he found attractive that he was on the phone. Sometimes women simply left their dates mid-meal to join him. One night the Beastie Boys brought a homeless man to dinner who’d asked them if they could spare some change. Even the odd exiled dictator made an appearance. The shah of Iran booked one table for himself and his wife, and three for his bodyguards. I noted their ankle holsters.

The waitstaff was made up of ambitious, creative young New Yorkers. Among them were Fidel Márquez, a painter; Masha Calloway, a fashion designer; and Darrell Maupin, who would open his own successful restaurant, Flamingo East. They and Robin Renzi, the dancer, became my close friends. Robin would later launch the jewelry line Me&Ro with Michelle Quan, who left Indochine for a modeling career. All I had going on outside of work were drawing classes at the New York Academy of Art a few days a week. I had not yet located any particular ambition. I went for dinner with friends, danced all night, and had sex all day. I remember being furious with Brian for a remark he made when I arrived at work: “You look like you just got fucked all day.” I was outraged, but it occurred to me later that he was absolutely right.

There was an ecstasy dealer who took to dropping by the restaurant around midnight. We’d take the pills toward the end of our shifts, hoping no customers would linger too long. After work we’d head to the clubs, needing catharsis and easily spending the money we had just spent hours earning. The Sisyphean irony of this went unnoticed. I was amused to discover that working at Indochine had a certain cachet. Waiters and waitresses were swept past the velvet ropes into all the clubs. I was initially surprised by the mini celebrity status conferred by waiting tables, but it says a lot about the era, which was all about tipping status on its head. Julian Schnabel was flipping burgers ten minutes before he became famous overnight with his broken-plate paintings. With his sensational-looking wife, Jacqueline, on his arm and New York at his feet, he seemed to be starring in his own biopic as he swept into Indochine night after night. “Jessica, get yourself a glass—have some of this Cristal,” he would say with a beneficent wave of his arm. It was the only restaurant in town where you could see Madonna, Sean Penn, Chris Walken, and Andy Warhol in one booth, John Waters and Divine in the next, and Henry Kissinger and his wife having a quiet dinner in another.

A certain high-powered lawyer was easily the restaurant’s most repugnant client, a considerable achievement. On one occasion he was approached by his waitress, Demetrious, a Black, bald, and beautiful torch singer who always wore huge brass earrings in the shape of Africa.

“Can I offer you something from the bar?” she asked him.

“Yes. I would like a different waitress,” he told her without looking up. She ignored him, went away, and returned calmly.

“I already told you, I want another fucking waitress,” he spat.

She shrugged. “I’m your waitress. I guess you’ll just have to deal with it.”

“GET THE FUCK AWAY FROM ME YOU UGLY BLACK BALD BITCH!”

She leaned in. “Sitthefuckdownandshutthefuckupyoudumbwhite-muthafucka,” she said in one breath. Beaten, he sat. I begged Brian to ban him, but Demetrious just shrugged it off. She was used to fighting her own battles and had already moved on.

At first, I was shocked by the overtly sexist behavior and banter at the restaurant. In the art world men did not compare the sex appeal of women in the presence of other women—or to their faces. There was rampant sexism and misogyny in the art world, of course, but it was generally more institutional and less visible to the naked eye. Men in the art world were less likely to openly grab one’s ass, or to make saliva-drenched comments about the run in your stockings inspiring in them an urge to bend you over a table. The art world had its share of knuckle-draggers—but the likelihood of being kneed in the balls by the objects of their desire kept them somewhat held in check. The women who raised me considered that feminism had “worked.” Their very existence was proof. No one thought the work was over—the ERA had failed to pass, after all—but the essential equality of women was beyond question, and the idea of acting coyly around men was considered absurd. However, the liberation train I’d been raised on had not reached restaurant culture. I was shocked to see so many women pushing out their tits, wiggling and giggling for their power-suited dates. Ironically, I’d been sheltered by my avant-garde upbringing.

I met Huy Chi Le on my first shift at Indochine. He was my age and had just arrived in New York from Vietnam. He spoke almost no English. Huy worked six nights a week at Indochine and seven days at another restaurant, working twice the number of hours to make the same amount of money as a waiter. When Huy was promoted at both venues to waiter, he kept both jobs, still taking just a half day off a week. He sent funds to his family and saved the rest. He established credit, obtaining an Amex gold card while we waiters were living out of tip envelopes and dancing all night. He bought a house in Brooklyn and sponsored his family to come over one by one. By the time Brian was ready to sell, Huy was poised to buy. He is now the owner of several businesses, a multimillionaire, and—with former manager Michael Callahan and former waiter Jean-Marc Houmard—co-owner of the still incredibly popular, and now legendary Indochine.

#3551. '16 and Pregnant' Alum Pleads Guilty in Man's Fatal 'Tranq' Overdose

Whitney Purvis has pleaded guilty to involuntary manslaughter and other charges more than a year after the former 16 and Pregnant star’s arrest in connection with a man’s fatal overdose.

Purvis, 34, was arrested in Georgia in July 2025 in the death of John Mark Harris, about a month after she shared the news that her 16-year-old son, Weston Jr., had died, Us previously reported.

According to Floyd County authorities, Purvis allegedly gave Harris a drug referred to as “Tranq,” containing a mixture of xylazine and fentanyl, resulting in his death, WMAZ-TV reported.

Purvis pleaded guilty on Friday, November 6, to three out of seven offenses she was facing in relation to Harris’ death, including involuntary manslaughter, illegal use of a communication facility and sale of a Schedule I or II controlled substance, specifically fentanyl, per the TV station.

She also filed a waiver of the right to withdraw her plea.

In pleading guilty to the three counts, Purvis specifically entered an Alford plea, meaning she maintains her innocence but acknowledges that the evidence against her would likely result in her conviction, Court TV reported.

According to Purvis’ arrest affidavit cited by the outlet, she allegedly gave Harris “Tranq” in February 2025.

Harris was 37 when he died at his Rome, Georgia, home, according to his online obituary.

Following his death, Purvis paid tribute to him in a message left on his obituary website, calling him a “great friend.”

“I’ll never forget you. Rest in peace and my condolences to your family and friends. I pray they are able to find some kind of comfort during this tragic time. I love you forever, John Mark. Love, Whitney,” Purvis wrote.

She was ultimately taken into custody by the Drug Enforcement Administration and Floyd County authorities in July 2025.

“Today, DEA Atlanta and local law enforcement arrested Whitney Purvis in Floyd County, GA on charges of involuntary manslaughter due to fentanyl poisoning,” Jae W. Chung, acting special agent in charge of the Drug Enforcement Administration, Atlanta Field Division, previously said in a statement.

About a month earlier, Purvis shared in a June 2025 Facebook post that her and Weston Gosa Sr.’s teen son, Weston Jr., had died.

“This is so hard to write. My beautiful son, Weston has passed away,” she wrote in the post. “He was only 16 years old. Life is so cruel and unfair. I just dont understand.”

Purvis told People that Weston had multiple medical issues, including Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and Addison’s disease, which she said led to him also having diabetes.

Following Purvis’ Alford plea, she’s facing up to 44 years in prison, per Court TV. Her sentencing hasn’t been scheduled.

Apple has finally released its very first touchscreen laptop—the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. I reviewed both the 14- and 16-inch models, and I can tell you that the tandem OLED is easily the best we’ve ever tested. That, along with a thinner and lighter design, blazing-fast M5 Pro/M5 Max performance, and epic battery life, makes it one of the best MacBooks available.

While the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is undoubtedly great, it’s proving to be one of Apple’s most divisive laptops. That’s not only based on what I’ve seen on social media, but also on what Tom’s Guide readers and followers have told us through polls and in the comments section of our TikTok videos.

To that end, I’ve scoured reactions to our MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display and selected highlights to give you a sense of what folks think.

From price and performance to features, here’s what Tom’s Guide readers and followers have to say about Apple’s new OLED MacBook Pro.

After the MacBook Pro with PROLED was announced and our initial hands-on with the laptop, we created a poll asking: Are you sold on the touchscreen MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR? with the four options you see above:

Based on a total 453 votes on our website, 144 votes went with “incredible tech, but $2,899 is way out of my budget,” followed up by 135 votes for “MacBooks don’t need a touchscreen — give me a standard M5/M6 laptop instead.”

“Touch, tandem OLED, and 2,000 nits make it worth the premium" received 131 votes, while “I want to see how third-party apps handle touch first” got 43 votes.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

I can’t say I’m surprised by these results, as the MacBook Pro OLED is now the most expensive Apple laptop, with the 14-inch model with M5 Pro starting at $2,899 and the 16-inch model with M5 Max starting at $3,399. And naturally, adding additional RAM, storage, and upgrading to a nano-texture display all significantly boost the price.

The usefulness of a laptop touchscreen is something I discussed in my review. While the touchscreen itself is extremely responsive and intuitive, it’s a feature that some laptop users (such as myself) don’t always need. You can save $900 by purchasing the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6, which starts at $1,999. Yes, that’s expensive too, but it’s still nearly $1,000 less than the starting price of the M5 Pro 14-inch PROLED.

That said, the tandem OLED touchscreen is worth it for some readers. Right now, it’s the brightest laptop display we’ve tested. It can even be much brighter than an OLED TV’s display. The screen is so vivid that others pale in comparison. If you can afford this laptop, I promise you won’t be disappointed by its mesmerizing display.

Many of the third-party apps I use daily, such as those from Google (Docs, Drive, Sheets), work perfectly, but there is still concern about how third-party apps handle touch. This is a fair concern, as developers have to optimize their apps for the touchscreen.

Given that it's still early days for the PROLED, issues could arise. This is something I plan to cover in greater detail if enough folks complain about their favorite apps not working as intended on Apple’s touchscreen laptops.

Commenters on our TikTok videos featuring the reveal of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display and our hands-on impressions are just as critical and skeptical about the MacBook Pro’s touchscreen.

User N7 Drones flatly says: “I see zero reason to have a touchscreen on my MacBook Pro!” While tk42121 says that “OLED is fine, but a touchscreen is worthless.” Another user under the handle of Reirei gives scorn and praise, saying that “Apple always late on tech but when they do it 10x better than others.”

I found the comment from Smooth Operator particularly interesting. “Why wouldn’t they do the screen flip to make it easier to touch the screen?” This is something I brought up regarding how comfortable it is to use a touchscreen laptop. A 2-in-1 convertible design would certainly make it easier for taking notes or drawing, though you’d also need Apple Pencil support—a feature the PROLED currently lacks.

While many comments on our TikTok videos weren’t the most positive, they weren’t all negative. For instance, krisnahafara said, “finally the logo [is] back.” Some other posts shared the same sentiment, though user Fernando Callo said: “Please, don't bring back the light-up logo to the rest of the lineup.” Guess they’re not a fan!

It shouldn’t be surprising that Apple’s first touchscreen laptop isn’t being universally praised.

While I think the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is the best laptop I’ve ever tested, its steep price point is hard to stomach for all but the most hardcore tech enthusiasts with deep pockets. I also think it’s fair to say that Apple is late to the touchscreen laptop party, even with the seamless integration of that technology.

This is an ongoing discussion, so let us know what you think about the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. Are you interested, or is the price keeping you away? Sound off below!

The Soundcore P31i earbuds are down to $32.99 (originally $59.99), which is as low as they’ve been, according to price trackers. At this price, most earbuds stick to the basics, so it’s unusual to see features like active noise cancellation and LDAC included here. That doesn’t mean they compete with premium pairs, but they do give you more to work with than you’d expect for under $35.

These earbuds are light, they fit well, and they don’t get uncomfortable after an hour or two, which isn’t always the case with cheaper earbuds. Battery life, too, holds up through a full day of use, with a little over seven hours on a single charge and extra top-ups from the case. The sound quality is better than expected for the price, though it leans toward bass-heavy tuning out of the box (you can tweak it in the app, but the app itself is not the most intuitive and takes some getting used to, notes this ZDNET review), and if you’re using a compatible device, LDAC support gives you the option for better audio quality.

There are also a few extras tucked in, like HearID for tuning the sound to your ears and an AI translation feature, though features like that feel more like a bonus than something you will use every day. As for its noise cancellation, it works, but expectations need to stay in check—it reduces steady background noise like engines and traffic, but it won’t match the isolation you get from more expensive earbuds. That lines up with its overall build, as well, which feels a bit basic compared to more expensive options.

#3545. Stephen Miller Into the Breach: How Susie Wiles’s Failures Portend Miller’s Future

There’s a time-honored tradition for new White House chiefs of staff: The outgoing chief invites former holders of the office, Republicans and Democrats, to a get-together (usually in the West Wing), where the newcomer is offered advice. But Donald Trump’s new chief, Stephen Miller—appointed in a jaw-dropping Truth Social post on Friday—won’t be getting a party. First, because the tradition applies only to a president’s first chief. Second, because no Democratic chief would likely want to be caught dead with Miller, a longtime basher of the opposition party. Shortly after hearing that Trump had picked the hard-right firebrand as his new chief, James Carville sent me a text that summed up the prevailing attitude: “This is like Caligula’s appointment of his horse as consul.”

It was different when Susie Wiles came to town. On the evening of November 19, 2024, she was the guest of honor at a dinner party thrown by Jeffrey Zients, Joe Biden’s outgoing White House chief of staff. They were joined by eight of Zients’s predecessors. It was an occasion for bipartisan bonhomie, a tradition started in 2008 by George W. Bush’s chief Joshua Bolten. In a spirit of goodwill and generosity, Bolten had thrown a gathering in his West Wing office for Barack Obama’s incoming chief, Rahm Emanuel. The informal meetup was intended as a way to convey the chiefs’ collective wisdom and experience—and to offer, in miniature, a nuts-and-bolts version of the transition of executive power that is a hallmark of American democracy.

Now evicted from her West Wing corner office, with the president’s agenda in tatters, Wiles has learned that fealty to Trump almost always ends badly.

On the night of the dinner for Wiles, however, a cloud hung over the occasion. Virtually no one at the table thought she could succeed as Donald Trump’s chief of staff.

For almost two years, Wiles was the second most powerful person in the West Wing. Had Trump been interested in governing, she might have helped him solidify a GOP majority in Congress for years to come. But she was unwilling, or unable, to save Trump from himself. On Wiles’s watch, he squandered his second term with a reign of revenge, retribution, and recklessness. Now evicted from her West Wing corner office, with the president’s agenda in tatters, Wiles has learned that fealty to Trump almost always ends badly.

And if past experience is any guide, Wiles’s replacement, Stephen Miller, may well crash and burn in even more spectacular fashion.

There was no one the president relied on or trusted more than Wiles. From their first meeting in 2015 at Trump Tower to her impressive stint as his winning 2024 presidential campaign co-manager, the “ice maiden” had Trump’s back. And he had hers—until last Tuesday’s epic Democratic blowout. Wiles would resign two days later. Indeed, the Republicans’ midterm apocalypse was an extinction event that not even Wiles could have survived.

Ironically, Trump’s savvy political strategist was the architect of what turned out to be a big blue bloodbath. “We’re going to win the midterms,” Wiles told me boldly when I interviewed her for Vanity Fair just a year ago. Even then, three months before Trump initiated a war on Iran, that was a ridiculously rosy prediction. The president’s approval rating was in the gutter. He’d failed to address, much less solve, voters’ primary concerns: affordability, inflation, health care, and housing—and had still not released the remaining Epstein files. How could a battle-hardened political pro like Wiles be so starry-eyed? The answer, I believe, is that in the fog of MAGA-land, she’d lost touch with the real world.

In almost every presidency, the West Wing is a bubble where like-minded acolytes engage in groupthink. But in Trump’s West Wing this phenomenon is exponentially magnified. It’s a parallel universe, one in which the 2020 election was stolen, violent insurrectionists are “patriots,” and the prosecution of political enemies—with scant evidence—is a presidential perk. (“Who would blame him?” Wiles said to me of Trump’s campaign to settle scores.) That, to my mind, is why Wiles seemed so stunned by the firestorm that erupted when her words appeared in my 10,000-word Vanity Fair series last December. She had no idea they would land like bombs on planet Earth.

Wiles invested Trump with almost otherworldly powers. He would lead the GOP to victory in the 2026 midterms, she believed, because of his preternatural ability to rally his base. That’s why, on the eve of the midterms, Wiles was all-in on sending Trump almost everywhere all at once, admonishing people to “vote like I’m on the ballot.” The trouble was voters saw all too clearly what she apparently couldn’t see: Trump was deeply unpopular; on his watch, the country was coming apart.

A year ago, when Wiles made her electoral prediction, I challenged her. “I admire your confidence about the midterms,” I said, “but the stakes are huge, right? And history is not encouraging. Incumbents do stuff and there’s a reaction. And usually, as Obama said, you get shellacked.”

Wiles seemed to shrug off that possibility. “Can you ever imagine Donald Trump saying that?” she said. “No, no.”

Wiles was right. Trump could never say such a thing—because he could never accept the fact that his electoral magic had waned. Neither, it seemed, could Wiles. But as his chief of staff and top political strategist, she was paid to know better.

Even before the election debacle, Trump had reportedly started privately inquiring about her on phone calls, although he lashed out at accounts of such purported conversations. Then, once the carnage sunk in, the die was cast. Wiles offered her resignation. And Trump accepted it.

At the start of her West Wing tenure, I believed Wiles stood a chance of succeeding. If Trump would listen to anyone, I thought, it was the loyal, organized, no-nonsense Wiles. Yet during 10 conversations with her over 10 months, I watched as she abdicated the most important duty of the White House chief: telling the president hard truths. Wiles told me she’d read my book, The Gatekeepers: How the White House Chiefs of Staff Define Every Presidency, and she understood the importance of heeding Reagan chief James Baker’s advice. “You do not serve your president well if you are just a yes man,” he said. In a phone call, she told me, Baker “reminded me that my job wasn’t to be a fangirl.” I asked Wiles, “Have you had any gut check moments where you had to tell the president something he didn’t want to hear?” She paused. “I probably have one a day,” she said. “But they’re over little things, not big.”

Wiles should have known that the midterms would spell disaster. She carried around a list of her priorities, on an index card. Number five: “Don’t forget about organized labor. Don’t forget about young Black men and women and Hispanics…because that’s the future of the country and the backbone of his support. And if we don’t convert those people to being enthusiastic Republicans, then if the Democrats were even just a little bit better, they might win an election.”

Miller is a zealot, a hard-boiled ideologue—an advocate of Trump’s notorious first-term Muslim ban, the brutal paramilitary tactics of ICE, the deployment of the National Guard to Democrat-run cities, and the lethal air strikes on boats in the Caribbean.

They might—and they did. And now Wiles is out, taking up shop, so Trump himself has said, within his political operation. Last November she hinted that she knew this day might come: “You go to bed at night, you say your prayers, you take stock of what the day was and what your day is tomorrow, and you get up and do it again…. So as long as that’s the case and the president’s pleased…” Wiles paused. “He could fire you tomorrow.”

She’s sensitive about her legacy as the first female White House chief. “I’m not an enabler,” she insisted. “I’m also, like, not a bitch. I try to be thoughtful about what I engage in, and what I disagree [with the president] about. I guess time will tell whether I’ve been effective.”

What about Wiles’s successor, Stephen Miller?

Miller is the antithesis of Ronald Reagan’s chief James Baker, a cool pragmatist who could push back on the president’s half-baked ideas. Miller, by contrast, is a zealot, a hard-boiled ideologue—an advocate of Trump’s notorious first-term Muslim ban, the brutal paramilitary tactics of ICE, the deployment of the National Guard to Democrat-run cities, and the lethal air strikes on boats in the Caribbean. He believes in a Hobbesian world, he has stated, “that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power.” Now he’ll be the last person in the room when Trump makes life-and-death decisions about law and order and war and peace.

The man who decreed that the president’s powers “are very substantial and will not be questioned” is now the official charged with questioning the president’s decisions. It’s hard to imagine Miller doing that without a personality transplant. He’s already alienated the House minority leader, and soon to be Speaker, Hakeem Jeffries, who has called Miller “a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands,” insisting, “I’ve got zero interest in working with that kind of individual.”

At the White House last November, after a Vanity Fair photo session, I spoke with Miller at length about the midterms, still a year away; about his portfolio in the Trump administration; and about the role of the White House chief of staff. Perched on a chair in the Roosevelt Room, he eyed me warily. He seemed impatient to get back to work. “I understand that your need for me is quite limited, right?” he said.

I asked Miller about his interactions with the president—specifically an Oval Office meeting in which he and Trump reportedly talked about blowing up boats in the Caribbean. “I would never talk about…whether a meeting occurred or didn’t occur,” he said, “or whether it was in a meeting that did occur, or was not in that meeting if it occurred, which I would never say either way.”

Miller was more forthcoming about Wiles’s prediction—that Trump and the GOP would triumph at the polls in 2026. “What about you?” I asked him. “I am confident that we’ll win the midterms,” he replied. History might be against them, he said, “but we have every expectation that we’re going to defy that history.” “Why?” I asked. Miller replied, “Because of the president’s unprecedentedly successful first nine months in office.”

What followed was a black-is-white, up-is-down litany of Trump’s accomplishments, a revisionist history that might have made Karoline Leavitt, another world-class propagandist, blush. “In no particular order,” Miller said, “the taming and defeating of inflation. As you know, we inherited record double-digit inflation and the president made his first priority to bring down the cost of living…cutting the price of energy by high double digits. For many Americans, gas prices have been cut in half since we took over.” None of this, of course, has proved true—but Miller was just warming up.

“And the passage of the largest package of tax cuts and reforms in American history in the form of the One Big Beautiful Bill. Fully securing the Southern border, the most secure border in history, zero illegal crossings, four months in a row. And also the largest number of deportations in American history…. The president has…achieved more in foreign policy than any president in our lifetimes, ending eight wars in eight months—which includes, but is not limited to, securing the historic peace deal between Israel and Gaza, Thailand and Cambodia, Congo and Rwanda, Azerbaijan and Armenia, Israel and Iran, and so on…”

Miller still wasn’t done. The president, he said, “has executed on every promise he’s made to the American people and that includes also taking back our culture and fighting against whether you call it radical leftism or woke or Marxism—a lot of people just call it plain crazy—but taking back our culture and restoring sanity to American life.

“It is my extraordinary privilege and blessing,” Miller added, “to be able to work for the president of the United States, to implement an agenda that I believe in wholly and completely and with every fiber of my being.”

I was there, of course, because I was writing a story on Susie Wiles and her West Wing team. I asked him, point-blank: “Would you agree, though, that it’s also the chief of staff’s job to tell the president what he doesn’t want to hear?”

“No, I wouldn’t say that,” Miller replied, finding fault with my framing of the question and insisting that this president wants to hear everything. “The chief of staff would never have to encounter the scenario you’re describing.” Miller said. “President Trump craves, he loves the every-minute detail of management, having every piece of information, having every side of everything, having inputs into the Oval Office from every square, every quarter, every person.”

As for the president’s staff, Miller said, their job is “implementing the president’s vision, the president’s directions, the president’s agenda, the president’s plans for the future…. We’re just here on his behalf to see that that is done.”

As the great political columnist Molly Ivins once wrote, “It probably sounded better in the original German.”

Chris Whipple is a contributing writer at Vanity Fair and a Fall 2026 Resident Fellow at Harvard’s Kennedy School Institute of Politics. You can follow him on Substack.

#3544. 10 Shows Like 'The Diplomat' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following its recently concluded fourth season, Netflix's political thriller The Diplomat has been renewed for a fifth season, and even better, it's the rare streaming show that seems to keep to a fairly regular schedule, meaning there's likely to be more of the Keri Russell-led espionage drama coming by late next year. If you're looking for something with the same political thriller vibes to watch in the meantime, here are 10 other series to stream now.

Diplomat creator Debora Cahn got her start on The West Wing, but honed her political-espionage craft on this show, for which she served as writer and, later, executive producer. The series begins with CIA case officer Carrie Mathison (Claire Danes) coming to suspect that decorated Marine Corps scout sniper Nicholas Brody (Damian Lewis), recently rescued from an al-Qaeda compound, has been turned and is planning a terrorist attack on the United States. As she has been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, her superiors don't give Mathison's suspicions much credence, kicking off a cat-and-mouse/is-he-or-isn't he? game between the two. As the show progresses, Carrie moves up the ranks until she's working directly for the president. Both leads won Emmys for their performances, and the series took the Outstanding Drama prize in its first year. Stream Homeland on Hulu and Netflix.

Focusing largely on the seedier side of international espionage, Slow Horses, based on the novels by Mick Herron, shares with The Diplomat a dry sense of humor about the consequences of institutional and human failures. With nods to the great spy dramas of John le Carré, Slow Horses updates the setting without losing either the thrills or the style of a time-honored genre. The “Slow Horses” of the title are a group of has-been MI5 agents—they’ve all made messes of significant jobs, but are still seen as having some use, if only in dull administrative tasks. Naturally, the members of the group (led by Gary Oldman's endlessly flatulent Jackson Lamb) find themselves in deeper waters than anyone thought them capable of navigating. Kristin Scott Thomas is the spymaster, navigating political pressures, misogyny, and her own unrepentant ambition in trying to do her job. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV.

An action drama that plays a bit like a spy thriller, The Night Agent stars Gabriel Basso as Peter Sutherland, an FBI agent who works overnights in the basement of the White House watching a phone that never, ever rings (dream job, honestly), until the night it does. Peter gets a call from Rose Larkin, a cybersecurity expert whose aunt and uncle were just killed; unbeknownst to her, they were also government operatives, and rescuing Rose sees Peter delving deep inside a web of conspiracy and corruption that plays out over three seasons, with a fourth and final on the way. While a bit more action-heavy than The Diplomat, it still plays in that realm of government secrets and conspiracies. Stream The Night Agent on Netflix.

There was a moment, around the turn of the millennium, when The West Wing seemed like a heightened but not entirely implausible picture of politics in action; its ripped-from-the-headlines style gave it an edge that allowed us to imagine smart, thoughtful people getting jobs in government, trying to do the more-or-less right thing despite systemic and personal flaws (it's also where The Diplomat's creator Debora Cahn started her TV writing career). The show's world can be a little frustrating when contrasted against our more explicitly appalling actual one, but it's a thoroughly pleasing fantasy nonetheless, with President Matin Sheen leading a White House staff through various diplomatic, military, and political crises. Stream The West Wing on Netflix and HBO Max.

Sidse Babett Knudsen stars as Birgitte Nyborg in this popular import. She's a minor Danish politician who watches other politicians fall to scandal and incompetence as she rapidly and unexpectedly ascends to the job of prime minister. The espionage and action are entirely incidental (but not nonexistent) here, as the show deals instead with the moral and political compromises that are seemingly intrinsic to statecraft. There's been talk of an American remake for years now, but you should just watch the original. Stream Borgen on Netflix.

Shonda Rhimes was already a powerhouse producer and screenwriter with several successful seasons of Grey's Anatomy under her belt when Scandal debuted, but its blend of political thrills and sexy, soapy drama truly solidified her brand—and her spot atop the modern TV landscape. Kerry Washington stars as Olivia Pope, head of the D.C.-based crisis management firm Olivia Pope & Associates (OPA), who is the person to call when you've got a PR disaster to fix. If you want to get a sense of the stakes involved, consider that Tony Goldwyn costars as Fitzgerald Grant III, who is both the president of the United States. and also Olivia's lover. Stream Scandal on Hulu and Netflix.

Téa Leoni plays Elizabeth McCord, a former CIA analyst who gave up that hectic life to become a political science professor. That's all going great until the Secretary of State dies under mysterious circumstances and she's called up by her old CIA boss, who's now the president, to take over the job. With her outsider's perspective and resistance to political considerations, she's surprisingly good at the gig, navigating foreign and domestic crises while also trying to figure out who the hell killed her predecessor, and whether they're coming for her, too. Stream Madam Secretary on The Roku Channel.

You could absolutely watch the original American take on this show, which stars Kiefer Sutherland—they have essentially the same premise—but this South Korean remake earns a few extra points by only running for a compact 16 episodes, making it far leaner and meaner. Education Minister Park Mu-jin (Ji Jin-hee) is fired from his job one day before an attack occurs amid an announcement of peace talks with the North, wiping out the entire presidential line of succession. His dismissal having not yet been finalized, the largely unambitious Minister Park is forced into the job, even as questions linger over the attack that put him in the role. Stream Designated Survivor: 60 Days on Netflix.

It's a different time and setting, but all the Keri Russell spy action you could want as a Diplomat fan. Set during the Cold War 1980s and created by former CIA officer Joe Weisberg, The Americans follows Soviet KGB intelligence agents Elizabeth (Russell) and Philip Jennings (the ever-reliable Matthew Rhys), living undercover lives posing as an American couple in the DC metro area—and raising their American-born children. The critically acclaimed show makes much of its period setting and a central conflict that places two spies in the heart of suburban America, even as they're tasked with undermining the Reagan-era government under which their children are growing up. Stream The Americans on Hulu.

A power struggle for leadership of an entire country is at the heart of this juicy political thriller. Prime Minister Park Dong-ho comes to believe that the president has been corrupted by powerful, wealthy individuals and companies (something that could only happen in South Korea, obviously). Deputy Prime Minister Jeong Su-jin sees the problem, too, but she's not so sure about his solution: He wants to have the president assassinated. But how much better is he than the man he would be replacing? And how pure are her motives in potentially putting herself in line for the top job? Stream The Whirlwind on Netflix.
