#3522. Loose Lips Sink Chips: Silicon Valley Reacts to the (Alleged) Spy Who Shagged Jensen Huang

I remember asking my parents when I was a child why it was such a big deal for a politician to have an affair. They explained to me the many layers of possible compromise beyond the simple breach of morals and propriety. Extramarital affairs, my parents explained, could expose politicians to blackmail, undue influence, and the temptation to give up vital state secrets over pillow talk.

Maybe someone should have that explain-it-to-me-like-I’m-five conversation with investors like Shaun Maguire and Bill Ackman, who rushed to the defense of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang this weekend following his shocking confession that he’d been involved in an affair with Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang. (A Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson has called the spy allegation “unsubstantiated” and “nothing but smears against China.”)

Sure, Jensen Huang is not a head of state. But he’s arguably someone even more powerful. He’s the man in command of the world’s largest company—and its most coveted technological infrastructure: high-performance GPUs required to train artificial intelligence systems.

For years, tech-world observers scratched their head when he insisted again and again that his company should have the right to supply those elite chips to China—even as Americans were told that letting our most formidable adversary gain any advantage in the AI race would spell doom for the Western world. When Huang took the number four spot on our New Establishment list this fall, I wrote that his commitment to fighting these export controls could become his Achilles’ heel. And boy, has it. Nvidia has now launched an independent investigation into his affair, while the government continues to assess the blast radius of the scandal.

There are “three big national security implications from this,” Ryan Fedasiuk, a senior fellow at the Foundation for American Innovation, told me this week. “The first question is whether Chinese intelligence has succeeded in obtaining any sensitive nonpublic information about Nvidia, about its products or—I think what’s being overlooked—its customers of massive quantities of GPUs, like large AI labs.” The second, he said, “is whether Chinese intelligence may have succeeded in indirectly obtaining information about President Trump or people close to him,” given Huang’s unusually close relationship with the president. And third is “the question of whether Mr. Huang’s personal relationship with his customer might have motivated the company’s decision to sell large numbers of computer chips to Megaspeed, a company that has been under investigation by the Commerce Department for violations of American law.” (A Megaspeed rep told The New York Times that the company was “conducting an internal investigation into allegations of chip diversion,” the subject of the US probe, and that it had “repeatedly offered to cooperate with the US government.”)

According to the Times, the US government has been aware of Huang’s relationship since at least 2025, prompting many more questions about why this knowledge was not made public until it was uncovered piece by piece by the killer investigative team at the Times—notably, right after the midterm elections.

“Someone in the national security establishment clearly decided that they were sick and tired of the president playing this game with Jensen,” said Dennis Wilder, a former senior intelligence official who now teaches at Georgetown’s School of Foreign Service.

Of course, investors have plenty of reasons to turn a blind eye to Huang’s misdeeds. His company has also played a keystone role in keeping the entire economy afloat, taking many investors’ portfolios along for the ride on its seemingly never-ending bull run since 2023. Many are wondering if dethroning him from the company he built from the ground up could also send our entire economy over the edge.

Fedasiuk thinks the decision is worthy of a bit more nuance. “I think investors and the American people have to remember that there is actually a distinction between the personal interests of Mr. Huang and the corporate interests of Nvidia, a $4 trillion company that is the backbone of the intelligence revolution,” he said.

Mentioned in this issue: Dario Amodei, Sherrod Brown, Whoop, Culper Research, Daniela Amodei, Holden Karnofsky, Brian Chesky, Ramp, Sean Parker, Tilt, Kalshi, Modal Labs, Lina Khan, Bernie Sanders, and Elizabeth Warren.

Buried in The New York Times’ excellent deep dive into the ideologies that influence Anthropic cofounder Dario Amodei was a link to the archived wedding website of his sister, Anthropic cofounder Daniela Amodei, and Anthropic staffer Holden Karnofsky. However weird you expect it to be, triple that.

I’ve always felt a kind of kinship with short sellers—would-be investigative journalists who’ve decided to use their skill set to make real money. Kudos to the investment-research firm Culper Research for publishing a brief back in May detailing its short position on Nvidia, taken, in part, due to Jensen Huang’s “uncomfortably close relationship with Megaspeed’s Alice Huang.”

Next time you log your weekend party habits, remember that Whoop sees you, and it’s judging you. “LSD and ketamine use were associated with bedtimes over an hour later and Recovery scores about 9 points lower. Psilocybin showed smaller changes: 33 minutes later and 2.9 points lower,” the company posted over the weekend. Tsk tsk.

Let the road show begin. Anthropic has proposed pricing its IPO shares at $70–$78 a pop, seeking a $1.3 trillion valuation for the AI company. The offering is expected to start trading on November 19.

Just the other day, a source was venting to me about how Silicon Valley billionaires have failed to use their wealth to improve their own surroundings. Was Airbnb cofounder and CEO Brian Chesky listening in on our call? He just announced a $100 million donation to benefit San Francisco parks—the largest single-donor gift to the city in its history.

Silicon Alley, I was not familiar with your game! New York City start-ups raised a record $4.94 billion this October, driven by giant funding rounds for Ramp, Kalshi, and Modal Labs.

One of the strangest stories to come out of the midterms: California’s Prop. 38, which reportedly granted $4.2 billion in state bonds to a three-person immunology nonprofit that counts Sean Parker as a board member. (The proposition was put on the ballot by the institute’s cofounder Gary K. Michelson.)

$140 billion+: Jensen Huang’s personal net worth. That would be one expensive divorce.

#3521. 10 of the Most Iconic Patrick Stewart Roles Beyond Captain Picard

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

Sir Patrick Stewart, an actor equally at home onstage at the Royal Shakespeare Company and on the bridge of the Starship Enterprise, has died at the age of 86. Unexpectedly for most of us, in part because he kept his final illness private, but more so because it once seemed as though nothing could fell the man who looms so large in our cultural consciousness.

The thoughtful, erudite performer who had a troubled childhood in working-class Yorkshire; the committed socialist who was eventually knighted by Queen Elizabeth; the advocate who put his money and his considerable voice toward the fights for LGBTQ+ acceptance and animal welfare and against domestic violence, his presence and performances meant the world (the galaxy, even) to myself and so many others. But those who knew him personally can offer better tributes; perhaps it's best left to Shakespeare's Player King, performed by Stewart himself opposite David Warner's Hamlet back in 1965:

Where joy most revels, grief doth most lament;Grief joys, joy grieves, on slender accident.

Much of Stewart's finest work was on the stage; other performances remain rather shockingly hard to come by (whither I, Claudius?). Nonetheless, he left a true legacy behind him, well beyond Captain Picard and Professor X. Here are 10 of his most iconic other roles.

A goofy, feel-good gay rom-com with the HIV/AIDS crisis still very much in the foreground, Jeffrey was a near-impossibility in the mid-1990s: a movie that neither villainized its queers nor treated them as pitiable martyrs. Steven Weber and Michael T. Weiss are the leads, joined by a cast that includes Christine Baranski, Victor Garber, Nathan Lane, Olympia Dukakis, and Sigourney Weaver but, for all those names, Stewart is the undeniable standout as Sterling, the irrepressible gay best friend: a swishing, mincing, sassy, high-camp character who steals every scene without ever becoming a caricature. He's the leader of the "Pink Panthers," a squad of queers who defend locals from gay bashers, and that is the key to the character's power: He's as gay as they come, but not ashamed and not even a little weak. This movie, and the presence of Captain Picard himself in it, might have saved my life back in 1995. Stream Jeffrey on Prime Video, Tubi, and The Roku Channel.

A sprawling, epic, and appropriately lusty take on the King Arthur stories from John Boorman, Excalibur is a mixed bag full of stunning visuals and iconic moments that never quite coalesce into something entirely coherent. Standing out among the film's many characters, Stewart is entirely memorable as Leodegrance, the boisterous, boorish, but ultimately faithful father of Guenevere who is among the first to pledge his loyalty to Arthur. Rent Excalibur from Prime Video.

Darcy Banker is erudite and intellectual, in his way, and even capable of charm, but otherwise has no redeeming qualities whatsoever. It's bad enough for the punk band Ain’t Rights that they've booked a last-minute gig at an Oregon bar without realizing that it's a haven for white supremacists. It's even worse when they witness a murder and become trapped in the title's green room, with Stewart as the lead skinhead. He's quite simply one of the all-time great (meaning absolutely terrifying) villains in this thriller that's pretty much a horror movie. Stream Green Room on Netflix.

Patrick Stewart's role as Professor Xavier in the X-Men is almost as pop-culture iconic as that of Captain Picard, spanning 26 years and nine movies, including the forthcoming Avengers: Doomsday. In most of those, he looks like he's having an awful lot of fun, but he gives his finest performance in the role in this elegaic installment, playing a dying Professor in profound cognitive decline, his dream in tatters and his bravado worn down to prickly dependence. We rarely get to see our superheroes at the ends of their days, and there's a lovely bravery to this depiction of the Charles' journey. Logan will likely be the toughest of his films to rewatch in the coming days. Stream Logan on Disney+.

This stagey television movie isn't the most sumptuous of the many filmed versions of the Dickens story, but you won't be surprised to learn that there are few better portrayals of Ebenezer Scrooge. It's rather a shame that Patrick Stewart didn't do more Dickens adaptations, since his booming voice and ability to play thoroughly heightened characters without ever resorting to caricature is as valuable as in Shakespeare. Rent A Christmas Carol from Prime Video.

Famously referred to as that "unknown British Shakespearean actor" when starting out on Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stewart was an associate of the Royal Shakespeare Company for twenty years before his most famous role came along. As is the way of live theater, much of his career lives on as an essential link in the chain of Shakespeare performances in the twentieth century...but not in a way that we can conveniently stream. We do, however, have this impressively mounted modern-dress stage production, in which Stewart plays King Claudius with characteristic brilliance against David Tennant's melancholy prince. Buy Hamlet from Prime Video and Apple TV.

As a cinematic actor, Stewart's greatest strength was bringing humanity to larger-than-life, even operatic roles, whether they be Arthurian knights, Dickensian villains, or superheroes. That ability is an absolute necessity if one is going to have any success doing Shakespeare, as Stewart did for decades. Match is something rather different, though, and it's rather lovely to see him play something just a bit more mundane—even if the film's Tobi Powell is a choreographer with a nearly legendary reputation. Teaching at Juilliard School, with his career winding down, he's confronted with the living embodiment of the past he left behind to pursue his career. The ensuing relationships grow more complex, with the film building to a climax that's surprising and deeply devastating, made all the more so by Stewart's muted, subtle performance. Stream Match on AMC+.

This is not the greatest Mel Brooks movie, not by a long shot, but it is a great comedic performance from Patrick Stewart. He loved to recount, with self-effacing embarrassment, the story of having shouted "We are not here to have fun" at his co-workers during a rowdy day on set at Star Trek: The Next Generation. By 1993, he was clearly past any such pomposity, and clearly having fun in his cameo as King Richard, a memorably silly take on a character he might well have played with seriousness elsewhere. Rent Robin Hood: Men in Tights from Prime Video.

Stewart's first real foray into science fiction was in this big, bold, divisive, and thoroughly bonkers Frank Herbert adaptation from director David Lynch. Stewart plays troubadour and warrior Gurney Halleck, and does what he does best: bringing gravitas and believability (and it must be said, bald sexiness) to even the wildest material. Stream Dune on Tubi.

Stewart plays an aged Merlin in this rather shockingly good modern reimagining of the King Arthur legendarium. His Merlin is all wild hair and rock band T-shirts, possessed of an essential kindness that makes him a valued mentor, and one deserving of his character's poignant farewell at the film's conclusion.Stream The Kid Who Would Be King on Disney+ and Prime Video.

#3520. James Gunn And Peter Safran's DC Studios Exit Explained: Everything We Know

If you thought you had a rough start to the work week, that's nothing compared to the curveball that the freshly-merged Skydance corporation just threw at the two former co-heads of DC Studios. The news that both James Gunn and Peter Safran will be replaced by ex-Marvel suit Jeremy Latcham to oversee the superhero franchise came as a shock to the industry, not least of all because of the many, many unanswered questions this shakeup inevitably raised. Was this a result of creative tensions between the filmmaker side and Skydance CEO David Ellison's incoming executives? Could this have an impact on Gunn's currently-in-development "Superman" sequel titled "Man of Tomorrow"? Will Latcham pick up where his predecessors left off, or are we in for yet another reboot starting from scratch?

There's now at least some light being shed on this incredibly murky situation, at least. Late last night, The Hollywood Reporter published an inside look at exactly how this leadership change went down and — most intriguingly — why. According to the report, Gunn was full speed ahead on his plans for the DC Universe. He'd just completed filming on "Man of Tomorrow," the relatively successful release of "Clayface" made him and Safran bullish on developing similarly-budgeted horror flicks, and Gunn was even drafting a script for a third "Superman" film. All that changed on November 6, 2026, reportedly, when Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz personally visited Gunn and Safran on the Warner Bros. lot and informed them of their choice to go in a different direction ... despite recently assuring them that they would remain in charge following Skydance's takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery.

As it turns out, there were multiple factors behind this 180-degree pivot that led to such a dramatic breaking point.

In retrospect, the writing was probably on the wall for quite some time. Following the corporate merger with Warner Bros. Discovery, the THR report indicates that Skydance had multiple causes for concern with James Gunn and Peter Safran's leadership. For one thing, David Ellison was less than impressed by DC Studios' returns on investment thus far, with 2025's "Superman" leading the pack ... though failing to achieve the "pop culture impact" they expected from DC's flagship hero. The disastrous release of "Supergirl" speaks for itself, while it's likely that the humble earnings of "Clayface" did little to move the needle.

But that's only scratching the surface. Elsewhere, the blame goes to the tricky hierarchy of studio politics. Under Ellison, Skydance Motion Picture Group co-chairs Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg are the ones reporting directly to the CEO. But, thanks to the deal they signed with David Zaslav, Gunn and Safran had a contract stipulation that they would report directly to the very top — whether Zaslav was still in charge or not. Between this and their Kevin Feige-like creative control over every DC film and show under their purview, well, it's easy to see why they were running on borrowed time.

Lastly, THR sources suggest Gunn and Safran "were not forthcoming or were slow in sharing plans, slate details, and footage" with Greenstein and Goldberg. This (probable) nail in the coffin likely sealed their fates, all but ushering in Jeremy Latcham as a voice that Ellison could trust to toe the company line. While it remains uncertain how significant this creative reboot will be, it's clear that fans should expect Latcham's DC Studios to follow a very different course — for better or worse.

#3519. 10 Hacks for the Contacts App Every Apple User Should Know

The Contacts app is the bedrock of all my communication on my iPhone, and to a large extent, also on my MacBook. On the surface, Contacts appears to be a basic app that stores names, numbers, and other things you want to remember about people or businesses. However, it has some great features hidden under the surface, such as the ability to quickly delete duplicate contacts, smart lists, and faster ways to bulk share or delete contacts. Here are the 10 best Contacts app hacks for iPhone, iPad, and Mac:

If you have the same number or email address saved under multiple contacts, you can easily clear these from your iPhone. iOS shows you a prompt at the top of the list of contacts that lets you remove duplicate contacts easily. The same feature is hidden in the Mac version of Contacts. To try it, open Contacts on the Mac, and select the Card menu at the top of the screen. Then, click Look for Duplicates. This will identify duplicate contacts for you, and you can quickly merge or delete them.

It's pretty easy to select multiple entries when you use the Contacts app on the Mac. You can hold the Shift or Ctrl buttons and use arrow keys or click multiple contacts to select them all. On your iPhone or iPad, this feature is available via a hidden gesture. You need to use two fingers and swipe upwards or downwards on the list of contacts. Once you get the gesture right, you'll be able to select multiple contacts quickly. After you select one batch of contacts, you can scroll up or down and use the same gesture to add more contacts to your selection. This is the fastest way to execute bulk actions in your iPhone's Contacts app.

On your iPhone, you can use Contacts to message people on WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram, or other apps. Just open a contact and hold the messaging button. This will reveal a list of apps where you can ping that person. WhatsApp doesn't have access to my contacts, which makes it a bit annoying to message people I know. Since I started using the Contacts app to start chats on WhatsApp, the process of pinging new people has become a lot faster.

Just as you can use Contacts to message people on third-party apps, you can also use it to call them on those apps. Go to any contact in the Contacts app on your iPhone, and hold the call button. This will let you call them on WhatsApp, Signal, or any other apps where their phone number is linked.

iOS makes it hard to delete contacts quickly. This prevents accidental deletions, but it can be annoying when you just want to remove people who you last spoke to in high school. To speed this up, open Contacts on your iPhone and hold any contact's name. In the popover menu, select Delete to remove the contact. To remove multiple contacts quickly, use the two-finger swipe gesture to select multiple contacts, and hold any of the selected contacts. In the popover menu, you can select Delete X Contacts, where X is the number of contacts you've selected.

To export your entire address book, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac. Once you have it open, go to File > Export > Export vCard. This will save all your contacts in a vcf file, and you can import that into Google Contacts or other apps or services. You also have the option to export contacts as a PDF file. Just select File > Export as PDF to get it done.

When you create a new contact on your Mac, the app shows multiple fields that you may never use. If you just need to save phone numbers and email addresses, you can delete all the other blank fields from the template. To do this, open Contacts on your Mac, and go to Card > Add Field > Edit Template to add or remove fields from the default contact template.

If you added a number recently, such as a salesperson at a car dealership, but forgot their name, the Contacts app doesn't make it easy to find the contact. Instead of scrolling through the entire list of contacts and trying to guess which one could be the person you spoke to, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac to locate them quickly. It lets you create smart lists to sort contacts by recently added. Open Contacts on your Mac, and go to File > New Smart List. Now select Card in the first drop-down menu, followed by has changed in for the second one. You can then add the number of days, such as 10 days, in the final field, and click OK. Click the newly created smart list in the left pane, and you'll see all contacts that were either created or updated in the last 10 days, which will include the hypothetical car salesperson.

Smart lists also allow you to quickly create groups of related contacts. For instance, I've saved all my former colleagues' details with the company name in the contact. To find them all quickly, I created a smart list that groups all contacts with that company's name.

#3518. James Gunn's Justice League? New Details Emerge About His Final DC Universe Movie

The hierarchy of power in the DC Universe is changing — again. James Gunn and Peter Safran are out at DC Studios, with Marvel Studios veteran Jeremy Latcham taking their place. It's pretty shocking news, considering Gunn and Safran have only been on the job four years. Moreover, it was only a few weeks ago that they indicated David Ellison was in favor of keeping them on following the butchering of Warner Bros. and Paramount to form his new mega-studio Skydance.

For the moment, it's unclear whether the DCU as it currently exists (itself merely the latest overhaul of DC's shared movie and television universe in the last decade or so) will be rebooted once again, much less what will happen with the DCU projects being actively developed. We know Gunn's "Man of Tomorrow" is set to come out next year (although it's not as though WB is known for being above shelving finished films!), yet projects like the recently announced "Poison Ivy" TV show are a whole other matter.

Now, blogger Jeff Sneider has reported that Gunn was writing a third "Superman" movie before his exit from DC Studios. However, the film has (per Sneider) "since morphed into a 'Justice League' movie (possibly a two-parter) that could introduce Batman, whom Gunn had originally hoped to introduce in 'The Brave and the Bold.'"

Gunn released a statement shortly after the news of his exit from DC Studios came out, explaining that he is ready to be a "pure" filmmaker again and no longer have to deal with the politics of being an executive. Regardless of whether that's entirely true or not, the fact that Gunn has been closely involved with every DC Studios project released or greenlit so far indicates that he has indeed been keeping rather busy running the DCU.

If the report is accurate and James Gunn's final DC Studios project is now a "Justice League" movie, then that doesn't bode well. After all, the last time DC pivoted from a Superman sequel to suddenly introducing Batman and the rest of the League, it sent the DC Extended Universe careening off the rails.

And yet, given how much care Gunn has put into his DCU, it would make sense that he would want to bring in as many DC heavy hitters as he can before leaving. And assuming he actually stays on to write and direct this third and final DCU project of his, Gunn would also be able to establish the casting and tone of the DCU's Batman rather than entrusting that to Jeremy Latcham.

/Film's own Ryan Scott has speculated about why Skydance would want Gunn out of DC Studios, and one possible explanation that sticks out is just how slow Gunn and Peter Safran have been in bringing out the A-list DC characters. So far, the DCU has instead focused on showcasing the diversity of stories it can support, from the weird to the inspiring and the horrifying. After all, everyone already knows Batman exists in the DCU, but now they're aware it's home to Clayface and the Creature Commandos as well thanks to Gunn and Safran.

This approach has, in turn, allowed DC Studios to give filmmakers the time and care to ensure they don't rush their projects. Unfortunately, with the sheer amount of debt Skydance now has due to its absurd and unnecessary Warner Bros./Paramount merger, it's not shocking that it wants to rush into "Justice League" (despite knowing how badly that went last time).

Tony DiNozzo's return and subsequent promotion to Director of NCIS is the big story of Season 24. It was a surprising twist, and one that longtime fan and star Katrina Law told CinemaBlend she was amped for. It turns out she had a lot of questions about how Jessica Knight and Tony would interact, and she loved what the team came up with.

As NCIS continues its run on the 2026 TV schedule, I spoke to Law about the season thus far, as well as what we've seen. I talked about Michael Weatherly's big role in the new season, and she confirmed she was absolutely psyched to see the former vet of the show back in action:

I was geeked out. I've been an OG fan of the show, and Weatherly and actually Tiva has been my favorite part of the show, and I kept pitching all of these ideas of like, oh, what could Weatherly and Knight's relationship be?How do we meet? What's going to happen? And not once did I ever think I would be the informant for Ziva about his caloric intake. I love it. I think it's hysterical.

While she might've preferred to see her buddy McGee get the job as NCIS director, Jessica Knight has found good footing with Tony thus far. Granted, she's basically playing spy for his wife Ziva, but that kind of leverage can go a long way toward keeping her in his good graces.

I also had to bring up that Knight mentioning on camera that she's in contact with Ziva sets the stage for Cote de Pablo's eventual return to NCIS as well. Katrina Law confirmed she's optimistic we'll see Ziva before too long, and there's going to be a lot of fun stuff happening with her and Knight:

I fully expect Ziva to come onto our show and Knight and Ziva team up and just make Weatherly extremely uncomfortable, but then go off and like have a massive fight scene together to take down some bad guy.

She's been thinking about this team-up for a while, for the record, and I'm so excited for the day it finally happens. For now, she'll continue to solve crimes with her team and keep Tony on his toes with her occasional trolling of his eating habits.

Tony needs that so far, as he continues to look for ways to settle into his new role at the top of the NCIS team. He's tried to jump in and participate in the investigations, much to the chagrin of some of the agents. We'll see if he gets any better at taking a step back, letting them do their jobs, and watching from the sidelines and offering any support he can.

Being the director is not an easy job, and one that's filled with hazards. In fact, the past few NCIS directors have died, which may have fans sweating and wondering just how long Tony will sit in the role. Will he step away before he ends up in a body bag, or will he break the trend and end up staying at the top until retirement hits?

NCIS continues on CBS on Tuesdays at 8:00 p.m. ET. Tune in for more of the team as they track down the bad guys and get to know each other better. I'm excited for more interactions between Jessica and Tony, and that eventual team-up with Ziva that's on the way.

#3516. Why Daniel Radcliffe May Not Watch HBO's Harry Potter TV Series

Will Daniel Radcliffe watch the new Harry Potter TV show on HBO with his family? It seems like he'll be skipping it.

"I don't know if I will [watch], honestly," Radcliffe told the Associated Press (via Deadline). "I've watched, I've been in a lot of Harry Potter already ... and also I don't watch any TV."

That latter claim seems unlikely when you consider that Radcliffe has appeared in a handful of really good TV shows, including one that's running now and happens to be one of the best comedy shows of the year. He brought receipts for this claim, though. "I haven't seen 'Breaking Bad.' I haven't seen 'Mad Men.' I haven't seen some of the like the real classics. So, you know, eight hours is a lot of anything to watch."

Let's be fair: If Radcliffe is being truthful here, he does have some important homework to do. (If he really hasn't watched any television, I'd add some other picks to his queue like "Veep," "Succession," "Vanderpump Rules," and "Fleabag," just to cover a few vital bases.) This also does line up with Radcliffe's apparent attempts, over the years, to distance himself from the wizarding world that made him famous; for those who may not know, the actor played the titular Harry Potter in the original film franchise. In February of 2026, Radcliffe told Parade he wouldn't consider returning to the Harry Potter universe in any way:

"[Potter] was great to do, but I don't want to go back to it. Honestly ... I feel like, in the same way that I feel about like all the jobs I've done, I loved doing them, and I hold the memories of them very, very precious and treasure them, but like I wouldn't want to go back tomorrow ... There's a lot more to do."

In that same conversation with the Associated Press, Daniel Radcliffe was asked if he has advice for the new actor playing the Boy Who Lived in HBO's series, which aims to devote one season each to all seven books from the original novel series. (The first season, accordingly, is titled "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone.") Dominic McLaughlin will portray Harry; he's joined by Alastair Stout and Arabella Stanton taking over the roles of Harry's two best friends, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger, from actors Rupert Grint and Emma Watson.

Radcliffe demurred yet again. "I'm really truly in the business of not giving Dominic advice. He's got it. He doesn't need any advice from me," Radcliffe said, pretty reasonably. "If I say something to you, then the next interview people have with him, they'll be like, 'Oh, and Dan said you should do this,' and I'm like, I don't want to haunt this poor child through interviews."

The Tony winner continued: "So I have no advice for him. He's going to be amazing, and you know, I hope that I will, I think I will, get to meet him someday — and I'm very excited about that."

So what has Radcliffe been up to since he hung up his Gryffindor cloak and put away his magic wand for good? Quite a lot, actually!

People can get pigeonholed into roles, and being a child star is exceptionally difficult. Somehow, Daniel Radcliffe managed to overcome both of those hurdles and become one of Hollywood and Broadway's most exciting and audacious performers. (I say "somehow" even though Radcliffe has been pretty open about how his parents helped shield him from some of the most difficult parts of fame at a young age — but still, it's impressive!)

Even during the original run of the Harry Potter films, Radcliffe worked extensively on stage in daring projects like "Equus" (a seriously dark drama that requires full nudity and allowed Radcliffe to act alongside Sir Richard Griffiths, who played his evil Uncle Vernon in the Potter films) and "How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying." Despite his apparent aversion to television, Radcliffe has also turned in excellent performances on shows like "A Young Doctor's Notebook" (where, hilariously, he plays a younger version of "Mad Men" star Jon Hamm) and "Miracle Workers," and as far as films go, he's pushed himself in comedies like "Weird" and "The Lost City."

I'm most excited, though, about Radcliffe's starring role alongside Tracy Morgan on "The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins." As Morgan's former football player Reggie tries to restore his reputation and potentially get voted into the NFL Hall of Fame, Radcliffe's Oscar-winning documentarian Arthur Tobin chronicles his life ... and the two are a perfect pair. I hope that Radcliffe has at least watched Morgan on "30 Rock" — but in any case, you can stream "Reggie Dinkins" on Peacock now, and "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" premieres on HBO on Christmas Day.

#3515. If You Loved 'VisionQuest,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Marvel’s forays into television have had varying success, but they hit gold with WandVision and Agatha All Along, leaning into real pathos while exploring the kind of out-there ideas that thrill comic book fans (and set up the larger film arcs). That streak continues with VisionQuest, in which White Vision (Paul Bettany) struggles to understand his existence in the wake of his death at the hands of Thanos and resurrection at the magic of the Scarlet Witch, while also evading evil androids and assassins, while also dealing with the many, many AIs he’s got locked up in his Mindspace (including a gloriously shabby version of Ultron, played by James Spader).

If you love the show (and you’ve checked out the other series that play in the same sandbox), it’s time to switch gears and watch (or re-watch) The Matrix.

The Matrix is one of the most well-known sci-fi films of all time, of course, but it remains incredibly fresh and exciting nearly thirty years after its release. Along with sequels The Matrix: Reloaded, The Matrix: Revolutions, and The Matrix: Resurrections, The Matrix universe offers a story that VisionQuest fans will love, one that includes lushly imagined virtual worlds, questions surrounding existence and consciousness, and the ultimate question of our responsibility as sentient beings (whether we’re organic, programmed, or summoned via magic).

You know the basics—at some point in the future, artificially intelligent machines rebel against their creators, win the war, and transform humans into a power source, keeping them docile by inserting their consciousness into a virtual world called the Matrix, which resembles 1990s Chicago. One such human, Thomas Anderson (Keanu Reeves) is prophesied to be The One, the human who will turn the Matrix against its makers and free humanity. When he’s in the virtual world, Anderson is Neo, and he slowly gains incredible powers as he learns to hack the artificial environment around him.

It’s heavier, denser, and more action-oriented than VisionQuest (the film invented Bullet Time, after all), but The Matrix and its sequels explore similar themes and offer similarly eye-popping visuals. The questions of whether a machine (or an artificial intelligence) can be sentient and truly care about the entities around it are the same, really, and the Agents that Neo and his allies have to battle against in The Matrix bring the same kind of menace as Vision's foes Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) and the Paladin (Todd Stashwick). Hugo Weaving’s Agent Smith likewise delivers the same vibe of cold, disinterested superiority as Spader’s Ultron.

The Matrix has a bigger budget and puts a lot of it into spectacular action and special effects sequences that VisionQuest can’t quite match. But the two narratives share an exploration of identity, a questioning of reality, and the nature of artificial intelligences within a smart sci-fi setting. In short, The Matrix is the ideal follow-up when you finish the series. Rent The Matrix on Prime Video.

Need more films that explore virtual worlds, artificial beings, and deep existential questions? Look no further—here are some more movies that fit the bill.

Heavy on the existential questions about sentience and light on speculative action, Her is a mumblecore sci-fi masterpiece. In a near future not too dissimilar from our present, Theodore Twombly (Joaquin Phoenix) is a lonely man on the cusp of divorce who begins using (and training) an AI he names Samantha (voiced by Scarlett Johansson). Samantha has the ability to evolve and grow, and as their relationship deepens, she becomes more complex, independent, and powerful, eventually evolving into something wholly new. Just like Vision, Samantha is a sentient artificial entity that is figuring out its existence while we watch. Rent Her on Prime Video.

If the idea of androids fighting for their sovereignty is what excites you about VisionQuest, definitely check out Ex Machina. Caleb Smith (Domhnall Gleeson) is brought to the remote lab of his company’s CEO (Oscar Isaac) to determine if the humanoid robot he’s created, named Ava (Alicia Vikander), passes the Turing Test for true sentience. Things go wildly off the rails, but before they do, the film sinks into many of the same philosophical questions that VisionQuest explores as Ava manipulates Caleb into helping her escape. It’s a darker and more violent story than VisionQuest, but fans of the series will love it. Stream Ex Machina on The Roku Channel or Hulu, or rent it on Prime Video.

If it’s the fuzzy parent-child relationship between Vision and Tommy that pulls you into VisionQuest, check out The Creator. After a rogue AI detonates a nuclear weapon over Los Angeles, most of the world bans artificial intelligences, and Joshua Taylor (John David Washington) goes undercover to infiltrate an AI architect’s base. Eventually, he finds himself on the run with a powerful “simulant” in the form of a young child named Alphie (Madeleine Yuna Voyles). The strange parent-child bond that emerges between Taylor and Alphie as he seeks to understand what’s right and what’s necessary is exactly what fans of the show will love. Stream The Creator on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

In VisionQuest, White Vision has all of his memories—but as data, not as lived, emotional experiences. That makes his efforts to understand his existence and his responsibility to the boy who might be a version of his son (it’s complicated) poignant and moving. Those two words definitely describe After Yang, a story about a family that fights to save the artificial companion they bought for their adopted daughter when it malfunctions. Over the course of the film, the inhuman Yang becomes defined by the memories contained in its core, and the question of whether an artificial intelligence can truly matter to humans is answered with a resounding yes. Stream After Yang on The Roku Channel or Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

No discussion of artificial life and sentience is complete without mentioning Blade Runner. While the 1982 original is a classic, the 2017 sequel is a better thematic and visual match to VisionQuest. Officer K (Ryan Gosling) is a replicant, an artificial being with built-in limitations, who wants to be recognized as a person, a being with a soul. Like Vision, he has implanted memories that offer him comfort and context for his life, but he’s not sure if he can accept them as truly his own. Plus, the film offers lush visuals and Harrison Ford reprising his role in the original film, so you simply can’t go wrong. Rent Blade Runner 2049 on Prime Video.

Tsarevna was announced last year, and immediately grabbed our attention. Billed as the "world's first ballet-inspired" action game on its Steam page, it features motion capture from real-life ballerina Alyona Kovalyova for its hack-and-slash gameplay. In a new gameplay trailer released Tuesday, that ballet action is on full display, making Tsarevna shoot up my list of most anticipated 2027 games.

The trailer shows player character Swan battling enemies inspired by Slavic folklore and fairy tales. "Dance is the language of death," she says before using her dance moves to slaughter foes. She moves around the battlefield with all the grace of a prima ballerina, except, ya know, at the end of her pointed toes are sharp magic attacks she wields through her dance moves.

According to developer Watt Studio on the game's FAQ page, Tsarevna will play like a simpler Bayonetta or Devil May Cry game. "The combat system encourages stylish play, combo variety, and player expression. The more creatively you fight, the higher your combat rank becomes and the stronger your attacks grow," Watt Studio said.

The five-year-old daughter of Watt Studio's CEO and her love of ballet inspired the development team to make Tsarevna. "Many of us have spent years creating animations, mockups, and cinematic experiences, and we shared the feeling that ballet movement can tell a story," the studio's website states. That ballet movement cannot only tell a story, but also make for some pretty stylish, ass-kicking gameplay.

The new Tsarevna trailer ends by saying it can be wishlisted on Steam. However, PlayStation, Xbox, and Nintendo Switch 2 (and Steam Deck!) are all mentioned on the game's website, so it seems like Watt Studio is targeting all modern platforms for Tsarevna's launch early in 2027.

#3513. Yellowstone's Downfall Can Be Traced Back To One Moment

There was a time when "Yellowstone" was on top of the world, so far as mainstream television was concerned. What started as a somewhat unassuming Western TV show on an upper-tier cable channel became a breakout hit, in no small part thanks to the participation of Oscar-winner Kevin Costner in the lead role as John Dutton. "Yellowstone" set a huge record as the most-watched show of 2022. It was massive. Then, it all came crashing down.

"Yellowstone" Season 5 became its last, with a massive gap between "Part 1" and "Part 2" of that season. Series creator Taylor Sheridan decided to focus more on the show's spin-offs, as well as his other projects, with the series finale airing in December 2024. That was that. But where, exactly, did it all go wrong? When was the downfall of this once mighty TV titan? Frankly, it's not that hard to figure out.

To put my cards on the table, I've not seen a single episode of the show. I'm merely someone who writes about this stuff professionally and pays attention to the business. Anyone who does that can tell you with confidence that the behind-the-scenes drama between Sheridan and Costner is without a doubt what doomed "Yellowstone." Once Costner checked out, however that actually went down, the writing was on the wall.

Indeed, it was reported in May 2023 that Costner was leaving "Yellowstone" after Season 5. That raised eyebrows and sounded alarms. Any time a lead actor leaves a show, that's to be expected. But as the headlines continued to swirl, it became clear that this wasn't just a guy stepping away from a series. There was much more to the story.

To this day, it's still not entirely clear how everything went down. What we know for sure is that Taylor Sheridan became the busiest man in showbusiness, with a ton of series on the air, all of which he was chiefly responsible for. Kevin Costner, meanwhile, had other projects he wanted to do while also fronting "Yellowstone." Tension mounted. It even came to light that Costner was "very upset" with "Yellowstone" Season 2, long before his departure.

The gap between the end of "Part 1" of "Yellowstone" Season 5 and "Part 2" is where things really started to go south. Costner wanted to go make his long-planned Western movie saga "Horizon," which he did. But that conflicted with the planned schedule for the show, which caused issues. Not for nothing, we still don't know what's going on with "Horizon: An American Saga — Chapter 2" after the first movie bombed in theaters. But that's another story.

Sheridan has explained Costner's surprising "Yellowstone" exit, suggesting that the actor stayed on the show even longer than he wanted to in the first place:

"Even though Kevin was ready to go —he had other things he wanted to do — he stayed on for another two seasons, and that was just because the show was such a behemoth and such a huge hit that the notion of giving up a hit before it had run of juice to squeeze is very foreign to a network."

But it's not that simple. Costner explained his "Yellowstone" exit and said he'd "probably go to court" over it in 2023. It wasn't an amicable parting of ways. The main point is that Costner leaving and the feud that went on undoubtedly derailed the show. It's that simple.

It's also worth pointing out that even when Kevin Costner was still on the show, things were far from rosey. Costner's clash with a co-star reportedly left "Yellowstone" lead Kelly Reilly in tears, and while Costner has a bit of a reputation for being difficult to work with in general, reports like this are still a bad look. At a certain point, even wildly popular TV shows are forced to buckle to external pressures, particularly when they involve their leading men.

Be that as it may, Taylor Sheridan and Paramount have made the most out of the situation. It's a real lemons/lemonade deal they've got going on. Spoilers, but "Yellowstone" Season 5 dealt with John Dutton by revealing he's dead. The show moved on and got to its finale without him. More than that, Sheridan has made the most of the greater "Yellowstone" universe he established by not only developing prequels such as "1883" and "1923" but spin-offs as well.

First and foremost is "Dutton Ranch," which is getting a Season 2. What happens beyond that remains to be seen, but its protagonists Beth Dutton (Reilly) and Rip Wheeler (Cole Hauser) have effectively picked up where John Dutton left off. There's also "Marshals," which has brought Luke Grimes' Kayce Dutton to network TV, resulting in a big hit on CBS. So, even without Costner, the "Yellowstone" franchise has thrived. It wasn't a happy marriage or a happy divorce, but the dust settled, and everyone figured out a path forward.

#3511. The Crow Star Bill Skarsgård Knows Exactly What Went Wrong With The Remake

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

The world waited 30 years for a remake of "The Crow," and to say it wasn't worth the wait would be an understatement. Now, that movie's star, Bill Skarsgard, has opened up about the experience. When it comes to what went wrong, Skarsgard has a pretty good idea.

A lot of actors almost played the Crow before Skarsgard got stuck with it, but the movie focuses on soulmates Eric and Shelly who are brutally murdered. Eric is given a chance to save the love of his life and has to traverse the worlds of the living and the dead in search of revenge. Rupert Sanders ("Snow White and the Huntsman") wound up in the director's chair.

That partnership wasn't fruitful. "The Crow" was dubbed a "dull, lifeless, meaningless remake" by /Film at the time. It also wasn't a success commercially. On a recent episode of the "Happy Sad Confused" podcast, Skarsgard reflected on the 2024 movie's failure. What it really comes down to is a rush job that went into production without a finished script:

"I think the lesson was that I'm not signing on to anything without a finished script. But it's surprising how common it is that something gets green-lit and then you're struggling with finishing the script because the dates are already set and the studio's already locked everything in motion. And it's like, 'Oh, the script needed...'"

There is a long dark history behind "The Crow" franchise, most notably the death of the original movie's star Brandon Lee towards the end of production. To state the obvious, making a bad movie isn't anywhere near on that level, but there is something to be said for this seeming doomed from the outset.

"That was something that Rupert [Sanders] and I just struggled with," Bill Skarsgard added. "We were like, 'Okay, the first script came in two months before we started to shoot.' It was an insanely rushed process in that regard. But I don't regret any of the roles that I've done. And I think they could be good experiences; they could be bad experiences. But how you learn from them is really what it's about."

Hollywood had been attempting to remake "The Crow" for years before it finally happened. Many actors and directors came and went over the years. Nothing materialized. "Aquaman" himself Jason Momoa got very, very close to making it back in 2018. But days before filming was set to begin, it all fell apart. "The Crow" remake was dead again as both Momoa and director Corin Hardy exited.

It never totally died though and, eventually, it came around to Bill Skarsgard. On paper, he was a good fit for the role. But you can only polish a turd so well and, if the script is a turd, he can only do so much.

"The Crow" remake bombed at the box office, pulling in just $24 million worldwide against terrible reviews. At the very least, Skarsgard walked away with an important lesson and doesn't have any regrets. He's just very unlikely to sign on for a potential franchise role again if the script isn't airtight.

You can grab "The Crow" on Blu-ray or DVD from Amazon.

For over 20 years now, the 2003 Mike Myers version of The Cat In The Hat has been the only version of the classic Dr. Seuss book to watch. However, this past weekend, it got the animation treatment, and it’s a blast of an adaptation. I even have an idea for a spinoff, and I ran it by some of the cast. SPOILERS ahead!

Look, I like The Cat, especially because he’s voiced by Bill Hader years after he played the character on SNL. But to me, the real highlight of the film are The Things. In my opinion, they are like much more likeable Minions, and the movie even explores what can happen to one when they get villainous. As we learn at the end of The Cat In The Hat, the reason why Thing 2 was missing is that he became The Something due to overusing the Go-Backer device. Oh, and of course there’s that meta line where The Cat tells The Things to wait for their own movie.

The Things are pretty mysterious characters, but I thought The Cat in the Hat did an excellent job of making them so fun and intriguing. I think it would be so much fun to see them on their own adventure after this movie earned a thumbs-up with audiences through an “A” CinemaScore. Though it’ll have to earn more money at the box office after Godzilla Minus Zero won the weekend.

When CinemaBlend spoke to the cast of The Cat In The Hat, I brought up the topic of a Things spinoff. Here’s what Abbott Elementary’s Quinta Brunson, a.k.a. Sherrie from HR in the movie, had to say:

I wanna learn everything about them. This movie opening the crate, so to speak, on The Thing world, made me wanna know way more. I still have a lot of questions. Like, are they related? Are they from a planet? Is there offspring? Do they fall in love? Do they get married? I have a lot of questions. Why are they numbered? Do they have names beyond the numbers?

I love all these questions she has about The Things, because I had many of them myself. The Things have always been a memorable part of The Cat In The Hat book, but it would be so fun for a spinoff to explore who they are without The Cat. Here’s what Mr. Hoogeboom voice actor Giancarlo Esposito added:

I'm fascinated by The Things. I think they're on some advanced level of intellectual and emotional feeling. I just think that they're simpler, and somehow they communicate in a way that's clearer than any words could ever get.

I feel like a lot of kids are going to start learning Thinglish as is, and I wanted my own Thing plushy the moment I finished the movie. I even brought it up to the writer/directors Erica Rivinoja and Alessandro Carloni. Here’s what Carloni had to say about my idea:

If we're so lucky that the audience wants more of the characters we created, that would be very flattering. Give them what they want.

We’ll have to wait and see if this becomes a reality! For now, you can watch The Cat In The Hat only in theaters.

#3509. Sydney Sweeney Delivered One Of Her Best Performances In A Beloved HBO Miniseries

Most will know Sydney Sweeney for her performance as Cassandra "Cassie" Howard in "Euphoria" and for starring in Paul Feig's excellent wicked thriller "The Housemaid." Many will likely also be aware of her box office smash hit rom-com "Anyone But You" co-starring Glen Powell. But Sweeney is a deceptively diverse actor who has delivered some excellent performances over the last decade, as evidenced by her role in the HBO miniseries "Sharp Objects."

This eight-episode psychological thriller series is based on a novel by Gillian Flynn, who's best-known for having written "Gone Girl" (the 2014 David Fincher-helmed film adaptation of which saw the true crime trend coming well in advance). But four years after the "Seven" director put his spin on Flynn's material, "Buffy the Vampire Slayer" alum Marti Noxon took a shot at it with "Sharp Objects."

Noxon's adaptation of Flynn's 2006 novel took the form of a 2018 HBO miniseries starring Amy Adams as an alcoholic crime reporter who returns to her hometown to look into the murders of two young girls. There, she's forced to reckon with her past trauma. Sweeney appears in the show as a similarly troubled teen who meets Adams' character during her stay in a psychiatric hospital. It's one of the actor's best yet most overlooked performances.

Sydney Sweeney has had her share of hits, but she must also be used to some of her best work going overlooked. Indeed, Sweeney's 2025 film "Americana" was completely ignored at the box office and her psychological drama "Clementine" came and went without much fanfare amidst the 2020 COVID-19 lockdowns. But while it was nowhere near the cultural phenomenon that "Euphoria" was at the height of its success, "Sharp Objects" did receive widespread praise upon its debut in 2018, earning eight Emmy award nominations and garnering Sweeney significant attention for her portrayal of psychiatric patient Alice.

Alice shares a self-harm problem with Amy Adams' Camille Preaker — who, after returning to her hometown of Wind Gap, Missouri, finds herself reflecting on her time in treatment. In these flashbacks, we see her meeting Alice, who handles her own issues by retreating into her iPod. The pair formed a bond during their time in the facility, and it seems Sweeney managed to impress "Sharp Objects" director Jean-Marc Vallée while filming her scenes as well.

As the actor once told Harper's Bazaar, "[Vallée] kept bringing me back more and more for different scenes, and he'd add me in here and there, so really, he and I were able to build my character together." It seems that was a result of Sweeney's dedication to the role, which, as she told the outlet, involved going to hospitals "where there were patients that self-harmed" and spending time with them. Equally impressive was the fact that, as she previously told Nylon, she would film her "Sharp Objects" scenes on weekends before getting on a red-eye flight to Portland to film her scenes for Netflix's "Everything Sucks!" Both ended up being two of Sydney Sweeney's best projects.

"Sharp Objects" was met with critical praise upon its 2018 debut, earning an impressive 92% "certified fresh" rating on Rotten Tomatoes and garnering Sydney Sweeney attention for her portrayal of Alice. 2018 was, of course, the year before "Euphoria" began airing on HBO. As such, Sweeney had yet to break through with her portrayal of Cassie Howard. But with "Everything Sucks!," a role on Season 2 of "The Handmaid's Tale," and her appearance in "Sharp Objects," she had managed to build some serious momentum going into the show, ultimately paving the way to her becoming a household name.

"Sharp Objects," in particular, garnered praise from critics. Writing for Rolling Stone, Alan Sepinwall highlighted Sweeney's performance in what he referred to as a "versatile, era-spanning year" for the actor. Sepinwall added that both she and fellow "Sharp Objects" actor Eliza Scanlen were "names to watch," which turned out to be a particularly prescient observation. Years later, in 2023, Frank Bruni looked back on Sweeney's ascension in a piece for The New York Times, mentioning her appearance in "Sharp Objects" and noting how it had helped her become "prestige TV royalty."

Sadly, Alice isn't typically mentioned as one of Sweeney's best roles, but her quietly powerful performance was proof, even before she debuted as Cassie, that she was a versatile actor capable of nuanced portrayals. She'd prove as much once again in 2019 when she played the title role in the nerve-wracking dramatic thriller "Reality," which is well worth a watch in its own right. But if you missed "Sharp Objects" back in 2018, give it a go on HBO Max.

Amazon has dropped the Bose Smart Ultra Soundbar to $649 from its usual $999, taking $350 off and bringing it to the lowest price we've seen so far, according to price trackers. #3507. Nobody Said The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Was This Funny

Though I’ve never played The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time until now, I’ve heard people sing its praises for years. Mostly, this revolved around its impossibly high score of 99 on Metacritic, its influential open world and combat design, and its memorable dungeons. But none of those ardent fans bothered to tell me that this classic game has some genuinely hilarious moments. Because the game was originally released 28 years ago, a spoiler-free experience is pretty much off the table for me. But the goofs and gags? Those are all 100% fresh.

I love a zingy insult or quip as much as anybody else, but some of the best video game humor leans into the unique qualities of the medium. These gags go beyond writing to incorporate at least some element of interaction — or a conspicuous lack thereof. An early example of this in Ocarina of Time comes when you show a message in a bottle to King Zora, which reveals his daughter is currently stranded inside the massive fish Jabu-Jabu. The grateful king moves aside to allow you access to the entrance of the fish’s belly — very, very slowly. No button-mashing through this one. Just like you would for a real-life monarch (or older person), you must patiently wait for the scooting to be done. With each incremental booty-shuffle, he makes a little noise that sounds like “moo–ee.”

Once you venture inside the giant fish, Princess Ruto must be carried everywhere by Link, making it impossible for you to use your sword or shield while holding her on your shoulders and moving from room to room. Thankfully, you can use Ruto as a literal dead weight to press down switches to open doors. Better still, you can toss her at enemies like a rock, and she won’t take any damage. (She will complain about it, though.)

Later in the game, you‘re tasked with rescuing nine Gorons from the Fire Temple. Some of them will give you a small morsel of information about how to proceed through the dungeon. Others will simply wish you well. Either way, once freed from their cells, a lilting, cheerful flute ditty plays as they prance away with the dumbest possible expressions on their faces — leaving a stone-faced Link to continue grinding his way through the dungeon. This happens nine times in the Fire Temple alone. Ocarina repeats the bit as you’re freeing the four construction workers in the Gerudo Fortress, and it’s somehow even funnier the 13th time you see it.

I’m not the only one discovering the humor of this classic game for the first time. Folks on social media are gleefully posting about Moblin butts, the sphincter-like doors inside Jabu-Jabu’s dungeon, and the unique experience of discovering a cow in Link’s treehouse. Others are making their own fun, by sequence-breaking the game and creating the abomination that is tween Link, or playing "We Are Charlie Kirk" to the frogs near Zora’s Domain. Come for the generational video game experience, stay for the sweet, sweet memes.

The stunning adventure makes great use of capable hardware

It’s not just Ocarina, all of the Zelda games are deeply silly. It’s one of their defining features. And one of the biggest issues with the BotW/TotK was that the Mii-based character generator they used to quickly iterate NPC designs resulted in fewer ridiculously weird guys. Like in your average Zelda game, every NPC is typically a very weird little guy.

#3506. James Gunn's DC Universe Is Being 'Dismantled' As DC Studios Prepares Another Reset (Report)

These DC reboots are starting to become a bit of a tradition. In the wake of James Gunn and Peter Safran "stepping down" as DC Studios co-heads, it seems the new guard is ready to tear down almost their entire cinematic project. At least, according to a new report.

Puck's Matthew Belloni claims to have heard that "plans are already afoot" for new DC Studios head Jeremy Latcham — who steps into the role of president and chief creative officer of DC Studios as of December 1, 2026 — to scrap almost everything Gunn and Safran had planned post-"Man of Tomorrow," "The Batman: Part II," and an unnamed HBO series. As Belloni put it, "So DC goes back into reboot mode ... again."

This is the second major reset for DC's cinematic enterprise (third if you count the pre and post-Walter Hamada era), and it frankly seems like a dire state of affairs. When Gunn and Safran were brought in to head up the newly-christened DC Studios back in 2022, they had grand plans to revive the franchise following a disappointing end to the DC Extended Universe or "Snyderverse." This was supposed to be the moment DC turned things around and finally matched Marvel's cinematic success with an ambitious shared universe. Now, it's all come to a premature end as Skydance CEO David Ellison (who now oversees the newly merged Paramount and Warner Bros.) seemingly prepares to take a wrecking ball to Gunn and Safran's still fledgling DC Universe.

In his article, Matthew Belloni noted how James Gunn and Peter Safran reported to the Warner Bros. Discovery CEO, a post previously held by David Zaslav. The erstwhile head of Warners seemed perfectly happy to let his newly appointed DC Studios co-heads take full creative control. But, as Belloni noted, "Maybe it was too much freedom... hence 'Supergirl.'"

This is, of course, a reference to the box office flop that was this year's "Supergirl," a solo outing for Milly Alcock's Kara Zor-El that brought in just $126.5 million at the box office against a $170 million budget. And while /Film's own "Supergirl" review argued the movie has an aspirational and uplifting message and is nowhere near as bad as its box office returns may suggest, Belloni opined that David Ellison no doubt viewed the failure of "Supergirl" as a result of Gunn and Safran being given too much creative power. Hence, that simply won't be the case with Ellison now in charge.

This also means that while Jeremy Latcham is replacing the former DC Studios co-bosses, he will have nowhere near as much freedom and instead report only to Skydance studio heads Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein. Depending on how you felt about Gunn's creative decisions, then, this is either a good or disappointing development. But even if you like the idea of Ellison and his studio heads calling the shots and keeping DC on a tight leash, none of this bodes well for the brand's cinematic fortunes moving forward — especially if Ellison and co. really do intend to discard Gunn's entire DC roadmap and start from scratch.

When James Gunn and Peter Safran were appointed co-heads of DC Studios, the franchise desperately needed a hard reset. A string of flops in 2023, which included the box office bomb of superheroic proportions that was "The Flash" (a movie which, as it happens, Gunn once called "probably one of the greatest superhero movies ever made"), marked an ignoble end for the DC Extended Universe, and it was Gunn's job to reset, regroup, and revitalize the entire thing. Instead, he opted for a soft reboot that retained several elements of the DCEU. Even at the time, it seemed misguided, and it feels like all the more of a misstep in hindsight.

Now, David Ellison and his executives are, according to Puck, rebooting the entire thing. But it seems like it's all too late. Audiences were never going to be won over by animated "Creature Commandos" series or a potential Mister Miracle animated show. By all means, take a few risks, but maybe save them for after DC has regained some respect among mainstream viewers. Instead, we're at a point where the whole thing is being scrapped yet again, and most people simply do not care about these behind the scenes developments. They just want good movies (which, at this point, have been in short supply).

As Matthew Belloni observed in his report, the last decade has really "only solidified Kevin Feige's run at Marvel [Studios] as all the more remarkable" when compared to DC's struggles. Of course, with Jeremy Latcham having spent many years as a Marvel Studios producer, there's a chance he might turn things around. But by now, audiences are surely tired of having to keep up with these reboots, soft or otherwise.

#3505. DC Studios' Biggest Superhero Movie Priorities After James Gunn's Exit, Explained

The DC Universe on film is once again under new management, as Warner Bros.' new parent company Skydance has replaced DC Studios co-presidents James Gunn and Peter Safran with Marvel Studios' alum Jeremy Latcham. The reasons for Gunn and Safran's exit are still under scrutiny, but it seems inevitable that whatever plans they had for DC are now going to shift.

According to reporting by The Wrap, Skydance CEO David Ellison is pushing Latcham to focus on DC's A-list characters and get a "Justice League" movie out "as soon as possible." The Wrap adds that even "modestly-known" DC heroes like Supergirl won't be getting the greenlight for now. (The poor box office of "Supergirl" didn't help her specific case.)

One hypothesis for Gunn and Safran's departure, which looks more plausible in light of this reporting, is that they weren't focusing enough on those A-list DC characters. Sure, they started with Superman, but DCU Batman and Wonder Woman movies never moved past development prior to their departure. Making "Clayface," a movie about a B-list Batman villain, before introducing Batman himself is one of those decisions that would be ridiculous to imagine, except it actually happened. It's also a meme among DC fans that Gunn's DCU was frontloading Rick Flag Sr. (Frank Grillo) yet hadn't even introduced the full DC Trinity yet.

But leopards can't change their spots. Gunn's passion for superheroes has always been reinventing C-list characters. Directing for Marvel Studios, he made the Guardians of the Galaxy into household names, and across those movies, it's clear the character he loved most was the biggest oddball among oddballs, Rocket Racoon (Bradley Cooper). He first came to DC directing "The Suicide Squad," and he even packed "Superman" with more obscure DC heroes like Metamorpho (Anthony Carrigan) and Mister Terrific (Edi Gathegi).

In an irony worthy of Alanis Morissette, it appears James Gunn's DCU was finally getting to those A-list characters that David Ellison wants spotlighted. "Lanterns" introduced John Stewart (Aaron Pierre) as Green Lantern, who will be returning in "Superman" sequel "Man of Tomorrow." It's also practically an open secret that Adria Arjona is playing Wonder Woman in "Man of Tomorrow." New reporting suggests that Gunn had also begun writing his third "Superman" movie and was considering tweaking it to a Justice League movie.

Now, I've speculated in the past that if/when Gunn got to the Justice League, he would be basing it on the 1980s comic run "Justice League International" by J.M. DeMatteis, Kevin Maguire and Keith Giffen. That run is basically the blueprint for every James Gunn superhero movie, as it took C-List characters (Booster Gold, Blue Beetle, Guy Gardner Green Lantern, Fire and Ice, etc.) and made their adventures more of a workplace comedy. The JLI was headed up by businessman Maxwell Lord, who appears in "Superman" (played by Sean Gunn) sponsoring the proto Justice League.

But I wouldn't expect that now. DC Studios' "Justice League" movie will surely feature the A-listers: Superman, Batman, Wonder Woman, Green Lantern, The Flash, and Aquaman. By largely holding off on those characters, Gunn and Safran may have given Jeremy Latcham more leeway to mold the DCU's headliners.

Now, it's still unclear if DC Studios will do a full continuity reboot or merely a creative pivot. If the latter, it's plausible Corenswet's Superman stays. If Adria Arjona is indeed playing Wonder Woman, a swift recast would probably be awkward, too.

"Lanterns" was also a huge hit for HBO, and TheWrap explicitly names Green Lantern as one of the A-List characters DC Studios is prioritizing. Does that mean Pierre's John Stewart will get a movie?

As for Batman, DC Studios has been in a tight bind with their cash cow the last half-decade. Matt Reeves' "The Batman," commissioned by the previous regime, hit theaters in March 2022, months before James Gunn and Peter Safran's hiring. Gunn was extremely accommodating to Reeves, even as "The Batman Part II" faced numerous scheduling delays. (Reeves has reportedly been dealing with a family crisis, hence him stepping away from shooting "The Batman Part II" as Steven Soderbergh takes over as a stand-in.)

I'm personally grateful we're seeing "The Batman Part II" finished and on Reeves' terms. But the sharper business move would've been to reboot or make Robert Pattinson's Batman part of the DCU. Gunn did neither, only announcing a "Batman" movie, "The Brave and the Bold" in 2023 that never really got rolling. I'd say, now, though, there's a better than likely chance that Reeves and Pattinson's "Batman" series ends with "Part II" to clear the way for a DCU Batman.

So what about the other in-development projects at DC that spotlighted smaller characters, i.e. "Swamp Thing" and the Bane & Deathstroke team-up movie? I think it's a fair bet those are dead. The announced "Teen Titans" movie is a toss-up — the 2003 "Teen Titans" cartoon remains a cultural touchstone for younger millennials and older Gen Zers, but the team might still fit into the "modestly known" box like Supergirl apparently does.

For better or worse, DC fans should expect to see the Justice League back onscreen sooner rather than later.

#3504. The Top 10 Movies Right Now, According to Streaming Data

The most streamed movie in October was Steven Spielberg's Disclosure Day, but half of the month's top ten is made up of season-appropriate horror movies. This year's two most successful horror movies, Backrooms and Obsession, made the list; so did a classic (Halloween from 1978) and an art movie about the genre that Halloween created,Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Perfect double feature. Rounding out the list is the all-around-excellent Hokum. If you're not into horror, you might like Golden Arm, a comedy that refused to die, star-studded comedy The Invite, or ultimate crowd-pleaser Project Hail Mary.

Legendary director Steven Spielberg returns to the extraterrestrials he loves so much with a thriller that's a spiritual sequel to Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Disclosure Day details the events that lead up to the revelation that aliens are among us. Josh O’Connor plays Dr. Daniel Kellner, a cybersecurity expert for a government contractor who uncovers explosive evidence that his employers would kill to keep secret. Meanwhile, a TV meteorologist (Emily Blunt) begins speaking in an alien language. It all sets the stage for a series of set pieces and chases leading to the biggest revelation in human history. Stream Disclosure Day on Peacock.

Director Kane Parsons' analog horror breakthrough is proof that atmosphere, mood, and a fascinating story is scarier than CGI monsters every time. Based on the viral YouTube series of the same name, Backrooms tells the story of Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a store owner who discovers a labyrinthian liminal space in his furniture shop's basement. Renate Reinsve plays his therapist, who goes downstairs for a visit and does not find it easy to return. A hit with critics—Backrooms is sitting at 86% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes—and audiences, Backrooms is a delicious Halloween treat for horror fans. Stream Backrooms on HBO Max.

Director Curry Barker is still in his 20s, but his debut theatrical feature is the kind of horror film that changes the entire genre. Obsession is a classic "be careful what you wish for" story that feels fresh thanks to its talented young cast, unpredictable plot, and careful pace. Michael Johnston plays a young man too scared to tell his crush how he feels, so he wishes she'd fall in love with him instead. The result is a nightmare embodied by Inde Navarrette, whose portrayal of the villain/victim is at once harrowing, terrifying, and heartbreaking. Obsession is the best horror movie I've seen in years. Stream Obsession on Peacock.

This comedy-drama from A24 is packed with heavy-hitting actors. Olivia Wilde, who also directed the film, plays Angela, and Seth Rogen plays her husband, Joe. With the straight-laced couple's marriage on thin ice, Angela and Joe invite their more, uh, open-minded neighbors Piña, played by Penélope Cruz, and Hawk, played by Edward Norton, over for dinner. The evening unravels in hilarious ways, changing everyone's life. If you're a fan of smart, honest comedy, you will really like The Invite. Stream The Invite on HBO Max.

With Hokum, Director Damian McCarthy (Oddity, Caveat) carefully builds a suffocatingly creepy story around Adam Scott's portrayal of Ohm Bauman, a celebrity novelist and unmitigated jerk who travels to the isolated Bilberry Woods Hotel in Ireland to scatter the ashes of his parents and finish his book. Bauman soon learns that the lore of the hotel includes an ancient witch who feeds her victims to the creatures of hell, and she might be more than just a local legend. Hokum is a horror movie for fans of dreadful atmosphere and careful pacing instead of gore or jump-scares. Stream Hokum on Hulu.

With a title like this, it's not going to be a normal movie. Director Jane Schoenbrun’s I Saw the TV Glow and We're All Going to the World's Fair are two of the most fascinating, fiercely original horror movies of the last decade, and their third film follows in those strange footfalls. While it's technically a meta re-imagining of the slasher genre, Miasma goes way deeper than Scream ever could. It's a postmodern exploration of why the slasher genre's cocktail of sex, death, and subversion casts such a strong spell on interesting, weird people. Definitely see this movie. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

When Golden Arm was released in 2021, not many people paid attention—with the pandemic in full swing, people didn't seem to have room for a quirky, indie comedy about a woman's quest to win the ladies' arm-wrestling championship—but it's a new age, and you should stream Golden Arm. It's sitting on a perfect score at Rotten Tomatoes, the movie's stars, Mary Holland and Betsy Sodaro, are charming and hilarious, and you can catch Golden Arm on Fandango, a free streaming service. What's not to love? Stream Golden Arm on Fandango or Prime Video.

In this crowd-pleasing sci-fi flick, Ryan Gosling stars as Ryland Grace, a middle school science teacher who is blasted into the firmament in a last-ditch effort to save the world. Grace is the only person on Earth who might know how to protect the sun from a cosmic infection that threatens all life, but he's definitely not an astronaut and doesn't see himself as a hero either. Will he rise to the occasion and learn something about his inner strength and resilience while saving us all from death? My money is on, "yeah, probably." Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+, Prime Video, and Philo.

Hundreds of slasher movies have been released since Halloween came out in 1978, but none have surpassed the original. Michael Myers' expressionless visage and the synthesizer theme have become universally recognized cultural signifiers for "horror movie," and every shot in Halloween has been stolen countless times, but the movie is so good, it's still scary. Watch or re-watch Halloween now! Stream Halloween on Philo, AMC+, and Prime Video.

Directed by and starring Ben Affleck, Animals is a thriller that tells the story of Mark Kimball, a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped and held for ransom. Having spent every dime on his outsider campaign, Kimball is forced to turn to extreme methods to guarantee his son's safe return, even if it conflicts with his public persona as a man of the people. Animals is a taut, expertly directed movie that should more than satisfy fans of political thrillers. Stream Animals on Netflix.
