#3489. 4 Upcoming Fantasy RPGs Better Than Waiting for a New Dragon Age

The fire’s burning low. The road ahead looks grim. The companion who has spent half your journey needling you clearly has something on their mind, and you’re one or two correct dialogue choices away from getting them to spill. You pick a reply. You feel it land. Then somebody makes a joke about cheese, and the tension breaks.

This is one of the many things the Dragon Age franchise does well. In this series, from Origins to Veilguard, you gather a party of real-feeling companions and grapple with party management. These are also tactical games — games where you need to pause your combat encounters, point at the biggest threat, and hope against hope that your mage remembers she’s standing in a pool of fire. They’re political games, full of nobles and templars quibbling about the fates of their respective territories and teams. And they’re games where consequences stick. A choice you made in a prologue will come back to bite you hours (or entire games) later, usually while you’re just minding your own business collecting elfroot for a salve.

It may be unlikely that we’ll see a new Dragon Age title anytime soon. (Earlier this month, former Dragon Age writer David Gaider said that “the golden days are over.”) Yet there are still campfires worth stopping at. If you miss that feeling of saving Thedas by day and hanging out with your party of oddball companions by night, check out these four upcoming RPGs. Consider this your recruitment screen.

You can never keep every companion happy in Dragon Age. Solasta 2 eases you into this never-ending quest for balance by starting you off with your family. You lead the Colwall siblings, orphans from a household tied to a religious order sworn against an evil called Shadwyn. Soon, the siblings travel to a new continent, where the opening city, Caer Mar, comes with rebels, factions, and plenty of trouble.

If you liked pausing Dragon Age to plan every fight, this turn-based tactical RPG (which has been in Steam Early Access since March 2026) offers plenty of occasions to plan. Positioning, line of sight, and high ground decide most battles, and D&D fans will appreciate the chance to use spells like Magic Missile and Shatter to deal damage. Between fights, as you trek your way across Neokos, your role-playing choices will influence your standing with the world’s factions — which, in turn, changes how the world responds to you. Cross the wrong faction, and the merchants may stop selling you the good stuff.

Solasta 2’s Early Access only covers part of Act 1 and comes with a low level cap — you can only get to level 4 at this time. Developer Tactical Adventures says it intends to stay in Early Access for about a year, and 1.0 will raise the cap to 10 and finish the main questline. While you wait, you can play the first game, Solasta: Crown of the Magister. It’s a crunchier D&D experience, so brush up on your spell strategy before you boot it up.

What if the Dragon Age: Origins prologue cast you as a vagrant with a bad attitude and no plan? In Outward 2, you play an ordinary person in Aurai, a dangerous world where most people never leave their hometown walls. You’ll choose one of three starting scenarios — a miner in the northern mountains of Tramontane, a homeowner in the underground city of Haboob, or a vagrant in Simeon’s Bastion. Then, you’ll get a background and personality traits like Hoarder, Gourmet, or Lone Wolf that change your dialogue, starting gear, and aptitudes.

Surviving Aurai will take more than a sword. Hunger, thirst, exhaustion, and weather threaten you as much as the world’s creatures do…and you don’t get mounts or fast travel to give you a quick way out of a tight bind. This game is more committed to realism (read: suffering) than your usual RPG. Armor weight will change how fast you move. If you want to stay mobile during a fight, you’ll need to drop your backpack. You can wield a different weapon in each hand, like a sword and shield, dual axes, or a mace and pistol, and trainers teach skills for a fee. But you can’t just be focused on survival: Your choices will pull you toward a faction that will shape your story. Will you join a budding mercenary company, a society of historians, or a humanitarian mission? What’ll happen after you do?

Outward 2 will support online and split-screen co-op, which means your companions can also be your IRL friends. While you wait for this title, play the first Outward if you like your fantasy with a side of hypothermia. Regardless, bring a friend. And a warm cloak, because the seasons in Aurai show no mercy.

Release date: Feb. 23, 2027 (Feb. 18 with the Premium Edition)

Where to play: PS5, Windows PC, Xbox Series X

This game’s not out yet, but Albion already has opinions about you. Here, you play as the hero of Briar Hill, “an ordinary person made extraordinary by fate.” From there, it’s up to you to decide what kind of hero you’ll be. Your built-in rival is Isabel, played by Hayley Atwell, a driven, powerful hero on a quest to right a tragic injustice. She opposes you and Humphry, her former guardian. With interpersonal conflict this charged, who needs a world to save?

Dragon Age taught us that the world should remember what you did, and Albion takes the lesson seriously. Your reputation affects how the world’s 1,000+ handcrafted NPCs treat you. That reputation can reshape the world around you and grow your power. Beyond reputation, you can romance villagers, have children with them, and start your own cozy life while chaos reigns above you.

Dragon Age blends dark subject matter with humor very well. Fable seems ready to carry on that particular mission. One of its spells, “Befowl,” turns enemies into chickens (and undead enemies into undead chickens, naturally). Isabel has an injustice to right and you’re standing in her way, so keep that chicken spell handy.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

If you ever wished you could replay your first Dragon Age campaign and fix just one decision, Clockwork Revolution might be your invitation to do just that. Dragon Age gave us choices that follow you from game to game. InXile’s first-person RPG explicitly lets you rewrite your own decisions to answer the question: Would anything change if you could reverse something from your past?

You play Morgan Vanette, a customizable member of the Rotten Row Hooligans gang in Avalon, a steampunk city whose factions run from the slums to the golden mansions. The villain, Lady Ironwood, already rules Avalon, and she’s been using time travel to keep it that way. Vanette and a band of allies set out to turn back the clock and right her wrongs.

Sounds standard, right? The twist, here, is how you go about doing that. You’ll use a device called the Chronometer to change key moments in the past. This sounds excellent in terms of instant gratification, but the effects of those changes threaten to ripple outward. The people closest to you feel it first, and the crew you return to after time shenanigans may differ from the one you left. Your allies, Ulysses, Nazim, Erasmus, Hazel, and Anne, have lives of their own, with stories that don’t revolve around you. If you enjoy political chess, Lady Ironwood gives you a rival to follow. A flying automaton named Prentice will guide you through the branching realities. You’ll build a character with attributes, skills, and gear, hack hostile automatons, and use an ability called Displace to toss an explosive barrel at enemies. Whatever you do, just change the past carefully, because your crew will remember.

#3488. The Cat In The Hat Is Another Box Office Flop Warner Bros. Can't Afford

Another weekend, another bad result for Warner Bros. "The Cat in the Hat" looked like it could help get Warner Bros. back on track at the box office. Instead? It became the latest in a string of flops that has defined the studio's year. Family-friendly movies have been very safe bets in recent years, and on paper, Dr. Seuss is very good intellectual property to exploit for a PG animated movie. But this didn't pan out as anyone had hoped.

Director Erica Rivinoja's "The Cat in the Hat" opened to a very disappointing $20 million domestically. It also pulled in just $10 million internationally, giving it a soft $30 million global start. That was only good enough for the number two spot, since "Godzilla Minus Zero" ruled the box office with a $30.5 million opening. Normally, it would be much safer to bet on the PG family movie over the R-rated Japanese monster movie. But this wasn't a normal situation, and instead, the animated movie was left fighting for scraps, relatively speaking.

The new movie sees the title character (voiced by "SNL" alum Bill Hader) take on his toughest assignment yet for the I.I.I.I. (Institute for the Institution of Imagination and Inspiration, LLC): to cheer up Gabby and Sebastian, a pair of siblings struggling with their move to a new town. It carries a reported budget in the $90 million range.

This major disappointment comes mere weeks after the Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount merger was made official, with the mega-corporation Skydance now ruling over both studios. That corporation is lousy with debt and it needs Warner Bros. to deliver. Unfortunately for CEO David Ellison and his new film chiefs, they're walking into a messy situation. They've got a ship to right.

The storied movie studio had a stellar year in 2025, with massive hits like "Sinners" and "F1" to its name. Warner Bros. set a huge record that year with six movies in a row opening to at least $40 million, but 2026 has not been nearly as kind.

Skydance inherited a string of massive flops from the Warner Bros. deal, with its 2027 slate also looking a bit uneven. Things could get worse before they get better, as evidenced by the performance of "The Cat in the Hat." Granted, the year should end on a high note as "Dune: Part 3" is just around the corner, but even that can't make up for everything that preceded it.

A very rough rule of thumb for theatrical success has always been a movie making 2.5 times its budget, given that theaters keep around half of all money from ticket sales. So just how bad has the year been for Warner Bros? The studio's bombs/disappointments include "The Bride!" ($90 million budget / $24 million worldwide haul), "They Will Kill You" ($10 million budget / $19 million worldwide), "Mortal Kombat II" ($80 million budget / $129 million worldwide), "Supergirl" ($170 million budget / $126 million worldwide), "The End of Oak Street" ($90 million budget / $121 million worldwide), "Practical Magic 2" ($75 million budget / $106 million worldwide), and "Digger" ($180 million budget / $50 million worldwide).

Yikes. Tom Cruise's "Digger" alone will lose as much as $250 million. Hits like "Wuthering Heights" and "Clayface," encouraging though they may be, can't come close to making up for losses that pile up for would-be blockbusters like "Supergirl." Unfortunately, this Dr. Seuss adaptation now joins this ever-growing list of crushing disappointments. Skydance and the new team has their work cut out for them.

#3486. Jennifer Lawrence's R-Rated Spy Movie Is One Of HBO Max's Biggest Streaming Hits

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

An R-rated spy thriller starring Jennifer Lawrence is finding new life on HBO Max. The Oscar-winner's 2018 movie "Red Sparrow" has become one of the streamer's biggest hit movies, nearly a decade after its original release.

Directed by Francis Lawrence, who had previously worked with Jennifer Lawrence on "The Hunger Games" movies, "Red Sparrow" is currently the eighth-biggest movie on HBO Max right now, per FlixPatrol. It sits just above "The Wolverine" and just below "The First Purge." Olivia Wilde's comedy "The Invite" is still HBO Max's biggest streaming hit, but the fact that an eight-year-old thriller is right up there with the streamer's current biggest movies is meaningful.

"Red Sparrow" sees Lawrence play a deadly Russian spy. The film centers on Dominika (Lawrence), a former ballerina forced to enter Sparrow School, a government program that thrusts her into a treacherous espionage game. She emerges as a lethal agent, but is trapped in a world she desperately wants to escape. Joel Edgerton ("Warrior"), Matthias Schoenaerts ("Rust and Bone"), Charlotte Rampling ("Broadchurch"), Mary-Louise Parker ("Weeds"), and Ciarán Hinds ("Rome") also star.

The movie is based on the novel of the same name by Jason Matthews. Before it turned into a Lawrence and Lawrence "Hunger Games" reunion, "The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo" director David Fincher and Rooney Mara were poised to reunite for "Red Sparrow." Darren Aronofsky ("Black Swan") was also set to direct at one point. But after much back and forth with a revolving door of A-list talent coming and going, it became a Lawrence starring vehicle. The results were viewed as underwhelming at the time.

Critics weren't terribly kind to the thriller upon its initial release. It currently holds a not-so-great 45% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes. /Film called "Red Sparrow" an "overlong waste of Jennifer Lawrence's talent" in our review from 2018. It also didn't resonate as well as Fox had hoped it would at the box office at the time.

Against a relatively steep $69 million budget, the movie pulled in $151 million worldwide. It was by no means a hit, especially relative to expectations. Keep in mind that Francis Lawrence and Jennifer Lawrence had a great track record together. "The Hunger Games: Mockingjay — Part 2" ruled the box office just a few years earlier, capping off a multi-billion-dollar run for that franchise. Not to mention that Lawrence was just a handful of years removed from her Oscar win for "Silver Linings Playbook."

Maybe it's because Lawrence remains a big star, with viewers seeking out stuff they haven't seen of hers before. Maybe it's because this sort of action/thriller is the perfect kind of "watch it on the couch" movie. Either way, what was once a disappointment is finding new life all these years later.

You can also grab "Red Sparrow" on 4K, Blu-ray, or DVD from Amazon.

#3485. ‘Victorian Psycho’ Review: Maika Monroe Scares Up a Very Different Kind of Final Girl

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on May 21, 2026 during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Bleecker Street will release the film in theaters Friday, November 13.]

Winifred Notty is the sanest person she knows, or so the heroine (or anti-heroine, depending on how you might see it) of Zachary Wigon’s “Victorian Psycho” is quick to tell anyone who will listen. Or not, as star Maika Monroe delivers that damning and darkly funny insight into Winifred’s soul via a prim voiceover that seems to exist for her own benefit as much as the audience she seems to imagine.

That’s tangled enough, but there’s also this: Winifred doesn’t really know that many people, mostly because just about everyone she’s come across in her life is dead. Still, sane! Ish. Well, it’s not called “Victorian Psycho” for nothing. Related Stories ‘Steps’ Review: A Disposable Fairy Tale Reminds Us That Cinderella Is Someone’s Hated Stepsister Too ‘The Debut’ Trailer: Julianne Moore Goes Full Julianne Moore in Jesse Eisenberg’s Riotously Funny Musical Theater Comedy

Adapted for the screen by novelist Virginia Feito from her own work, the book comes recommended alongside its predecessor, “Mrs. March,” for anyone drawn to entertainment with “psycho” in the title.Beloved scream queen Maika Monroe (“It Follows,” “The Guest,” “Longlegs”) may be switching sides here, offering a twist on who horror fans root for once the blood starts flowing. (Hint: it’s the psycho.)

When we first meet Winifred, the Victorian-era governess is bound for her next assignment to teach the children of Mr. and Mrs. Pounds (Jason Isaacs and a sneaky-great Ruth Wilson, respectively) at their sprawling Yorkshire estate. “This won’t be like the other times,” she tells herself, winking mightily at how all those other times turned out. Our Winifred sports dead eyes and a rictus grin she works so very hard to fix in place. It’s even better when she attempts to imitate those around her, all the better to approximate “being human.”

No question, there’s something very wrong with Winifred. But what? You’ll find out soon enough. Possessed of “a darkness” she cannot shake, Monroe’s Winifred practically vibrates with the need to hold things together. It does not always work for her, but it is nearly always funny, deliciously and dementedly so.

Wigon and Freito don’t balk at the “psycho” promise of their story, as Winifred happily whacks away (often literally) at everyone icky, from gardeners to nurses (Thomasin McKenzie) and, yes, at least one baby. Killing scenes are elegantly, amusingly cut by editors Dustin Chow and Lance Edmands and designed for maximum gasps. Blood flows, then spurts, then pools. Sometimes it gets on Winifred’s face or her collar. She moves on, grimly and happily.

Cinematographer Nico Aguilar brings a similar energy to his work, shooting in and through keyholes, swinging his camera like a clock pendulum, even briefly adapting the perspective of a swallowed (redacted, for spoilers) as it travels into Winifred’s belly. It’s playful and gross, wholly fitting the material. Mostly, it’s so dark and fucked up you can’t help but laugh. OH! Did they do that? Yes, yes they did.

Possessed by the notion that she’s meant to be a part of the Pounds family (who would want to be? these aristocrats are monstrous), Winifred continues to fray. Bloodlusty audiences will be charmed by her go-for-broke attitude (more like go-for-the-throat), plus a steady stream of visual cues as to her current state. Dreams and nightmares merge, she’s haunted by the Pounds’ family mascot of a wild boar (particularly in an ever-morphing tapestry), and she simply can’t stop sneaking into places to stare at people while they sleep.

Clocking in at a tight 90 minutes, some changes to the also-slim book are smart, while others dilute its darkest impulses. Gone is the countdown to a Christmas massacre, which frames the novel; hell, gone is the whole Christmas massacre. Freito’s script leads up to a different sort of celebration, doing away with many of the most colorful supporting characters in the process (Mrs. Fancey, we hardly knew ye!).

That choice isn’t disastrous, although the execution of the big! final! event! is oddly watered down. Here it’s imagined as a battle of Winifred’s wills… but, erm, what wills? The book and the film each offer enough reasons for why our heroine is the way she is, Wigon’s film oddly bisects her spirit by implying she’s not fully on board with all the evil she commits.

For fans of the novel and its wonderfully unrepentant star, this choice might rankle; it’s also odd that Freito would go this route with her own adaptation. “Well, that’s not my ‘Victorian Psycho’ — and she’s not. That’s such a shame because for much of the film, she’s even better. By tempering her impulses and inner monologue, the film ends with less of the giddy gore that makes the rest of it such a dark treat. Dare we say it? We would have loved for this one to go full, ahem, boar.

“Victorian Psycho” premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Bleecker Street will release it in theaters on Friday, September 25.

#3483. PlayStation Officially Cancels Live-service Shooter Fairgames

Sony's latest game cancellation adds to a long list of failed GaaS projects

Sony has canceled Fairgames (aka Fairgame$) three years after the live-service shooter was announced, Bloomberg reported on Tuesday. No one at its developer, Haven Studios, is getting laid off, and instead Haven will support other Sony Interactive Entertainment-owned studios, according to that report.

Farigames recently held a playtest and, according to an internal email reviewed by Bloomberg, feedback from that playtest didn't live up to PlayStation's expectations. "While the test demonstrated strong operational excellence, live ops readiness and community engagement, player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set," executives Sean Decker and John Doyle said in the email. With "challenging market conditions in the PVP shooter genre," Sony decided to cancel the game.

Fairgames reportedly had been reworked multiple times since its 2023 reveal. It would have been the debut game from Haven, which was founded in 2021 by former Assassin's Creed producer and Google Stadia Games and Entertainment head Jade Raymond, who has since left the studio. Haven was acquired by Sony in 2022.

Back in 2022, Sony announced a huge push for live-service games, aiming to release at least 10 by 2026. While games like Helldivers 2 and Gran Turismo 7 have been steady live-service hits, Sony's push has largely failed. Concord is the most notable misfire, as it was actually released before Sony reversed course and shut it down shortly after launch in embarrassing fashion.

A live-service God of War game, a multiplayer The Last of Us game, and many others were canceled before they could see the light of day. PlayStation studios working on live-service games, including London Studios, Firewalk Studios, and Bluepoint Games, were all shut down in recent years. In June, Sony laid off most of the Destiny team at Bungie, as "Destiny 2 fell short of expectations" with players. Recently, Horizon Hunters Gathering was reportedly delayed so it can be rebooted in response to negative player feedback (which sounds not too dissimilar to the Fairgames situation).

#3482. I tested a compact gaming PC the size of two Xbox Series X consoles — and it delivers desktop RTX 5070 power without the noise

The GMKtec Neo-X1 Pro delivers desktop-tier gaming performance and remarkably whisper-quiet acoustics in a compact 14.6-liter chassis. Its soldered mobile CPU and steep SFF price tag keep it from being an automatic purchase for everyone, but if you want high-end living room portability with room to swap your GPU down the road, it’s an impressive machine.

Impressive, near-silent gaming performance

Built-in carrying handles make it easy to move

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The GMKtec Neo-X1 Pro is a desktop gaming PC with a twist. Unlike other large, bulky desktops, it’s remarkably compact with a volume of 14.6 liters, making it even smaller than the HP Victus 15L.

Known for making some of the best mini PCs, the Neo-X1 Pro is GMKtec’s first-ever small form factor (SFF) gaming tower. To get its design this small without overheating, the company used a custom all-in-one liquid cooler paired with a high-end mobile AMD CPU. However, the Neo-X1 Pro still packs in a desktop-grade Nvidia RTX 5070 dedicated GPU.

I’ve been using the Neo-X1 Pro as my daily driver for both work and gaming for the past two months, and it has continued to impress me. From its compact design — complete with carrying handles — to its near-silent performance even under load, this gaming desktop certainly delivers. Just as if you built your own SFF PC, you are paying a premium for its more compact size.

My GMKtec Neo-X1 Pro review will help you decide if this is the best gaming PC for you or if it’s worth going with something with a slightly larger case for less.

2 x USB-A, 1 x USB-C, 1 x 3.5mm audio combo jack (front), 1 x HDMI 2.1, 1 x DisplayPort 1.4, 4 x USB-A, 1 x USB-C, 1 x 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet, 1 x 3.5mm audio jack (rear), 1 x HDMI 2.b, 3 x DisplayPort 2.1b (Nvidia RTX 5060 Ti)

2 x USB-A, 1 x USB-C, 1 x 3.5mm audio combo jack (front), 1 x HDMI 2.1, 1 x DisplayPort 1.4, 4 x USB-A, 1 x USB-C, 1 x 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet, 1 x 3.5mm audio jack (rear), 1 x HDMI 2.1b, 3x DisplayPort 2.1b (Nvidia RTX 5070)

The GMKtec Neo-X1 Pro delivers a stellar PC gaming experience without taking up your entire desk. Games look and run great thanks to its Nvidia RTX 5070 GPU, while the custom all-in-one liquid cooler keeps acoustics so quiet that I often forgot there was a high-powered gaming rig humming right next to my monitor.

At 13.78 × 6.50 × 10.43 inches, the Neo-X1 Pro is an impressively compact gaming PC. In fact, it’s roughly the same size as having two Xbox Series X consoles side by side on your desk with a pair of carrying handles bolted on top.

Inside its well-packed box, you’ll find the PC itself alongside a standard power cord, an HDMI 2.1 cable, and a pair of antennas. Once you unbox the Neo-X1 Pro, all you have to do is screw on those antennas and plug it in to get started.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

On the front of the Neo-X1 Pro, next to its signature green power button, there’s a 3.5mm headphone/microphone combo jack, two USB-A ports, and a USB-C port. I really liked having two full-sized ports up front for the 2.4 GHz USB dongles for my controller and other peripherals.

Around the back, the power receptacle for its 850W SFX power supply sits at the very top alongside the motherboard connections. Here, you get four USB-A ports, a 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet port, a single USB-C port, an HDMI 2.1 port, a DisplayPort 1.4 connection, another set of audio jacks, and the gold connectors for the Wi-Fi antennas. Right underneath them, the Neo-X1 Pro’s RTX 5070 provides a single HDMI 2.1b port along with three DisplayPort 2.1b connections.

You’ll probably want to position the Neo-X1 Pro on the right side of your desk. The left side panel is perforated, giving you a glimpse at its internal components, including the RTX 5070 from Zotac. On the right side of the case, circular cutouts bring cool air in alongside another strip of ventilation holes at the bottom. While you won’t see it when you’re sitting down, I really like how the top of the case features GMKtec’s iconic neon green all the way across.

From the instant I had it set up and powered on, the Neo-X1 Pro surprised me: all I could hear was a faint hum in the background. Even under load while running demanding games, it remained whisper-quiet compared to gaming desktops I’ve built and other pre-builts I’ve tested in the past.

With an AMD Ryzen 9 9955HX3D processor and 64GB of DDR5 memory, my review unit handled my everyday workload — which consists of multiple Chrome windows with dozens of open tabs and light photo editing in GIMP — with ease. Considering the generous system RAM alongside the 12GB of VRAM on the included RTX 5070, the Neo-X1 Pro could easily pull double duty running large local AI models just as comfortably as it plays games.

Despite relying on mobile silicon, the Neo-X1 Pro held its own in our benchmark tests against the HP Omen Max 45L we reviewed recently. While its single-core and multi-core Geekbench scores fell slightly behind the desktop-class 9950X3D inside the Omen Max 45L, it pulled ahead in our SSD speed test (which measures transfer speeds moving a 25GB file). At just over two minutes, the Neo-X1 Pro’s HandBrake encoding time (converting a 4K video file down to 1080p) was also impressive, trailing the massive Omen tower by only 21 seconds.

If you’re looking for a rig that is compact yet potent and don't want the headache of hunting down SFF components or managing tight clearances yourself, the Neo-X1 Pro presents a capable prebuilt alternative to building your own mini-ITX battle station.

Speaking of gaming, the Neo-X1 Pro delivers and then some thanks to its full-size RTX 5070 from Zotac. All of the games I tried looked great and played smoothly, though you’ll likely need to lower the resolution or enable Nvidia’s DLSS if you want to push native 4K or beyond.

To put the Neo-X1 Pro to the test, I downloaded and installed Resident Evil Requiem. Exploring the Wrenwood Hotel as Grace Ashcroft was downright creepy, but navigating the Wrenwood City Streets as Leon showed me what this rig is capable of. From the rain beading off Leon’s leather jacket to the blinding vehicle headlights cutting through the foggy street while fighting off the newly infected, the entire opening sequence looked stunning on my 4K monitor.

In benchmark tests at our lab, the Neo-X1 Pro frequently surpassed triple-digit frame rates at 1080p without DLSS enabled, and even at 4K, Forza Horizon 6 reached 96 fps on High settings. For heavier titles like Black Myth: Wukong, dropping down to Medium settings brought it within striking distance of 60 fps in 4K (51 fps). While you'll need to make occasional graphic tweaks on demanding games, the Neo-X1 Pro handles recent titles at stable frame rates without breaking a sweat.

After running through tests on a standard 4K display, I brought the desktop into my office to see how it handled gaming on the Innocn E49M1R. Even at a massive 5120 × 1440 resolution, performance stayed rock solid in Red Dead Redemption 2 without any visible tearing or stuttering. That said, finding space for the Neo-X1 Pro on a desk alongside a flat, 49-inch super ultrawide monitor is definitely a challenge.

With those two handles on top, moving the Neo-X1 Pro from room to room was an absolute breeze. Whether you want to hook it up to the living room TV for big-screen couch gaming or haul it over to a friend’s place for a weekend session, this SFF PC is well-suited for quick transport. However, I’d be hesitant about carrying it onto a flight given the effort it takes to safely break down and secure its internal components.

The Neo-X1 Pro is a quiet, cool, and capable gaming PC. However, like most small form factor machines, it comes with classic trade-offs: cramped internals that make upgrades tricky, and a noticeable price premium for shrinking everything down.

In order to see what keeps the Neo-X1 Pro running so quietly, I decided to open it up. To do so, I just had to remove two screws on the side panel, and the whole thing slid off as you’d expect with a traditional desktop PC.

Under the hood, you can see the Zotac RTX 5070 running along the bottom, complete with a built-in support bracket to prevent GPU sag over time. Above it sits GMKtec’s custom AIO liquid cooler, which commands the lion's share of the case’s 14.6-liter interior.

Much like the Minisforum G1 Pro I reviewed, you have to work around and partially dismantle the cooling assembly if you want to upgrade the Neo-X1 Pro’s RAM or storage. If you choose to brave the process, you could swap out the pre-installed dual-channel 32GB sticks for two 48GB sticks to reach a whopping 96GB of memory. There is also an unused secondary M.2 NVMe slot, meaning you can configure up to 16TB of high-speed SSD storage overall.

While its CPU is soldered permanently to the motherboard, the Neo-X1 Pro holds one massive advantage over the G1 Pro. Since it relies on a standard rear expansion bracket and ships with an 850W SFX power supply, you can actually upgrade GMKtec’s rig down the line with a standard off-the-shelf GPU — provided the replacement card is under 310 mm (12.2 inches) in length and sticks to a strict dual-slot design.

Given the potent hardware GMKtec packed into the Neo-X1 Pro, you likely won’t need to upgrade anytime soon. Even so, while working inside this dense chassis will be second nature to seasoned SFF builders, beginners will find servicing and upgrading components noticeably daunting.

In the world of desktop PCs, opting for a compact case over a standard mid-tower almost always commands a higher price tag. From specialized SFX power supplies and custom low-profile coolers to the dense chassis engineering itself, small form factor PCs occupy an expensive niche.

Although the base Neo-X1 and its more potent sibling, the Neo-X1 Pro, originally started at $2,099 and $2,899 respectively at launch, their prices have crept up like most electronics as a result of RAMaggedon. The standard Neo-X1 now costs roughly what the Pro originally did, and the Neo-X1 Pro can reach as high as $3,699 at full price (though it is frequently discounted to $3,199).

Even accounting for parts being more expensive across the board, that isn’t pocket change. You could likely assemble a comparable full-sized DIY gaming desktop for less cash, but you would be trading convenience for the cable-routing headaches, tight thermal clearances, and endless compatibility checks that come with building an SFF machine yourself.

The best way to frame the Neo-X1 Pro is to compare it to Valve’s Steam Machine. While Valve’s compact cube targets couch play with modest, fixed internals, the Neo-X1 Pro brings far more graphical muscle and actual hardware modularity to the living room. You are undoubtedly paying a steep premium for its compact 14.6-liter footprint, but in return, you get couch-friendly portability with enough breathing room to upgrade your RAM, storage and even graphics card down the road.

The GMKtec Neo-X1 Pro is a capable, quiet, and compact gaming PC that delivers desktop-class performance in a much smaller footprint than traditional towers. The top-mounted handles make it easy to haul between rooms or take to a friend’s place, while the full-sized desktop RTX 5070 GPU handles modern AAA titles with ease.

While the AMD Ryzen 9 9955HX3D is permanently soldered to the motherboard, it holds its own remarkably well, delivering near-desktop speeds despite its mobile roots. The interior layout can look intimidating for beginners, but the chassis is straightforward to open, leaving room for future storage and graphics upgrades.

Make no mistake: this compact rig demands a steep price premium, and patient, experienced builders could assemble a comparable DIY machine for less. Even so, if you have the budget and want heavy-hitting gaming performance without surrendering half your desk, the Neo-X1 Pro delivers on its promises. It stands as an impressive, well-engineered debut for GMKtec's push beyond the mini PC space.

#3481. Avengers: Doomsday Billboard May Have Spoiled Thor's Biggest Power Upgrade Yet

Doomsday is almost upon us, and no, I'm not talking about Joe Russo's wretched vision of an AI garbage future. I am, of course, talking about he and his brother's latest Marvel team-up movie "Avengers: Doomsday" which may have just been partially spoiled by, of all thing, a billboard.

Per a Twitter/X post from Marvel Updates, new "Doomsday" billboards have gone up in Shanghai, one of which depicts Robert Downey Jr.'s Victor Von Doom summoning an energy blast. The other, however, is a bit more interesting. It shows Florence Pugh's Yelena Belova/Black Widow, Chris Evans' Steve Rogers/ ex-Captain America, Chris Hemsworth's Thor, and James Marsden's Scott Summers/Cyclops similarly wielding their various powers. But some fans have pointed out that the lightning surrounding Thor — who's seen holding his battle axe, Stormbreaker — appears yellow as opposed to the usual blue hue used in previous films and the "Doomsday" trailers themselves.

New banners for 'AVENGERS: DOOMSDAY' have been spotted in Shanghai. pic.twitter.com/iCOsrgdumJ

— Marvel Updates (@marvel_updat3s) November 10, 2026

This is notable, because it suggests Thor could be using a hugely powerful force known as the Odinforce in "Doomsday." This power, previously unused by the character in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, was created by the Kings of Asgard, and it could prove pretty handy in the Avengers' upcoming clash with Doctor Doom. For now, it remains unclear whether this billboard actually does spoil the inclusion of Odinforce in "Doomsday," but it would make a lot of sense for Thor to power up ahead of his battle with RDJ's villain. The only thing is, there's a major trade-off that comes with using this particular power, which could mean Hemsworth's hero is about to take a long nap.

The Odinforce comes with a big caveat. Those who use it must enter what's known as Odinsleep, whereby they become unconscious while recharging. If the Shanghai billboard does, in fact, show Thor using the Odinforce, that could spark a dramatic storyline for the character.

For some reason, Chris Hemsworth's hero has been given the character arc of Ross from "Friends." He started out as a fearless and formidable leader before demonstrating a more humorous side and eventually becoming a bit of a joke himself. 2019's "Avengers: Endgame" in particular was accused of fat-shaming the grief-stricken Thor, concluding the God of Thunder's journey from serious warrior to silly superhero. Even Hemsworth told GQ that 2022's "Thor: Love and Thunder" was "too silly," adding, "I think we just had too much fun."

When the remarkably dull "Avengers: Doomsday" teaser trailers debuted in early 2026, we did at least get our first look at a much more serious Thor, who will clearly be a lot less "silly" in the upcoming team-up movie than he has in other recent MCU projects. All of which is to say that allowing him to wield the Odinforce in "Doomsday," which could involve a major sacrifice, would be a nice way to treat the character more seriously, providing a dramatic storyline that perhaps sees him willingly embrace Odinsleep in his attempt to overpower Doctor Doom and save his friends.

As unimportant as it may seem to the uninitiated, the appearance of heroes' powers in "Avengers: Doomsday" is clearly something to which Marvel Studios pays close attention. We've already seen the studio upgrade the look of Doctor Doom's power energy to more closely resemble the famous Kirby Krackle of the comic books. As such, the color of Thor's lightning isn't as trivial at it may seem.

This isn't technically the first time fans have spotted hints of the Odinforce in "Avengers: Doomsday" promotional material either. Back in July 2026, Earth 616 posted on Twitter/X highlighting promotional art in which Thor is shown holding Stormbreaker with orange/yellow lightning surrounding the weapon.

Thor's lightning in the MCU has always been blue-white pure electrical power channeled through Mjolnir or Stormbreaker.

The yellow-gold lightning in this promotional poster is completely different from anything we have seen before.

In the comics the Odinforce manifests as... pic.twitter.com/4JQKlPte14

— Earth 616 (@MarvelExrth616) July 12, 2026

The post also points out that Thor prays to Odin in his "Doomsday" teaser trailer, saying, "Lend to me the strength of the All-Fathers, so that I might fight once more." All of this combined with the latest billboard revelation suggests we'll be seeing some sort of upgraded Thor in "Doomsday," though at this point, none of the speculation has been confirmed by Marvel.

Whatever happens, it seems the Russo Brothers have a much more serious story planned for Thor in "Doomsday," which is good news. Trailers have shown the character trying and failing to attack Doctor Doom and delivering solemn speeches to the various heroes who gather together to take on this latest threat to the MCU. Gaining the power of the Odinforce would be an exciting development that allows Hemsworth's character to finally regain his standing as one of Marvel's most formidable heroes.

"Avengers: Doomsday" hits theaters on December 18, 2026.

#3480. Casey Bloys to Receive the Milestone Award at 2027 PGAs

The Producers Guild of America (PGA) has announced that Casey Bloys, the newly instated co-chair and chief content officer of Skydance Direct-To-Consumer, will be honored with the Milestone Award at the 38th annual Producers Guild Awards on Saturday, February 27, 2027, at the Fairmont Century Plaza in Los Angeles.

The PGA’s Milestone Award is meant to honor individuals or teams who have made historic contributions to the entertainment industry. Past recipients include Louis B. Mayer, Walt Disney, Alfred Hitchcock, Steven Spielberg, Sherry Lansing, James Cameron, Bob Iger, Donna Langley, Ted Sarandos, George Lucas and Kathleen Kennedy, Charles D. King, Dana Walden, and Jason Blum. “Considering Hollywood’s recent history, no one is more deserving of the Milestone Award than Casey Bloys. Over the last decade, Casey has had a front row seat to all the disruption and consolidation facing our industry. All the while he has remained a true and steadfast champion of the creative process,” said recently elected PGA presidents Donna Gigliotti and Mike Farah in an official statement. “He is a friend to producers, writers, actors and everyone who has dedicated their lives and careers to entertainment. Casey and his talented team help shepherd television that shapes our culture, stands the test of time, and protects the originality of storytellers. While Casey is never one to seek the spotlight, the Producers Guild of America is proud to recognize the breadth and depth of his exceptional career with the Milestone Award.”

“Receiving the Milestone Award is an incredible honor, particularly from an organization that represents so many of the people I’ve had the privilege of working alongside throughout my career,” said Bloys in his own statement. “I’ve always believed our job is to create an environment where talented people can take risks, tell ambitious stories and do their best work. I’m enormously grateful to the Producers Guild for this recognition and to all of the producers, storytellers and colleagues who have been part of that journey.”

In his new role at Skydance, Bloys oversees all original programming for HBO Max and Paramount+ in addition to strategy, operations, communications, and performance across the company’s streaming platforms.

Since becoming President of HBO in 2016, Bloys has led the development and production of award-winning and critically acclaimed series like “Succession,” “Euphoria,” “Barry,” “Girls,” “Veep,” “Insecure,” “Mare of Easttown,” “Big Little Lies,” “The Pitt,” “The White Lotus,” and many more. That has resulted in HBO and HBO Max’s original television programs receiving 21 Emmys across eight original programs this past year, as well as several other industry awards. Seven of Bloys’ current original series also saw cross-platform audiences averaging a milestone number of more than 15 million U.S. viewers per episode.

#3479. Amazon Prime Members Can Get Two Free E-Books in November

You can get thousands of free e-books over the course of 2026 if you know where—and when—to look. All year long, Amazon is offering free Kindle e-books to readers, with new opportunities popping up every month. In November, Prime members can get two free Kindle e-books from Amazon's First Reads program.

Amazon First Reads is a program aimed at Prime members that offers early access to new e-books across many genres, as curated by First Reads editors (one of many Prime Member benefits). Prime members can choose to download one free e-book every month from a rotating list—though some months that number is bumped up to two, usually with a free short novel—and non-members get them for a discounted price. These e-books can be read on any compatible Kindle device or via the free Kindle app.

Go to the First Reads landing page to see the full list of e-books available this month. Once you find a book that seems interesting, click the "Shop Now" button from the First Reads landing page. Make sure you’re not being redirected to the Kindle or Amazon mobile application, because you won't see the free book option there; instead, use your internet browser on your phone or computer.

Make sure you’re not clicking the ”Pre-order for...” button, as that will direct you to pay. Instead, click the “Read for Free” or the "Buy Now with 1-Click" button under the "First Reads" banner on the book's Amazon page (don't worry, you won't be charged). #3478. Alexander Skarsgard And Olivia Colman's Romantic Fantasy Movie Is A Sleeper Box Office Hit

A sleeper box office hit has emerged. The movie in question is the romantic fantasy flick "Wicker," which stars Alexander Skarsgård ("Godzilla vs. Kong") and Olivia Colman ("The Favourite"), who was part of one of the most shocking Oscar upsets of all time, we might add. Now, she's leading one of the fall season's sneakiest hits.

Directed by Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson, "Wicker" opened in theaters on the weekend of October 23, pulling in a solid $5.7 million domestically on a reported $10 million budget. That's not bad, but it debuted at number five on the charts, and it's easy for movies like this to slip by pretty quickly. However, it's managed to hold very well, even as "Godzilla Minus Zero" ruled the box office this past weekend.

As of this writing, "Wicker" has earned $20 million domestically to go with $9 million internationally for a $29 million running total. It hasn't dropped more than 24% on a single weekend, either, meaning that it still has a lot of gas in the tank. Thus, on top of already being in a good position thanks to its reasonable budget, it's on track to profit theatrically before VOD and streaming are even factored in.

Sad to say, that's not the case all too often for smaller, non-franchise movies these days. The film's backer Black Bear has also had a rough start as a distributor in Hollywood, with its Sydney Sweeney vehicle "Christy" flopping at the box office in high-profile fashion last year. This is the hit Black Bear needed.

"Wicker," as it were, centers on an ostracized fisherwoman (Colman) who commissions the local basketmaker (Peter Dinklage) to weave her a husband (Skarsgård). But when this creation proves unexpectedly extraordinary, jealousy and upheaval threatens their quiet village.

It's good news for the movie business in general when a new distributor can emerge on the scene and find success — especially with Warner Bros. and Paramount having recently merged under one roof. Add in Disney having already absorbed Fox in 2019, and Hollywood continues to shrink. So, as much as Black Bear has struggled in the past, it's starting to figure things out.

Indeed, it's been tough sledding for the studio up to this point. Recall that Henry Cavill and Jake Gyllenhaal's action movie "In the Grey" bombed at the box office earlier this year after Lionsgate dumped it and Black Bear picked it up. Matthew McConaughey's "The Rivals of Amziah King" didn't pan out for the studio, either. But if it can emulate the success it's finding with "Wicker" (which is easier said than done, admittedly), there's reason to be optimistic.

Broadly speaking, both theaters and the Hollywood system could use more sleeper hits like this. 2026 has had a lot of bright spots at the box office, among them "Obsession" and "Project Hail Mary," but having smaller movies that can thrive is key to a healthy marketplace. Brad Pitt's survival thriller "Heart of the Beast" also became a sleeper hit while you weren't looking, but that was an expensive movie with an A-list lead. It's not quite the same thing.

Instead, "Wicker" feels closer to Disney turning "Barbarian" into a sleeper hit in 2022. That, in turn, paved the way for director Zach Cregger to make hits like "Weapons" and "Resident Evil." So, yes, we could absolutely use more movies like "Wicker." At the right place and with the right premise, more original, non-franchise ideas can still thrive.

#3477. 10 Best Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave Replacements

It's been several weeks now since Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave was released for Nintendo Switch 2, and fans around the world are still exploring this massive game. While you could easily sink hundreds of hours into playing through every Flame Lord's story, you may be wondering what to play after your adventures in Dagda are through. Worry not: we've compiled a list of games like Fortune's Weave to keep your strategic skills sharp while you wait for the story expansion DLC that's slated to be released sometime in 2027. While many of the games on this list are strategy RPGs, some incorporate other standout elements of Fortune's Weave, like its tournament-focused story or the opportunity to recruit dozens of allies.

If you enjoy negotiating tricky terrain and periodically swapping your character classes in Fortune's Weave, the 2025 remake of Final Fantasy Tactics will be right up your alley. While it's not quite as difficult as the 1998 PlayStation original, FF Tactics demands that you engage deeply with its job system and figure out which team compositions are necessary for a specific battle. You are very much expected to grind via "optional" skirmishes, even on normal difficulty, and that challenge leads to a satisfying sense of mastery. A surprisingly grim yet moving story about the exploitation of common people by the nobility makes this one worth revisiting again and again.

2023's Engage didn't manage to inspire a thousand ships like Three Houses, mostly because the story is pretty flat and forgettable. But it's still well worth playing, because the combat and maps are extremely fun. The central gimmick, Emblem Rings, allow you to equip anyone in your squad with the skills of a past Fire Emblem hero, allowing for some truly bonkers synergies and limitless possibilities for customization. Build a strong enough bond between a character and an Emblem, and they'll be able to inherit some of that Emblem's skills permanently. Engage has plenty of social-sim elements and overworld exploration, but for some reason I feel far less remorse about ignoring them here than I do in Fortune's Weave.

Are you the type of Fire Emblem player for whom permadeath is the only option? Then you'll vibe with the tough battles in this 2019 strategy game from indie developer Chucklefish. Wargroove features 12+ unique Commanders, each with a special ultimate ability called a "Groove" that charges during combat, like healing powers or building walls. My favorite commander is Caesar, a golden retriever in stately silver armor that's festooned with a plume of red feathers. In one mission, he and his troops enter an abandoned stronghold, only to find that it’s been overrun by rogues. These ruffians soon learn a harsh lesson: underestimate the dog general at your own peril. He's a beautiful boy and I will murder anyone who lays a finger on him.

This tactical RPG from Sega does away with grid-based maps, though it's similar to Fire Emblem in that you'll control an assortment of class types in turn-based combat. The watercolor aesthetics are unique and charming, but don't expect a ton of narrative depth from the game's anime riff on the Second World War. Thankfully, the combat is a far richer and deeper experience, thanks to elements like tanks, ordinance, snipers. The maps offer plenty of variety in terms of terrain, obstacles, and weather, and there are around 50 characters to recruit, each with their own unique abilities and perks. But don't get too attached; they can die permanently if they're wounded in battle.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

Sega's '90s entry into the strategy RPG genre hasn't enjoyed the decades-long success of Fire Emblem, but it still has plenty of memorable maps to enjoy, including a giant chessboard and a series of floating rafts. The story is bare-minimum hokum, even by '90s RPG standards: think "the magical seal has broken on ancient evil." But an assortment of truly unique characters — including a werewolf, a phoenix, and checks notes a flying jellyfish with ice magic make Shining Force 2 well worth checking out for retro game fans. If all the social sim elements and calendar management in Fortune's Weave stress you out, you'll find none of that here: just sweet, sweet grids punctuated by the occasional town. If you have Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack, you can find it in the Sega Genesis library.

If you enjoyed gradually unlocking the world map in Fortune's Weave, Vanillaware's 2024 tactical RPG takes a similar approach to exploration as you liberate towns and gather resources. The main story is pretty standard — you're tasked with assembling an army to overthrow the evil empire — but the optional adventures and character-driven missions have more meat on the bone. Like Fortune's Weave, Unicorn Overlord features more than 60 characters to recruit across a variety of classes. In a fun riff on the typical tactics formula, you'll combine those characters in squads of up to five for turn-based combat. You can even customize the order in which your skills and passive abilities trigger to maximize their damage-dealing potential. Vanillaware's painterly environments and character designs help make the experience easy on the eyes, too.

The Hundred Line is a choose-your-own adventure story first and a tactical RPG second. Even so, there's plenty for Fire Emblem fans to sink their teeth into. While your characters can't die permanently for plot reasons, their best attacks only unlock when they're close to death. Limited turns and massive waves of enemies encourage a high-risk, high-reward approach. You can use all your action points in a given turn, or save up a bunch to unleash hell all at once. While there are plenty of intricate, grid-based battles to chew on, its greatest similarity to Fortune's Weave is getting to see a variety of perspectives on crucial events. The Hundred Line features more than 20 distinct story routes and 100 unique endings. (And it was one of our favorite games of 2025!)

Did you spend countless hours befriending the various warriors scattered around Dagsion in Fortune's Weave, even if some of those recruits never even made it to the front line? If so, you should check out Konami's Suikoden series, especially the first two games, which got a lovely remaster back in 2025. These turn-based RPGs allow you to recruit 108 characters to join your fledgling army, though not all of them are playable. Some will perform vital functions around your castle, like running various shops, manning the storeroom, and even enabling fast travel. If you only play one game in this series, make it Suikoden 2. It chronicles a continent engulfed by war due to the bloodthirsty ambitions of Luca Blight, one of the most loathsome video-game villains of all time. In terms of sheer brutality and love-to-hate factor, Luca gives Fortune's Weave's Divine Emperor Dagda a serious run for his money.

First things first: Atlus's 2024 RPG features turn-based combat, rather than the map-based battles in Fortune's Weave. Beyond that, though, there are a ton of similarities between the two. Metaphor also blends a massively consequential fighting tournament with a popularity contest, as your group of heroes must gain renown across the land by accomplishing daring feats of bravery. While the game features eight playable characters, you can befriend dozens more through the Persona-like Follower Bonds system, which opens up new job classes as well as combat and exploration perks. And speaking of exploration, like Fortune's Weave, there's an extensive overworld map to explore during your free time, which allows you to unlock side quests, take on optional battles, and complete bounties.

Square Enix hasn't made a ton of strategy RPGs, and honestly, we're not sure why. Every time the company dips a toe in this pond, the results are usually something pretty special. That's the case for this 2022 tactical RPG co-developed with Japan-based studio Artdink. There are some overlong cutscenes you'll want to button-mash through, but the maps here are unique and well-designed. If you're a clever tactician, elevation, bodies of water, and even environmental obstacles like mine carts can all be used to turn the tide of battle in your favor.

#3476. All the Health and Fitness Products You Didn't Realize You Could Buy With HSA Funds

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), it's that time of year: Use those funds, or you'll lose them. Luckily, there are plenty of clever ways to spend your remaining FSA funds on qualifying healthcare costs—some that you may never have considered as "qualifying."

For instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch (even the latest Fitbit Air). At least, that's what plenty of brands like Whoop, Oura, and even Nike want you to think. Is the process really as straightforward as the marketing suggests? Here's what to know about all the unexpected ways you can spend your FSA funds before the end of the year.

Right off the bat, when it comes to most of these fitness trackers and smartwatches, your HSA/FSA dollars won't be able to cover the entire purchase; instead, you'll save an average of 30% on eligible health purchases.

There is some more fine print, although it’s not as tricky as you might think. For the most part, if a device is necessary for treating or monitoring a specific medical condition—and not just “general wellness”—it could be eligible to purchase with those pre-tax health dollars.

The main “catch” here (as I’ve previously explained) is proving that device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN). Your LMN is basically a doctor's note required to classify certain purchases as qualified medical expenses under IRS guidelines, proving that the device will be used to treat a legitimate medical condition, such as obesity or a heart condition. Let’s take a look at what you can actually expect if you want to get a fitness wearable approved as a medical necessity.

When it comes to securing your LMN, you might not even need to make a doctor's appointment, thanks to third-party players like Truemed. When you browse sites like Coros, Amazfit, and more, you'll see the option to “Pay With Truemed” at checkout. From there, you'll be asked a few questions about your health circumstances, and you’ll be matched with a provider to determine your eligibility. If you qualify, you’ll get an LMN that will allow you to use your HSA or FSA funds to complete your purchase—all without ever having to meet with your primary doctor.

Truemed is one of the most popular payment platforms in this space, with the company claiming on its site that “90% of LMNs are issued within seven hours.” I spoke with Truemed’s co-founder and CEO Justin Mares to find out how it works behind the scenes. After you take that short survey about your health, an independent licensed provider reviews your answers before deciding whether the purchase looks medically necessary. If it doesn't, Truemed won't bother forwarding the request at all. Because Truemed screens your case before it has a chance of getting denied, those approval numbers get to stay mighty high. And the reality is, most Americans will have at least one health marker—like weight or cholesterol levels—that they can self-report to prove that, say, a Fitbit Air is necessary tool for prevention and maintenance.

For the purchases that do go through to a medical professional, approval turns out to be surprisingly straightforward. It comes down to the idea of "standard of care" in general. “If you go into a doctor's office and say your family has a history of high blood pressure,” Mares says, “your doctor probably is not going to ask for lab work before they'll talk to you about it. They simply take you at your word and help you manage the risk.” Proving HSA/FSA eligibility works on that same standard fairly often, according to Mares. You're not submitting a stack of medical records; you're answering a simple intake form about your health history, and a licensed clinician uses that, plus their own judgment, to decide whether a given product is appropriate for you.

Before you get your hopes up too high, FSA/HSA eligibility for wearables is still far from a free-for-all. An LMN only covers you, personally, for a specific product from a specific merchant, and it's usually tied to a specific condition, like cardiovascular risk, pre-diabetes, sleep issues, chronic pain, and so on. Some employers' FSA administrators scrutinize wearable purchases more closely than others, and even a fully compliant LMN doesn't guarantee your plan will approve the claim. Some companies (like Coros, for one) are more transparent about walking customers through the required medical consultation at checkout, while other brands market "HSA/FSA eligible" prominently without explaining that the LMN step is what actually makes that true. Luckily, I’ve saved you some time and rounded up some of the major wearables—and other unexpected items—that you might be able to prove as FSA/HSA eligible.

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. These tend to draw more scrutiny from plan administrators simply because they're marketed as lifestyle products first, so the strength of your intake answers matters more here than it does for something obviously medical, like a blood pressure cuff.

If cardiovascular monitoring, training load tracking, or heart rate accuracy is relevant to a documented health concern, these watches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches. Sadly, no Garmin watches are HSA/FSA-eligible. Still, the following Garmin-brand products are eligible for an HSA/FSA purchase:

You can filter by HSA/FSA eligibility and browse all eligible Garmin items here.

Think adjustable dumbbells, rowing machines, and connected bikes. It's the same logic doctors use when they tell a patient with pre-diabetes or high cholesterol to start exercising regularly; if a clinician is willing to attest that structured exercise is part of your treatment plan, equipment that enables that can qualify. For instance, here are some HSA/FSA eligible products from Nike Strength:

The common thread across all of these is that the product itself doesn't determine eligibility—your health history does. A Whoop band might be an easy approval for someone managing a cardiac condition, but it'll get more pushback for someone with no relevant health history at all. If you're curious whether something on your wish list might qualify, it's worth filling out the intake process just to see how creatively you can spend those pre-tax health dollars. However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste.

#3475. This '60s Japanese Thriller Is One Of The Best Movies Streaming On HBO Max

Ben Affleck's new kidnapping thriller "Animals" made a splash on Netflix this year — at least in terms of viewership. Critics dismissed the picture, and justifiably so, given how shaky the "Animals" script is. Yours truly clocked that "Animals" is basically an unauthorized remake of Akira Kurosawa's "High and Low," and I was not the only one.

In both movies, a rich man who has just invested all his money in a venture (a business takeover in "High and Low," a mayoral campaign in "Animals") receives a phone call that his son has been kidnapped. Except, the ransomers mistakenly took one of his much poorer employee's sons — so, does he still bankrupt himself to save a kid that isn't his?

I would highly suggest turning off Netflix and flipping over to HBO Max (where "High and Low" is currently streaming) to watch Akira Kurosawa show you how it's done. Several of the filmmaker's classics are currently streaming on there, including "Seven Samurai," "Rashomon," "Throne of Blood," and "Yojimbo." Like with "High and Low," all of those movies also star Toshiro Mifune, Kurosawa's go-to leading man at his peak. But "High and Low" is my personal favorite of the bunch and Kurosawa's magnum opus.

Kurosawa is distinguished for his samurai movies or Jidaigeki (Japanese historical dramas). He often adapted William Shakespeare's plays, too, moving their stories from Europe to to the east: "Throne of Blood" is literally just "Macbeth" in feudal Japan, and it's one of the best "Macbeth" movies to boot.

"High and Low" stands out in that collection for its contemporary setting and source material. (It's adapted from a procedural novel, "King's Ransom," by American author Ed McBain.) While he may not have had the Bard to draw on this time, Kurosawa still made some pure cinematic brilliance.

If I were ever tasked with assembling a list of "old" and/or international movies to convince people that black and white or non-English-language movies can be great, "High and Low" would be on there, 100%. That's not just because it's great (it is), but it's great popular entertainment: a taut suspense thriller and investigative procedural. It's not at all "pretentious," as untrained viewers might call it.

"Someone wants a ransom for the wrong kid, but only you can pay it" is also a great moral dilemma for a thriller and one that slots neatly into anywhere in the world with class disparity. That's why "High and Low" has been remade in many different settings. We know what a hero would do in this situation, but we're not sure if Kingo Gondo (Toshiro Mifune) is a hero from the beginning.

Now, the movie wisely stacks the deck in Gondo's favor so he doesn't come off as an aloof rich guy. He wasn't born rich, he worked his way up, so he knows what losing everything is like, and that makes the sacrifice extra painful. And while he works in shoe manufacturing, he's got a creative spirit. He's planning a leveraged buyout because he wants to make high-quality shoes his way instead of saving money on a cheaper product.

Would you sacrifice all your savings and life's work to save an innocent child? You probably just answered "yes," but it's still an abstract question for you. "High and Low" portrays how someone would act when the choice and its consequences become real. The most impressive balancing act in the movie is that it both does and doesn't feel like a foregone conclusion when he agrees to pay the ransom.

"High and Low" doesn't end when the ransom gets paid. The kidnapper escapes, setting off the second half, where Gondo is largely absent and the police characters take over to try and find the kidnapper. "High and Low" is as bifurcated as its title, with the two halves divided by setting: Gondo's hilltop mansion in the first half, the town below in the second, with the train sequence where Gondo delivers the ransom as a fitting bridge. (It's worth noting that a more literal translation of the original Japanese title, "Tengoku to Jigoku," is "Heaven and Hell.")

During that first half, Kurosawa uses Gondo's living room like a theater stage. Even confined to a single house, the picture looks huge. The screen is wide enough that you can keep track of each character's movements, and the film blocks no frame carelessly. The contained setting, and immense pressure placed on Gondo, still give the first half a claustrophobic feeling. The second half entering the town below is a pressure release, but your attention doesn't go slack because there's still a mystery to solve. The ending of "High and Low," where Gondo and the kidnapper finally come face-to-face, is a triumphant denouement.

Many great American filmmakers have looked to Akira Kurosawa, like "The Godfather" director Francis Ford Coppola. Watching "High and Low," it's easy to understand why.

#3474. ‘The Rings of Power’ Season 3 Review: Amazon’s ‘Lord of the Rings’ Series Is Just Going Through the Motions

The charges against Amazon’s epic (and epically priced) “Lord of the Rings” series, “The Rings of Power,” stacked up quickly. The first two seasons were pretty good by blockbuster standards — and I wasn’t alone in saying so — but the record-breaking costs, as well as the franchise’s lofty pedigree, set expectations higher than Great Eagles can soar. When the most expensive TV series ever made struggled to yield the requisite viewership spikes and comparable cultural impact, the claws came out.

Showrunners J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay’s series was, among other prominent complaints, a lackluster imitation of Peter Jackson’s films and an all-too-obvious ploy to become TV’s next “Game of Thrones.” Even when the visuals wowed, the characters weren’t memorable enough (save for the dwarves), the stories weren’t fun enough (again, except for the dwarves), and the twists weren’t smart enough. (The dwarves, in their infinite wisdom, did not partake.) Perhaps most damning for a show paid and made for an audience of one, Jeff Bezos’ pet project didn’t get J.R.R. Tolkien’s text — at least, not on at any depth. Related Stories Casey Bloys to Receive the Milestone Award at 2027 PGAs ‘Victorian Psycho’ Review: Maika Monroe Scares Up a Very Different Kind of Final Girl

On the whole, these criticisms weren’t enough to spoil a flawed but ambitious saga. Sure, “The Rings of Power” was made with too much deference to the past and too little innovation for the present — repeating itself (and other “Lord of the Rings” adaptations) while lacking the deft touch and sweeping imagination viewers crave from their greatest fantasy series. But it was still thrilling in its spectacle, from sets to sound design, costumes to vivid colors. (“House of the Dragon” it was not.) Episodes easily conveyed the filmmakers’ giddy excitement for the next big battle scene, the next big twist, and the next big moment in their Tolkien translation. All that money was on the screen, where it belonged, and dreams of spending it elsewhere — like, say, on many shows instead of just one — were set aside when Mount Doom erupted and the Siege of Eregion was underway.

I say all this, dear reader, not just as a handy recap of where things stand for yet another series with lengthy breaks between seasons, but to establish my position on a franchise that’s reached its sudden, somewhat unexpected nadir (for now, at least). While flaws were evident before, “The Rings of Power” Season 3 is undone by them. The listless episodes aren’t just hamstrung by additional exposition and a dearth of deadly combat; there’s a lingering wariness to it all, as if the filmmakers have run out of surprises and settled for treating their adaptation like the supplementary material it’s based on.

The third season begins with a recap of its own: Five years have passed since the Elven city of Eregion fell, and Sauron (Charlie Vickers) controls more of Middle Earth than ever. His army of orcs are tracking down the rest of the titular rings, which are safe(ish) with the elves in the luxe strongholds of Lindon and Rivendell, as well as my beloved dwarves in the sonorous mines of Khazad-dûm. But the Dark Lord himself is right where we left him, trying to forge the one ring to rule them all. Celembrimbor (Charles Edwards) was the only Elf who knew how to forge it, and now that he’s dead, Sauron grows more desperate by the day.

Not that you could tell from Vickers’ affectless portrayal. In “The Rings of Power,” the Australian actor is saddled with an arguably impossible task: Take the very presence of evil — which Tolkien so profoundly established in readers’ limitless imaginations as “an image of malice and hatred,” before Jackson sagely (and cinematically) channeled that energy into a giant, all-seeing eye — and embody that transcendent menace within a guy who looks like the guitarist next door. Vickers was able to hide his Sauron in plain sight during Season 1, when no one knew who Halbrand really was, but the big reveal didn’t lead to a bigger (or more sinister) performance, and attempts to lend human dimensions to evil incarnate similarly suffered.

What Sauron means to the series is more powerful than what he does on a scene-by-scene basis, and Season 3 throws that balance way out of whack. Absent significant conflict elsewhere, the story keeps returning to Sauron and his schemes, but none of his scenes have enough juice to elevate him to adequate levels of intimidation. A lengthy climactic sequence near the end of the season deploys shifting aspect ratios, operatic music cues, and dead-eyes stares aplenty, but they don’t add up to the riveting spectacle its creators intended. Instead, they only remind audiences how little Season 3 has to show off, not to mention how misguided some of those showcases can get.

Númenor, with its warring cousins Míriel (Cynthia Addai-Robinson) and Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle), remains a bland, human-centered snooze-fest. (My god, these people are boring.) The desert empire of Rhûn fares slightly better with Ciarán Hinds’ Dark Wizard (those eyebrows!), but the man long known and now confirmed as Gandalf (Daniel Weyman) is still little more than a mysterious symbol. (Just wait ’til you see him… put on his hat?)

And what’s become of Prince Durin (Owain Arthur), Princess Disa (Sophia Nomvete), and my rambunctious, sunless dwarves? You’d think lifelong cave dwellers would thrive in a season that’s lost a considerable amount of its light (times are tough in Middle Earth, and “The Rings of Power” has never been subtle), but my feisty friends are stuck in a plot so predictable it’s all but spelled out in the very first episode by accident! (When the wisest dwarf speaks, we all know to listen.)

New additions feel slotted in, as if emotional attachments are expected to emerge from name recognition alone (sorry to Celeborn, Galadriel’s long-lost hubby), while old favorites are nowhere to be found. (Nori and Poppy are entirely absent through seven episodes.) Others that do show up aren’t developed thoroughly enough to support their dramatic turns, like the Southlands boy turned tree-chopping, Mordor-enslaved man Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin), or get wasted in order to prop up other, less compelling characters, like Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova).

Perhaps “The Rings of Power” Season 3 is just a temporary dip — the midway point of a five-season plan that needs to set the table so we can feast for the two final seasons. Even if that’s the case, it’s no excuse. “The Lord of the Rings” may engender enough goodwill to give “The Rings of Power” a little leeway, but a full season lacking in evident ingenuity and attentive investment is enough to strip away the nostalgic sheen.

The biggest slight against the series has always been its status as a prequel: Based on appendices to “The Lord of the Rings,” this is the story the movies ran through as an epilogue, so it’s going to take a little extra sumthin’ sumthin’ to prove expanding into a five-season series is warranted. Instead, we’re given the same ol’, same ol’. Not everything needs to be realized onscreen just for the sake of seeing it happen, step by step, beat by beat, ring by ring. Yet bearing witness to the inevitable is Season 3’s greatest ambition.

“The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” premieres Wednesday, November 11 on Amazon Prime Video with four episodes. Two episodes will be released November 18 and 25 to complete the season.
