#3455. You Can Get Microsoft Visual Studio Pro 2026 on Sale for Just $30 Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Microsoft’s flagship development tool, Visual Studio Professional 2026, reduces much of the friction that used to come with large projects, and it’s on sale for just $29.97 on StackSocial right now, which is far less than what most developers expect to pay for a professional-grade IDE.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a desktop-only Windows product built as a 64-bit application, designed for people working on real-world codebases. Think multi-project solutions, long build times, and code that’s touched by more than one person. In day-to-day use, the biggest benefit is the context the software provides while you work. Visual Studio 2026 supports C#, C++, .NET, ASP.NET, Blazor, and .NET MAUI, so you can move between desktop, web, and cross-platform projects without switching tools. You also get Hot Reload, which helps reduce rebuild time by letting you edit code in .NET and C++ apps and see changes immediately. And CodeLens adds useful context right inside the editor—who last edited a method, which tests cover it, and whether recent changes broke anything—without forcing you to dig through menus or version history. The software’s AI-powered IntelliCode suggestions also feel more restrained than flashy. They tend to fill in logical patterns based on your existing code. It saves time on repetitive work, but you’ll still want to read what it writes.

Collaboration is another area where this version earns its keep. Live Share allows teammates to jump into a debugging or editing session without cloning the repo or matching environments. That’s useful for code reviews or troubleshooting, but it depends heavily on a stable internet connection. System requirements are also worth noting: While it can technically run on 4GB of RAM, 8GB or more is far more realistic, especially for larger solutions, and storage needs can balloon depending on workloads, reaching well over 100GB in some setups. Also, it doesn’t support 32-bit systems and won’t run on mobile devices or Chromebooks. For developers already working in the Windows ecosystem, this is a solid long-term license. For everyone else, those limitations can be deal breakers.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a full-featured, 64-bit IDE for Windows designed for developers working on complex, multi-project codebases, and it's on sale right now for a one-time price of $29.97 on StackSocial.

#3454. MCU Star Teases Potential Avengers Return After Massive Character Death

WARNING: This interview contains MAJOR spoilers from VisionQuest season 1, episode 8, "Forever."EXCLUSIVE: One of the newest players in the Marvel Cinematic Universe bites the dust.

Since 2021, the MCU has continued to expand the franchise on the big screen, but also through the world of television, following Disney+'s launch, allowing new and established characters from the beloved superhero property to get their time to shine on the streaming platform. While the Avengers are about to enter their next era with Doomsday and Secret Wars, Marvel Television is officially ending one with the completion of the latest TV series.

In an exclusive interview with ScreenRant's Andy Behbakht for VisionQuest, T'Nia Miller, who boarded the WandaVision trilogy series as Jo Carrington/Jocasta, discussed the death of her character in the major finale of the Disney+ Original. While she became a big casualty in the Phase 6 drama, things may not be over for her just yet.

As the VisionQuest post-credits scene showed Ultron still having Jocasta's drive, the actress was asked if she had been told what the future may have in store for her, or if she, like audience members, is also waiting to learn her fate beyond the latest Marvel TV show. Miller commented, "Oh, I'm there with the rest of you. I'm in Ultron's hands, so let's see what happens."

If she gets the option to return to the MCU timeline, Miller shared how she would love to tap into some of Jocasta's larger mythology from the comics, as she has history with Earth's Mightiest Heroes themselves. The Free Rein alum commented that "I would like to see her starting to set about right what she started. I know in the comic book she works alongside the Avengers, and so I'd love to see some of that. That would be great. That'd be super cool, but yeah, I think I'd like to see what Jo Carrington started."

Yeah, that would be great to see an Ultron and Jocasta spinoff of some sort. What would that look like?"

As of writing, it has yet to be revealed what the future has in store for several VisionQuest characters, excluding the big setup for one major hero in Avengers: Doomsday. Given that the focus is to finish the remainder of the Multiverse Saga, it may not be until Phase 7 that viewers learn about what will happen to some of these players.

#3453. Stacy Keach, ‘Fat City’ and ‘Mike Hammer’ Star, Dead at 85

Stacy Keach, the highly prolific screen and stage actor known to audiences for his television role as the private detective Mike Hammer and other tough guy characters, died of heart failure on Tuesday at his family residence in Magdalenka, Poland. He was 85.

Keach’s death was confirmed by his wife, Malgosia, in a statement sent by representation at Guttman Associates.

“It is with profound sadness and a broken heart that I announce the passing of my darling husband, Stacy Keach, who passed away on November 10, 2026, at our family home in Magdalenka, Poland,” reads the release. “After a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure, Stacy peacefully departed this world. He fought for so long, with extraordinary courage, determination and strength. He was a true warrior, facing his illness with the same remarkable spirit and resilience that defined his life.” Related Stories How Nicholas Britell Packs Conflicting Emotions Into the ‘Jay Kelly’ Score Adam Sandler Looks Back on His Early Days in Hollywood at IndieWire Honors

She continues: “Stacy was not only a legendary actor, admired and loved by audiences the world over, but also my beloved husband, my companion and the heart of our family. His passing leaves an immeasurable emptiness in our lives. But his extraordinary spirit, his unforgettable voice and the love he gave so generously will remain with us forever.”

Keach rose to the stature of one of the preeminent classical stage actors in the United States through the ’60s and 70s, venturing into avant garde productions and playing roles like Falstaff and Hamlet in his early career. He first appeared on Broadway in 1969, playing Buffalo Bill in Arthur Kopit’s “Indians,” for which he received a Tony nomination. He was also a four-time Drama Desk award winner.

It was after establishing his onstage bona fides that Keach was tapped to play the detective Mike Hammer for CBS’ television film “Murder Me, Murder You,” adapting the character of Mickey Spillane novels that had previously been brought to the screen in noirs like “Kiss Me Deadly.” The film spawned a three-season run of “Mickey Spillane’s Mike Hammer,” with nearly 50 episodes and two more TV movies featuring Keach as the tough PI. A revival, “Mike Hammer, Private Eye,” was produced in the late ’90s.

In film, Keach established his star in 1972 with early featured roles in John Huston’s classic boxing drama “Fat City” and Richard Fleischer’s intense cop thriller “The New Centurions,” along with a starring role of Doc Holliday in Frank Perry’s 1971 Western “Doc.” Though he never quite rose to marquee stardom, Keach’s character actor skills were called upon regularly by Hollywood, oftentimes playing military authorities in titles ranging from “Up in Smoke” to “Escape from L.A.” to “Truth.” In 1980, he starred in, co-wrote and executive produced the Walter Hill Western “The Long Riders,” alongside his brother James Keach.

Other notable credits for Keach include the lead of “Exorcist” creator William Peter Blatty’s horror oddity “The Ninth Configuration” (1980), the voice of the mysterious villain Phantasm in the classic superhero animated feature “Batman: Mask of the Phantasm” (1993), and the Bakersfield-loving father to George Clooney’s movie star in “Jay Kelly” (2025).

Born June 2, 1941 in Savannah, Ga., Walter Stacy Keach Jr.’s family moved to Pasadena after his drama teacher father signed a day-player contract with Universal. Keach attended University of Calfornia, Berkeley and later studied theater at Yale School of Drama and the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art.

Along with Malogisa, Keach is also survived by his their children, Karolina and Shannon; their grandchildren; their spouses; and his brother, James.

#3451. 7 Netflix Shows That Are Perfect From Beginning to End

Chris is a UK-based film and TV writer, editor and occasional filmmaker. For more than a decade, he has written news, reviews and features covering movies, television and pop culture. He has also made short films and worked in video production, giving him experience on both sides of the screen. Chris runs the We Love Movies More Than You TikTok channel and has a particular interest in overlooked and short-lived TV shows.

When Netflix first revealed it was going to make original TV shows and movies, the rest of the industry was doubtful that the company that used to mail DVDs in the post would pose any real threat to the established network structure. Now 15 years on, we’re drowning in streaming services making TV shows at a rate that’s almost impossible to keep up with.

In that time, Netflix has had some serious hits, plenty of misses, and an alarming habit of canceling TV shows far too soon. While some of their biggest originals couldn’t stick the landing, all the shows on this list started strong and ended in a satisfying way, even though two were canceled before they could reach their planned endgames. To keep this list from being largely populated by Mike Flanagan and adaptations of Harlan Coben books, you’ll find no miniseries here. From the return of The Karate Kid to one of the best sci-fi series of the 21st century, these Netflix TV shows are all perfect from beginning to end.

A belated sequel series to the 1980s classic The Karate Kid didn’t have to be this enjoyably heartfelt or this good. A middle-aged Johnny Lawrence (William Zabka) finds himself broke and at a low point, but he finds renewed purpose when he meets bullied teenager Miguel (Xolo Maridueña). Reopening his old karate dojo reawakens a decades-old feud with former rival and successful business owner Daniel LaRusso (Ralph Macchio). Over the six seasons, Johnny and Daniel have more than one rematch, steadily become friends, and begrudgingly train the next generation of champions together.

Cobra Kai rarely takes itself completely seriously, and that’s part of its overwhelming appeal. Fights break out between LaRusso’s Miyagi-Do and Johnny’s more aggressive Cobra Kai students, truces are made, and ghosts from their past return in the form of John Kreese (Martin Kove), Ali Mills (Elisabeth Shue), and Terry Silver (Thomas Ian Griffith). Yet Cobra Kai is more than a nostalgia grab with a training-montage-friendly soundtrack. The expansive young cast can more than hold their own, forging friendships and rivalries as they step out of their sensei’s shadows.

There’s no shortage of TV shows that put usually law-abiding people in circumstances that force them to break the law. Yet Ozark takes a different approach: the main characters are morally compromised from the start. Jason Bateman stars as financial advisor Marty Byrde, who has spent a decade laundering money for a cartel, but after his business partner is caught stealing, Marty has to uproot his family to the Ozarks to launder hundreds of millions of dollars.

Laced with dark humor and unexpected turns, Ozark keeps the tension mounting through its four seasons as each problem they solve only creates a fresh crisis that threatens to unravel them. While all the performances are electric, the show’s MVP is Laura Linney as Marty’s wife Wendy. She goes from a bored stay-at-home mom who gave up her career to someone getting dangerously comfortable in the criminal world; Wendy is in her element, making shady deals and power plays. For her, it’s about letting her true self take the wheel after years of being on autopilot. Not all crime dramas are so willing to take their characters to such dark places and still keep their audience completely invested, but Ozark manages that right up until the final credits roll.

Created by Joe Penhall and produced by David Fincher, Mindhunter is the second show on this list to end prematurely. Set in the late 1970s, the series charts the groundbreaking work of the Behavioral Science Unit. FBI agents Holden Ford (Jonathan Groff) and Bill Tench (Holt McCallany) team up with brilliant psychologist Wendy Carr (Anna Torv) to interview some of the most notorious serial killers to understand how they think and build psychological profiles that may help catch other killers.

Much like Fincher’s Se7en and Zodiac, Mindhunter focuses more on the psychology behind the murders and the toll it takes on the team that’s trying to make sense of the madness. The interviews with Edmund Kemper (Cameron Britton) are incredibly tense. He speaks calmly and intelligently about the truly terrible things he has done. The first season is more about gathering information; the second puts their theories into practice by investigating the Atlanta child murders. Now that Fincher won’t be renewing his deal with Netflix, a revival seems unlikely, but the two existing seasons are an engrossing and frequently disturbing crime drama from a master of the genre.

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

Tina Fey and Robert Carlock’s effervescent sitcom might have a premise that sounds like an emotionally devastating crime drama, but Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt is one of Netflix’s best original comedies. Kimmy Schmidt (Ellie Kemper) emerges alongside three other women from a bunker they’ve been held in for 15 years under the rule of a charismatic cult leader (Jon Hamm). Once the media frenzy dies down and the shock that the world didn’t end wears off, Kimmy sets out to start a new life in New York City.

Kimmy’s upbeat resilience is tested by everyday life, and her lack of people skills often gets her into trouble, but her newfound friends help her in their own, often odd ways. Deluded out-of-work actor Titus Andromedon (Tituss Burgess), a wild-card landlady (Carol Kane), and her unhinged socialite boss (Jane Krakowski) all become her eclectic support system. As you’d expect from the makers of 30 Rock, the jokes arrive fast and ridiculous, with a supporting cast full of scene stealers. Even though the interactive special Kimmy vs. The Reverend has been removed alongside all of Netflix’s choose-your-own-adventure-style shows, the four seasons remain a joyfully absurd comedy masterpiece.

Proving that adult animation could be more than just obscenities and crass jokes, BoJack Horseman was an early Netflix original and one they’ve yet to surpass. Created by Raphael Bob-Waksberg, the series stars Will Arnett as the titular washed-up actor, with his days on a hit sitcom a thing of the past, along with his sense of purpose and relevance in the ever-changing entertainment industry. He attempts to mount a comeback by writing a tell-all memoir, and the publisher sends ghostwriter Diane (Alison Brie) to get an up-close-and-personal look at the horse behind the star.

Intertwined with Hollywood satire and the obvious comedy mined from a world where anthropomorphic animals and humans live side by side, BoJack Horseman is a far deeper show than its glossy animation suggests. Delving into his traumatic childhood, his adult depression, and problems with addiction, BoJack continuously tries to work on himself, but his self-destructive nature becomes hard for his friends to sit by and watch. The writing never excuses his behavior or shies away from showing the hurtful repercussions of his actions or paints the road to recovery as anything less than hard work. While the series has a constant melancholy, BoJack Horseman is a beautifully woven story that uses a horse to show us what it means to be human.

Baran bo Odar and Jantje Friese’s elegant German sci-fi series frequently appears on lists of Netflix’s best original shows, and with good reason. The small town of Winden has known many tragedies, and many of its residents have spent generations hiding secrets that connect four families in unexpected and unsettling ways. Grappling with his father’s sudden death and the mysterious disappearance of his friend Mikkel, Jonas (Louis Hofmann) embarks on a journey to uncover the past and prevent an apocalyptic future.

Few TV shows have successfully pulled off such ambitious creative swings and told a richly complex yet rewarding story, but Dark makes it look easy when all its puzzle pieces fall into place. Despite the global ramifications, the emotional stakes of its time-travel mystery remain personal, especially in the complicated relationship between Jonas and Mikkel’s sister, Martha (Lisa Vicari). Naturally, for a series that deals with grief, time travel, and alternate universes, there’s a lot to take in, so repeat viewing is almost essential, as even slower episodes prove vital by the time it reaches its heartbreaking conclusion.

While Liz Flahive and Carly Mensch’s 1980s-set series was another TV casualty of the COVID-19 pandemic, with the final season canceled after filming the first episode, GLOW remains perfect from beginning to end. Out-of-work actress Ruth Wilder (Alison Brie) attends an open audition held by B-movie director Sam Sylvia (Marc Maron) to try out for a new television series, The Gorgeous Ladies of Wrestling. Among the diverse mix of women looking for a second chance or their big break, Ruth’s former best friend Debbie (Betty Gilpin) arrives to confront her and ends up joining the team.

Their rivalry eventually spills into the wrestling ring, with Debbie taking on the heroic role of Liberty Belle and Ruth playing Russian villain Zoya. All the cast completely commit to their wrestling personas no matter how outlandish; they each bring something different and make the women behind them feel real. For all the neon lights, spandex, and training montages to iconic '80s music, what sits at the heart of GLOW is friendship. From characters learning to stand on their own to the tentative steps Ruth and Debbie take to rebuild their fractured bond, GLOW is a heartfelt series that prizes characters as much as power slams.

#3450. How to Try 'Audio Intelligence' on Your Apple Watch Early

It has been a big year for Apple. There's a new CEO, prices have increased across the board, and there's been a seemingly endless rollout of new devices, including two new Apple Watches: the Series 12 and the Ultra 4. All things considered, these watches offer only minor upgrades over the previous models, shipping with new heart rate monitors and the latest S11 processor. But one of the biggest new watch features, "Audio Intelligence," is also the most controversial—and it's rolling out in beta today.

Audio Intelligence is Apple's branding for a new set of features exclusive to the Series 12 and Ultra 4. These features use the new Apple Watches' hardware, along with on-device and cloud-based AI, for tasks like sound and music identification as well as dictation. "Sound Recognition" can alert you to important sounds, like alarms and doorbells, while "Music Recognition" can automatically display songs playing around you—but these aren't the features you'll hear talked about in discussions of Audio Intelligence.

Rather, everyone is up in arms about "Live Rewind" and "Siri Recap." These Audio Intelligence features passively "listen" to your conversations throughout the day, and, using AI, deliver summaries of what was said. When you double-click your Apple Watch's crown to use Live Rewind, you'll get a loose transcript of the last 15 seconds of conversation it overheard, while Siri Recap can show summaries of all your in-person chats throughout the day. You can even configure a schedule for when your watch is "listening" for recaps—e.g., only run during work hours. Apple suggests each is intended to help jog your memory; maybe you use Siri Recap to remember important discussions you had that morning, while Live Rewind is meant for moments where you forget what someone just said. (As opposed to asking them to repeat themselves, I suppose.)

Apple's claims may or may not assuage your fears, but it seems the company is pushing on ahead regardless. Apple is releasing Audio Intelligence as part of iOS 27.3, which launches in beta on Tuesday. If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, you can try it out today, assuming you enroll in Apple's latest beta version.

To do so, you'll need to sign up for the Apple Developer program, since iOS 27.3 is rolling out first for devs. This program used to require a $99 fee, but you can skip it now if you opt for the free account. Once you enroll your Apple Account in this program, you can open your iPhone, head to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, and choose "iOS 27 Developer Beta." Go back one page, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install iOS 27.3 when it's available.

#3449. Ruaridh Mollica Breaks Down What VisionQuest Finale's Epic Reunion Means For His MCU Future

VisionQuest's Ruaridh Mollica discusses the major finale moments of the WandaVision spinoff, the massive MCU reunion, and Tommy Maximoff's MCU future.

WARNING: This interview contains MAJOR spoilers from VisionQuest season 1, episode 8, "Forever."

Since Phase 4, one of the big successes to come out of the Marvel Cinematic Universe was the WandaVision series, bringing Elizabeth Olsen's Scarlet Witch and Paul Bettany's Vision together for their own solo adventure. As the MCU timeline was beginning its era of original TV shows on Disney+, the nine-episode project emerged with tremendous success, while also kicking off the beginning of a new trilogy.

After Agatha Harkness' breakout debut in the Phase 4 series, it led to Kathryn Hahn headlining her own spinoff, with Agatha All Along. However, despite Wanda freeing Westview, which seemingly meant the end for her kids that she had created through magic, that was far from the case, as the Phase 5 offshoot revealed that Wiccan had survived.

In true comic book fashion, his soul managed to inhabit Billy Kaplan's body, with Joe Locke playing the teenage version. After managing to save Tommy, it was time for the speedy hero to get his time to shine by becoming one of the central figures in VisionQuest, which serves as the finale to the trilogy, with Ruaridh Mollica being cast as the other Maximoff twin.

With the end of VisionQuest season 1, viewers have been able to follow Tommy's complex journey as both Thomas Shepherd and the son of Vision and Scarlet Witch. A few weeks ago, I was honored to speak with the Scottish actor for ScreenRant about not only giving the MCU audience a lot of payoffs for the WandaVision trilogy, but also bringing a new era to Speed, including some of the pivotal moments in episode 8, "Forever."

Over the last couple of years, the MCU has begun to introduce more LGBTQ+ characters across the big and small screens, with Tommy being canonically bisexual, which made this role a personal one for the star, who is also openly bi. Throughout VisionQuest, it doesn't get explored or established, but as I asked Mollica if there were discussions about whether the Phase 6 drama would address it, he assured comic readers who are seeing him adapted in the franchise that this incarnation of Speed is bisexual.

Ruaridh Mollica: "I think Tommy knows he's bi. I think that a specific queer relationship isn't explored in this particular section of his life in the show. I really hope that will be explored in the future. I think as a bisexual actor playing a bisexual role, I do feel there's moments where I'm watching me do something in a scene, and I'm like, 'Oh yeah, that was very queer!' [laughs] I hope that it exists in who he is and in elements of his personality rather than in his specific relationship during the show. But yeah, I do think Tommy's probably been with guys before the show happened, or in other timelines."

The tragic backstory for Thomas, before Tommy's soul got transferred, was a driving factor in how it influenced the dynamic between the orphan and Vision, with Mollica elaborating why it stands out as much as it did.

Ruaridh Mollica: "I think it's one of the biggest parts of his backstory. Like, other than the complexities of the Tommy Maximoff side, ultimately, the Thomas Shepherd side of everything is heartbreaking. Thomas has been alone for so much of his life. Life has not been easy for him. He is a hustler and a grifter for a reason. He is out on the streets and stealing things, and he doesn't trust probably anyone other than Lisa that, at this time, he's had a string of foster families that have never understood him. I think, to have the potential promise of finally having a father like that, is all he really wants. [All] Thomas Shepherd wants is to be loved by a parent, and suddenly that is shown to him, and it might be possible. And obviously, then there's all the complexities of the Tommy Maximoff side and the impossibility of that interaction as a whole. But I think his backstory of being an orphan is so important for the yearning and the desire of that father-son relationship, and the desire to have a mother as well."

Similar to how Agatha All Along followed Billy and allowed him to express his perspective on Wanda, that also became the case for Tommy on VisionQuest, but very differently. While Locke's hero shared his conflicted feelings for his mother, Mollica's character is someone who looks at the Scarlet Witch in a very different regard, with past episodes revealing that he can relate a lot to their mom, which became one of the most emotional components throughout these eight episodes. Obviously, everyone is now waiting for the full Maximoff reunion, as Mollica reflected on how he envisions the perfect reunion between Speed and Wanda.

Ruaridh Mollica: "I would obviously love that reunion to happen. I don't know how I would envision it. I think, based on how we've seen the reuniting of Tommy, Billy, and Vision, I would assume that the same feeling [from] that moment would translate into the feeling of reuniting with Wanda."

It was only a matter of time before the twins finally found each other, as Locke reprised his role as Wiccan in VisionQuest episode 8, bringing him and Mollica's Speed together in a heartfelt reunion that viewers have waited to see since 2024. However, little did these actors know that they would work together outside the MCU, as the two of them got cast in West End's Clarkston.

As rewarding as it becomes for viewers, it means just as much for Mollica himself. During our interview, he shared with me how it was a gift to get to bond with his on-screen brother through VisionQuest, while also building a dynamic that would help them on stage in Clarkston.

Ruaridh Mollica: "Filming that moment was amazing. I love the finale of the show, [episode 8] is my favorite episode because it feels like this big moment of everything coming together in this really f-----g epic way. It is a story all about family. And so when we're there trying to save Vision, and I can't do it alone anymore, and my brother finds me again and comes out of his portal, and we do it together - that broke my heart. It was powerful, even when we were shooting it, and then I love that we have this beautiful hug with our father that resembles the comics, when it's Billy and Tommy hugging Wanda.

It really paralleled that for me, and yeah, I just thought it was such a beautiful moment to shoot, but like you said, watching that moment, I teared up, and I, I was there. And in terms of our relationship going forward onto the play, we met for the first time doing this, so we got to spend a lot of time together on set, and I guess, playing brothers, there's a closeness there, and we get along really well anyway. So it definitely helped us bond a lot more before the audition process, and then we spent a lot of time together anyway, leading up to the play, and then got pretty close in rehearsals and everything like that."

There may not have been an official "like uncle, like nephew" mantra, but the VisionQuest finale gave Speed not only his own iconic superhero moment, but also a clever way to nod towards his uncle from another universe. As Tommy is mastering his speed more, the final episode sees him getting to have a very X-Men: Apocalypse-esque scene a la Sweet Dreams. When asked if this was a clever way to pay homage to Evan Peters' Quicksilver, but with their own spin, Mollica shared the following:

Ruaridh Mollica: "I think with that moment, we needed to have Tommy's superhero moment, his moment of, 'I am Tommy Maximoff,' - and that line gave me chills whenever I was reading it before we shot it. I was like, 'That is the epic superhero moment,' and he gets to zoom-zoom off and have his hero moment, and then Terry, what he loves to do as a writer, a creator, filmmaker, is then flip the moment on its head and be able to kind of laugh at it. And I think by slowing it down, it allowed for the family dynamic to exist in the epic moment, and I thought that was just perfectly [descriptive] of the show. It is superhero, and it is epic, but it's a father and son who are still trying to figure out their relationship. So even in the most epic moments, they are bickering, and that moment definitely allowed that to happen, and also just poke fun at the superhero moments that exist."

As Billy got his Wiccan suit in Agatha All Along, I asked Mollica if Tommy was meant to officially get his Speed costume in VisionQuest. It turns out, the MCU spinoff was very close to making it happen, as he had even been measured for a superhero uniform. However, he elaborated on how they decided to hold off on that for a very good reason.

Ruaridh Mollica: "It's so interesting you say that, and actually, I've not told anyone this yet, so this is exciting. Yes, I got completely measured for a full superhero suit. We were gonna make it. It was gonna happen in the finale at some point. But then Terry, exactly like you said, couldn't find a way for [Tommy] to just appear in a suit. He wants the show to be as grounded in reality as possible, especially my character, who really, I feel like grounds everything back to London and the real world and everything like that. There was never a moment where he could just find a superhero suit, or turn up in it, and it breaks that connection [to] reality. We were able to get the superhero goggles because they came from Paladin, and that was a way that could be worked in. And then we changed the costume to be a bit more green and tracksuit-like to reflect the superhero suit, and I think that was a really good choice. I think I like that, and also it leaves us wanting more. "

ScreenRant: "I also took the jacket as a nod to what we saw little Tommy wear in WandaVision as a nice little homage in that way."

Ruaridh Mollica: "Yeah, totally. Sarah Young, our costume designer, she was so on top of making sure there were so many homages to the original characters."

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

By the end of the VisionQuest finale, Tommy has become more comfortable with his powers, as he is learning to discover just how powerful he is. But how powerful would Mollica say Speed is at this point?

Ruaridh Mollica: "I think he's pretty comfortable. I think that was the first time he'd used his speed to that level, and he obviously realized that he needs to eat more before he does that. I think now that he knows that if he carbs up, he could sustain himself for a lot longer. And I think he's probably experimenting with that after that moment. And I think he's still got a lot to figure out, especially about how far does his phasing go? His ability to affect the atomic structure of atoms using his speed. How far does that go? I think his power could be pretty massive, so I think he still [has] a lot to learn."

While VisionQuest completes this trilogy, many have expressed wanting to see the MCU finally adapt Avengers: Children's Crusade. When I asked if a potential spinoff like that is something he, Locke, and the Marvel Studios folks have discussed, while also addressing whether he knows where Tommy is going next, he is just as curious.

Ruaridh Mollica: "I honestly don't know. I don't know. We'll have to wait and find out. I hope to know as well."

Nevertheless, Avengers: The Children's Crusade or maybe even a Young Avengers spinoff is something he would be more than down for.

Ruaridh Mollica: "Totally. I mean, I loved reading it, and it would be a privilege. But I cannot say anything, I don't have that information [laughs]"

At the time of this interview being conducted, Mollica was in London, which is where Avengers: Secret Wars will film in the near future. With the world speculating who is in the Phase 6 finale, when I asked him if Tommy might be popping up in the 2027 ensemble, as it would make sense for Speed to be part of the cast after VisionQuest, the star laughed with a "No comment!" response.

Another crucial figure in Thomas' life is Lisa Molinari, played by Lauren Morais, with the WandaVision spinoff showcasing how important she has been to him. In a lot of storytelling, there is sometimes the scenario where a man becomes a female character's entire world or arc, but VisionQuest instead flips it on its head, where it's almost reversed.

Throughout the season, viewers have been able to see that, prior to reuniting with Vision, Lisa is very much what Tommy's world is heavily dependent on. When asked if that was something that he and Morais consciously worked into that dynamic, or if it was something that they both felt, 'We're gonna flip the script a little bit from what we usually see in these kinds of relationships', he shared the following:

Ruaridh Mollica: "Yeah, I think that was something Terry did really well, just with the writing and the characters. And I think me and Lauren naturally had just a fun rapport, and yeah, I think that was mainly down to the writing, but also kind of where Tommy comes from. Lisa means so much to Tommy in that sense because she is powerful. She is cool, I think she's probably taught him a lot over the years."

ScreenRant: I'm glad she survived, and you guys are both together by the end, and you're with Paladin now. That was a dynamic I was not expecting to see be so much fun. Todd is, obviously, awesome, as you know, so I'm glad that you all made it out alive. I'm hoping that is something that we see more of in the future.

Ruaridh Mollica: "Yeah, that was so cool leaving that dynamic with Paladin and having them together at the end. I thought that was such a beautiful way to tie that section off, as well as our section, and leave things open."

Credit: Anna Maria Tinghino/Future Image/Cover Images

After his big MCU debut, what is next for Mollica beyond the Marvel brand? The Franchise alum is busy with several projects, which happen to involve a few names that are no strangers to the superhero genre.

Ruaridh Mollica: "Right now, I'm filming a Paramount show called Laird, which will be super cool. It's kind of like Yellowstone, but in the Scottish Highlands, and that's with Kenneth Branagh, and that'll be cool. And then there's a motorbike racing movie called The Isle of Man Tourist Trophy Race with Channing Tatum coming out next year, and that'll be fun."

From working with the great filmmaker behind the MCU's first Thor movie to Gambit himself, it was not lost on the VisionQuest co-star that he was collaborating with both of them.

Ruaridh Mollica: "It's so bizarre. I was literally talking to Kenneth about it the other day. It's like, 'Oh my god, because you directed Thor,' and then we had a whole moment talking about that, which was pretty cool. "

All episodes of VisionQuest are streaming on Disney+.

#3447. Ridley Scott’s 10/10 Sci-Fi Masterpiece Officially Won’t Return in 2026

2026 will be remembered as a bumpy year for the great Ridley Scott, who finally returned to sci-fi after nearly 10 years away from the genre. Scott tapped widely known stars, including Josh Brolin, Jacob Elordi, and even Margaret Qualley, to feature in The Dog Stars, but the film eked out only $39 million at the box office. The budget for the film was never publicly disclosed, but it was reported to be anywhere between $75 million and $100 million, which makes it a total box office disaster. Scott isn’t taking some time to reevaluate after the woeful performance of The Dog Stars, either – he’s returning to the screen next November for a Treasure Island reboot starring Hugh Jackman as the titular pirate. The movie is expected to begin shooting early next year, which will leave a tight window to hit its release date.

In this later stage of his career, Ridley Scott isn’t directing as many movies as he once was, but he remains involved in projects across the board through his Scott Free production banner. For example, it’s been almost 10 years since Scott directed his last Alien project, Alien: Covenant, but he produced the last few franchise installments, such as Alien: Romulus and Alien: Earth. The latter project, written and created by Fargo scribe Noah Hawley, premiered back in 2024 and was a massive hit with critics and audiences, prompting FX to bring the show back for Season 2. Production on Alien: Earth Season 2 kicked off earlier this year, and while there was an initial wave of optimism that the show would return before the end of 2026, it can now be safely assumed that it won’t be released until 2027.

Most of the stars whose characters survived the events of Season 1 are expected back in Season 2, but there are plenty of exciting new additions to the cast as well. Both Peter Dinklage and Jerome Flynn are among the new stars joining the Alien: Earth Season 2 cast, but this won’t be their first time working together. The duo spent years playing the pair of Tyrion Lannister and Bronn in Game of Thrones, the hit HBO fantasy series that was on the air from 2010 to 2019.

Check out the first season of Alien: Earth on Hulu or Disney Plus and stay tuned to Collider for more updates and coverage of the second season.

#3444. Why I'd Choose the Oura Ring 5 Over the Cheaper Ultrahuman Pro

Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro is now officially on sale in the U.S., which makes this the perfect time to consider how this new device compares to the reigning champ in the smart ring market, the Oura Ring 5. Here's the short answer: While there’s a lot to like in the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, ultimately I think the Oura Ring 5 is just better at doing its job.

I’ve spent plenty of time with both rings, and admittedly, many of the differences between the two will come down to personal preference—for example, do you like the biohacking concept and the “next best actions” suggestions in the Ultrahuman app, or do you favor the soothing vibes of the Oura app? But when it comes to the devices themselves, there are big differences between them in terms of size, cost, and overall ease of use. Here’s my take on each, and why Oura is still my top choice.

The Oura Ring 5 is impressively small, and when you have to wear something on your finger, size matters a lot—and generally, smaller is better. The Oura Ring 5 is the smallest and most comfortable smart ring I’ve ever worn. I have a ton of photos here comparing it in size to other smart rings (including RingConn, older Oura rings, and an older Ultrahuman); suffice it to say, the Oura Ring 5 wins this category easily.

When it comes to the interior fit, both rings are similar: mostly smooth on the inside, without any intrusive bumps. But considering the overall shape and feel, the Oura Ring 5 is just more comfortable to wear throughout an entire day.

The Oura Ring 5 comes with a plug-in charger, which isn’t very convenient, but will get the job done. You can buy a slim, rounded charging case that easily fits in your pocket for $99. You need to match the size of the case to the size of your ring, and the charging case is not compatible with earlier versions of the device. It’s good for 30 days of charge, according to Oura.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro comes with a charging case that is heavy and bulky with prominent corners, but good for an extra 45 days of battery life. The case fits any size of Ultrahuman Ring Pro, but is not compatible with previous versions. You can have the case play sounds if you’ve misplaced it.

The Ultrahuman ring lasts slightly longer on a charge: up to 15 days, according to the company, versus six to nine for the Oura Ring 5. The Ultrahuman ring also has several different battery modes, with “chill mode” lasting me about two weeks when I tested it. The company says some users are finding the latest software update extends battery a bit further.

To sum up: the Ultrahuman ring lasts longer on a charge and has more capacity in its charging case. You also get the charging case for free. But the Oura Ring 5’s charging case is smaller and much easier to carry around. Once again, we’re looking at two decent options: The Oura case is more expensive for what you get, but it’s also nicer to use.

Oura is the most expensive smart ring out there, and it requires a subscription. That makes it the priciest option, giving Ultrahuman an opening to beat it simply by virtue of being cheaper. But this one is closer to a wash, depending on the choices you make. If you’re looking for the cheapest possible smart ring, well, you’d probably end up with something else entirely, like a RingConn Air. But between the Oura Ring 5 and the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, the latter is cheaper than the Oura Ring 5...but only if you’re saying no to all the extras. Let me break it down.

The Oura Ring 5 costs $399 for the shiny black and silver models, and $499 for gold, rose, and the matte versions of the black and silver. The subscription costs $5.99/month (or $69.99/year, which is only a $2 savings), and the Oura is basically useless without the subscription.

Here's how the cost works out on an annual basis:

Oura Ring 5 in black or silver: $399 + $5.99/month subscription = $470.88 for one year, $542.76 for two years

Oura Ring 5 in other colors: $499 + $5.99/month subscription = $570.88 for one year, $642.76 for two years.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro is $479 for all colors, and there is no subscription for basic use of the ring. But you can't necessarily stop there, because the Ultrahuman app includes “PowerPlugs” that will give you extra features or analysis screens. Some are totally free, including the caffeine window,  smart alarms, a new parent mode, and a limited version of the cycle and ovulation tracker, but others carry a monthly fee. And if you consider all the optional subscription fees for different PowerPlugs, they can quickly add up:

HealthEx, to connect medical records: $4.99/month

Most people probably wouldn't choose all of them, but even if you just wanted, say, respiratory health and cycle & ovulation pro, you’d quickly outstrip the price of an Oura Ring’s subscription. On the other hand, Ultrahuman also offers an Ultrahuman Max plan for $9.99/month or $99.99/year that includes all the PowerPlugs mentioned above, plus the Les Mills workouts that normally run $11.99/month. That's cheaper than subscribing to all of the options individually, but it will also make the Ultrahuman Ring Pro more expensive than the Oura Ring 5: $578.99 total for one year, or $678.98 for two years. In short, if you want everything that each ring has to offer, the Ultrahuman will cost you more.

Here's the big caveat: I wouldn't recommend bothering with most of the PowerPlugs. For example, "UltraSync for Tesla" recommends settings for your car based on how rested you are, which will be useless if you don't have a Tesla, and probably even if you do. "Cardio adaptability" measures a metric that Ultrahuman says is subtly different from HRV; Oura doesn't measure this adaptability metric, but it's not clear to me whether it's even worth measuring at all (I'd argue probably not).

Ultrahuman's respiratory health PowerPlug ($3.99/month) records sounds while you sleep, which Oura doesn't do; but Oura reports breathing disturbances based on the ring's data, which Ultrahuman doesn't do. Ultrahuman's feature is more expensive.

Ultrahuman offers a premium version of its cycle tracker for $3.99/month, while Oura has a partnership with Natural Cycles that cost $149.99/year. Either will provide more detailed (and, each company says, more accurate) cycle tracking than the basic tracking each app provides without the extras. Oura's option is more expensive.

Ultrahuman's HealthEx Powerplug ($4.99/month) displays information from your medical records throughout the app; Oura lets you import your medical records for free, but uses them mainly in the Advisor (chatbot) and dedicated areas of the app. Ultrahuman's option is more expensive.

Oura's app gives you scores for your readiness, sleep, and recent activity, and it tracks how stressed you seem to be throughout the day. A message at the top of the main screen gives you advice for what to do that day—for example, scaling back your workouts if you seem to be tired or stressed. Ultrahuman does pretty much the same thing, giving you a "next best action" that changes throughout the day, but tends to stick to predictable themes: get more activity if you've been sitting, and that sort of thing.

Both give detailed breakdowns of the factors that contribute to your scores, and both likely overstate how useful their scores are (you don't actually need to change your workout plans just because you had a less-than-perfect night of sleep). But the apps handle the basics pretty similarly: Both have partners and integrations, and you can book blood tests through either app, if you want to do that for some reason.

Ultrahuman gives you a bit more guidance on circadian rhythms, urging you to get in extra steps during certain times of day, and offering to micromanage your caffeine intake. It has a "longevity" tab that puts your long-term habits in terms of how many years they are supposedly subtracting from (or adding to) your lifespan, including measurable metrics like VO2max and a few things that are more inscrutable, like arterial stiffness.

Oura has a whole tab of "vitals" that it calculates from your day-to-day data, which I find more useful than Ultrahuman's data views. The items here include "resilience," which compares your stress to your recovery; a "symptom radar" that can sometimes flag when you're sick; and metrics of sleep regularity and how you're breathing. And, of course, you can check your "cardiovascular age" to see how much younger (or older) you should feel.

Overall, I prefer Oura's approach because the metrics make more sense, are easier to find, and are less likely to feel like they're going way out on a limb relative to the underlying science. Ultrahuman wants you to feel like a cutting-edge biohacker; Oura does a bit more to keep things down to earth. It is a bit funny to remember that both apps, and their wealth of data, are basically just pulling from heart rate readings throughout the day and night. Neither app gives you any truly important information the other doesn't, but Oura's makes more sense to me.

Updated 11/10/2026 to note that the Ultrahuman Ring Pro's stated battery life is up to 15 days, not 8-10 days.

#3443. macOS 27.3 Golden Gate public beta 1 now available, here’s everything new

Following the release of macOS 27.3 developer beta 1, Apple is now rolling out the first test build for users enrolled in the public beta. Here’s what’s coming

Contrary to macOS 27.2, it looks like Apple had quite a bit in store for macOS 27.3 and its counterparts.

In addition to expanding Siri AI to four more languages, including Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese, the system also introduces several new Safari features, including Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode for websites, and the ability to organize and manage tabs using Siri AI.

macOS 27.3 also adds native Markdown rendering to Quick Look, allowing users to preview .md files with proper formatting instead of raw Markdown syntax.

The update also expands Siri AI’s capabilities across Apple’s own apps, allowing users to perform more complex actions in apps like Messages, Music, Calendar, Photos, and Reminders, as well as manage files and folders.

Apple is also introducing new tools for third-party developers to create advanced Siri AI integrations using Markdown-based instructions, allowing the assistant to coordinate multistep actions across different apps.

Users who enjoyed the wallpaper introduced with the new touchscreen MacBook Pro will also find a new screensaver called Pro Lighteensaver, which features light moving along the metallic-looking lines that form the word “PRO.”

Earlier this week, Apple also confirmed that macOS 27.3 will introduce new checks for potentially harmful content shared through public iCloud links. Starting with the update, files and photos shared using the “Anyone with the link” option will be checked by Apple, which may remove flagged content or take action against accounts that violate its policies.

The release build for macOS 27.3 public beta 1 is 26C5035r, which is the same as the developer build.

If you’d like to join Apple’s free public beta program, visit beta.apple.com.

#3442. Five Creative Ways to Spend Your FSA Funds Before the End of the Year

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), you know the drill: Use the funds before the end of the year, or lose them. Unfortunately, chances are slim you can pack the rest of the year with doctor's appointments. Does that mean your hard-earned funds go to waste? Definitely not. You can spend your remaining FSA funds on other qualifying healthcare costs. And what counts as "qualifying" might surprise you—for instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch.

As the end of the year approaches, here are all the ways you can spend any leftover money in your FSA balance.

Many over-the-counter medications and health items are FSA-eligible, including pain relievers, cold medicine, bandages, dental care products, menstrual products, and more. Scan your medicine cabinet and make a list of anything you need to stock up on.

FSA/HSA eligibility for smartwatches and other fitness wearables is real, but the main “catch" (as I’ve previously explained) is proving the device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN).

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. Similarly, smartwatches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does, as long as you can link a relevant documented health concern. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches.

If you want to get creative with it, the official FSA store lets you filter by "surprisingly eligible." Similar to the section above, for some of these items, you'll want to brush up on how exactly to get an LMN to justify certain tech as FSA-eligible for you personally. In the meantime, go crazy and snag yourself Epsom salt for $8.99, Supergoop! sunscreen for $38.00, or perhaps a snazzy massage gun for $349.99.

Knee braces, wrist splints, compression socks, and other orthopedic items can help relieve chronic pain issues. Rather than wait for these issues to rear their heads down the line, use FSA money to offset the costs of these fixes now. If you use eyeglasses or contacts, consider using your FSA dollars to update or refresh your prescriptions. Don't forget to stock up on eye drops and lens solution, too.

If you have medical procedures scheduled for early next year, many healthcare providers will allow you to pre-pay the estimated costs this calendar year using FSA funds. This includes dental work, physical therapy, chiropractic visits, Lasik eye surgery, and more.

However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste. After all, it came out of your paycheck. Check in with your employer’s rules for any balance remaining on Dec. 31 this year, so you aren’t left forfeiting your hard-earned funds. You can find a complete list at the FSA store here.

#3440. VisionQuest Finale Officially Confirms Return Of Major Avenger

WARNING: This article includes MAJOR spoilers from VisionQuest season 1, episode 8 finale.The Marvel Cinematic Universe just dropped its biggest twist for 2026.

Throughout its run since Iron Man kicked off the MCU timeline in 2008, the franchise has seen various heroes and villains connect with audience members worldwide, whether they are passionate comic book readers or casual moviegoers. While many characters have met grim fates over the many phases, the dead don't always stay dead.

The airing of the VisionQuest finale, episode 8, "Forever," came with perhaps the biggest post-credits scene for any Marvel TV show. The final seconds of the installment see Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom making his latest collection, as he is seen taking Elizabeth Olsen's Scarlet Witch, taking the audience back to her final moments in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, revealing that Wanda Maximoff is, in fact, alive.

This comes after years of the actress being asked if she would ever return to the franchise, especially for Avengers: Doomsday and Avengers: Secret Wars. Even prior to the VisionQuest post-credits scene and the launch of the show in general, Olsen had denied that she would be showing up in the WandaVision spinoff.

While Marvel Studios has yet to formally announce Scarlet Witch being in Avengers: Doomsday, it is more or less a given at this point, with the Phase 6 series being the final project to release before Anthony and Joe Russo's ensemble feature. With Victor von Doom uttering the words, "Scarlet Witch, awaken. Your powers will be mine," as she opens her eyes, it's clear that she will play some part in his massive plan in the December film.

#3439. 'NCIS' Star Katrina Law Warns the Entire Team Will Break in Season 24

Amanda M. Castro is a Network TV writer at Collider and a New York–based journalist whose work has appeared in Newsweek, where she is an Associate Editor, and The U.S. Sun, where she previously served as a Senior Consumer Reporter.

She specializes in network television coverage, delivering sharp, thoughtful analysis of long-running procedural hits and ambitious new dramas across broadcast TV. At Collider, Amanda explores character arcs, storytelling trends, and the cultural impact of network series that keep audiences tuning in week after week.

Born and raised in Puerto Rico, Amanda is bilingual and holds a degree in Communication, Film, and Media Studies from the University of New Haven.

Editor's Note: The following contains spoilers from NCIS Season 24, Episode 3. NCIS Season 24 has given longtime fans a reason to celebrate Michael Weatherly's return as Tony DiNozzo, but the team won't ride that nostalgia wave forever. According to Katrina Law, the job's emotional toll is about to catch up with Jessica Knight and her colleagues in ways viewers haven't seen before. The actress, who has played Knight since Season 18, tells Collider that the team will face a breaking point this season, with some particularly revealing episodes still ahead.

"I think this season you really get to see a lot of Knight's vulnerability in a way that you've never experienced before," Law says. "This season, you get to see her break in a way that you haven't seen before." And Knight won't be the only one struggling. Law adds that viewers will see "the entire team break" in a way the series hasn't explored before, making the aftermath as important as the moments that lead to it.

Before those emotional storylines unfold, however, the November 10 episode, "Speechless," gives Law a very different reason to remember Season 24. The installment marks the acting debut of her seven-year-old daughter, Kinley Andreen, who plays a young girl caught in the middle of a frightening investigation. It's a family milestone for the actress, but it also brings a personal connection to an episode built around the lengths a parent will go to protect their child.

Knight has spent much of her time on NCIS proving she can handle whatever comes through the doors at headquarters. A former member of the agency's REACT team, she joined the Major Case Response Team after the deaths of several colleagues and the arrest of her former team leader. She's since become an established part of the group, but Law's comments suggest Season 24 will ask something different of her: What happens when the agent who used to hold it together can no longer do so?

Knight has already experienced significant personal and professional upheaval throughout her time on the series. Law's tease, though, points to a more exposed side of the character, one that hasn't necessarily had the same space to emerge amid the team's investigations. The actress is particularly interested in seeing audiences connect with that vulnerability, especially as the other agents face their own emotional struggles.

Law says two upcoming episodes have already been filmed, and she credits writer Scott Williams with understanding how to bring out the characters' emotional depths. "I think Scott Williams does such justice to the characters when it comes to their emotional depths and bringing out the best and the worst in them," she tells Collider. For Law, what makes the story worth watching is how the team comes together and moves forward after reaching that breaking point.

Tonight's episode, "Speechless," gives Law a chance to share the screen with someone she knows better than anyone: her daughter, Kinley. The seven-year-old makes her acting debut as Chloe Sims, an eight-year-old girl the NCIS team discovers hiding alone in her apartment after her Marine mother disappears.

Chloe is frightened and initially reluctant to help, but she has a surprising skill that could give investigators the breakthrough they need. Her fluency in Mandarin becomes an important part of the case, creating an unexpected connection between the young witness and Knight. Law tells Collider that the character's appearance makes that ability all the more striking, describing Chloe as a blonde-haired, green-eyed girl whose talent will surprise viewers.

The casting also makes the episode's central themes hit a little closer to home. The investigation revolves around a missing mother and a child left to navigate a frightening situation, while Law is experiencing the unusual privilege of playing opposite her own daughter. She says watching Kinley move from being her little girl to a young actor stepping into character was unlike anything she'd experienced.

Law's behind-the-scenes experience was just as memorable as what audiences will see on screen. In her Collider interview, she recalls watching Kinley switch into character, suddenly becoming Chloe rather than the little girl she knows at home. "I would literally kind of see my daughter disappear and then this little actress pop up," Law tells Collider. "It was surreal, but then I would also kind of see my daughter peeking through, looking for the validation of like, 'Mommy, am I doing a good job?'"

A great detective is really just a personality with a method attached, which is why we keep remaking the same four of them. Here is yours, what it says about you, and the case for them being the best in the business.

You let people think you are not a threat and then you simply never go away. Columbo is the only major detective show that tells you who did it in the first ten minutes, because the pleasure was never the puzzle, it was watching a rich man slowly realise he is in trouble.

You are the most interesting person in the room and you know exactly how to use it. Rian Johnson built Blanc as a gentleman detective who is also an outsider everywhere he goes, which lets him be charming at people who would never otherwise talk to him.

Everybody tells you everything, and you have never once asked them to. Jessica Fletcher is a crime novelist from a small town in Maine who is so warm and so obviously trustworthy that suspects confess to her essentially as a social courtesy.

You expect to be lied to and you are almost never disappointed. Chandler wrote Marlowe as a man with a rigid private code in a city that has none, which is why he takes the case, solves it, gets nothing out of it and takes the next one.

Kinley's Mandarin-speaking abilities also connect to Law's family. The actress, who is half Chinese and speaks fluent Mandarin, explains that her mother has been instrumental in passing the language down to the next generation. "Pretty much every day my mom will sit down with Kinley and go over her Mandarin skills and teach her," Law says. "So it's been passed down through generations to Kinley, and she's upholding her family traditions."

One challenge Law hadn't quite anticipated, though, was balancing all her responsibilities on set. She was Kinley's mother, acting coach, scene partner, and fellow performer at the same time. At one point, she tells Collider, she even had to remind her daughter to look at her rather than directly into the camera. Kinley eventually pointed out that she was looking at her mother, prompting a laugh from Law.

The actress also explained why allowing Kinley to act on NCIS doesn't mean she's changing her approach to protecting her daughter. Law has deliberately kept Kinley off social media, but the young girl wanted to take part in the show and was already familiar with its cast and crew after years of visiting the set. With her mother beside her throughout filming, surrounded by people she already knew and trusted, she says it was an especially comfortable introduction to acting.

Of course, Kinley's debut isn't the only major development adding extra excitement to Season 24. Weatherly is back as Tony DiNozzo, and Law is just as enthusiastic about his return as longtime viewers. An original NCIS fan herself, the actress describes the decision to bring Weatherly back as a brilliant move by the network.

She didn't expect Jessica to get involved in Tony's return. Law pitched several ideas for how Knight might interact with Weatherly's character, but never expected Ziva David (Cote de Pablo) to pull her into their history by asking her to keep tabs on him.

"I kind of love it," Law tells Collider, explaining that the unexpected setup creates a fun relationship between Knight and Weatherly. It's an interesting position for Jessica, who now finds herself caught up in a dynamic that predates her time on the team.

Law has a few ideas about where that connection could go. When asked what she'd like to see for Knight this season, she didn't hesitate: she wants Jessica and Ziva to finally share the screen, preferably in an action sequence or an interaction that leaves Tony thoroughly uncomfortable.

For a franchise that's been on television for more than two decades, it has found new ways to bring its characters together while making room for the next generation. Season 24 is doing both, giving viewers the nostalgia of Tony's return while promising a much more vulnerable side of the agents they've spent years following.

"Speechless" offers a particularly personal entry point into that larger story, but Law's comments suggest the emotional challenges ahead won't be limited to one case. With two more character-focused episodes already in the can, Knight and her teammates could be heading into some of their most difficult moments yet. And if Law gets her way, perhaps a certain former Mossad agent will be around to make things even more interesting.

The NCIS Season 24, Episode 5, "Speechless," airs Tuesday, November 10, 2026, at 8 p.m. ET / 7 p.m. CT on CBS.

#3438. These 10 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

Apple dropped the first developer beta for iOS 27.3 on Tuesday. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These new actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

#3437. Report: Apple’s planned $7 billion bond sale attracts four times as much demand

Apple has filed a preliminary prospectus with the SEC outlining plans to issue seven series of bonds. Here are the details.

Over the past week, several Big Tech companies have turned to the bond market to raise billions of dollars amid growing investments in AI infrastructure.

Meta, for instance, just raised $15 billion through a US bond offering, followed by another €9 billion (roughly $10 billion) in European bonds. Earlier this week, Alphabet raised €6 billion (approximately $6.7 billion), while Microsoft completed a $25 billion bond sale last week, its first since 2017.

Apple has also turned to bond sales in the past to raise billions of dollars.

Previous offerings include those in 2015, 2019, 2020, and 2021. Most recently, Apple raised $4.5 billion through a four-part bond offering in May 2025, which attracted approximately $10 billion in investor orders.

Earlier today, Apple filed a preliminary prospectus with the SEC outlining plans to issue seven series of bonds maturing between 2028 and 2036.

However, while other Big Tech companies have been borrowing heavily amid growing AI infrastructure investments, Apple’s filing makes no specific mention of AI.

Instead, the company says it intends to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, potentially including stock buybacks, dividends, acquisitions, and debt repayment, as it has done in previous bond offerings.

And while the prospectus didn’t specify how much Apple intends to raise, Bloomberg reported soon after that the company is targeting approximately $7 billion, with investors already placing orders totaling around $31 billion.

According to Bloomberg, strong investor demand has also helped Apple secure more favorable borrowing terms, with investors willing to accept lower interest rates than those offered by Microsoft, Meta, and Oracle in their recent bond sales.

All of this is happening amid a massive tech sell-off, which saw the Nasdaq 100 plunge more than 6% at one point today, with Nvidia shares falling about 8% and the S&P 500 dropping nearly 4%.

Apple’s own stock is also taking a hit, trading down 1.49% at the time of publication, but it is faring better than those of its Big Tech peers, whose stocks have become more closely tied to the AI spending boom.

Be that as it may, Apple is expected to finalize the size and pricing of its bond offering soon, potentially as early as later today, after which the company will file the definitive terms with the SEC.
